कोट.etymology: Borrowed from English coat ('sleeved outer garment, suit jacket'), which entered Middle English from Old French cote ('tunic, overgarment'), ultimately of Frankish origin (*kotta, 'coarse woollen cloak').

history.meaning: outer tunic -> tailored jacket or overcoat

कोट.notes: Masculine in Hindi (मेरा कोट); English alveolar -t is adapted regularly with retroflex ट (koṭ).

कोना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit कोण (koṇa, 'angle, corner'), via Prakrit कोण (koṇa).

rootFamily.gloss: side; next to (के बगल में / बगल वाला 'adjacent, side')
middle; centre (के बीच 'between / in the middle of')

कोमल.etymology: Hindi कोमल (komal) is a learned tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit कोमल (komala, 'tender, soft, delicate, charming'). Although its deeper Indo-European root is uncertain, some scholars link it to Sanskrit कुम / कम् ('to love, desire') or early Indo-Aryan roots for young, supple shoots. In Sanskrit poetry and Ayurveda, कोमल describes soft petals, gentle speech, and delicate touch. In modern Hindi and Hindustani classical music, it serves both as an everyday literary adjective for gentleness and as the technical name for a flattened musical pitch.

कोमलता.etymology: A tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit कोमलता (komalatā, 'softness, tenderness, delicacy'), formed from the adjective कोमल (komala, 'soft, tender, delicate') with the abstract feminine suffix -ता (-tā, analogous to Latin -tās and English -ty). In musical and literary Hindi, कोमलता expresses gentle touch, soft phrasing, or tenderness of manner.

कोयला.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit कोकिल (kokila) or more directly Middle Indo-Aryan *koïla / *koyala, ultimately related to Old Indo-Aryan *kokila- / *kūla- ('glowing ember, blackened wood'; compare Prakrit कोइल / कोयल koïla, 'charcoal'). Note the exact phonetic merger with कोयला from *koïla in northern Indo-Aryan, giving Hindi कोयला (koylā) for both mineral coal and artist's charcoal.

कोरा.etymology: Inherited Indo-Aryan adjective कोरा (korā, 'unbleached, untouched, blank, sheer').

कोर्टयार्ड.etymology: Borrowed into modern urban and hospitality Hindi from English 'courtyard', used alongside native आँगन (ā̃gan). English 'courtyard' combines 'court' (from Old French cort and Latin cohors, 'enclosed yard, retinue') with 'yard' (from Old English ġeard, 'enclosure, garden', cognate with Latin hortus). Both halves historically meant an enclosed open space, reinforced together into a single compound.

कोशिश.etymology: The noun 'कोशिश' (kośiś) is borrowed from Classical Persian 'کوشش' (kōšeš), meaning 'effort', 'endeavor', or 'attempt'. The Persian noun itself is derived from the verbal root of 'کوشیدن' (kōšīdan), which means 'to strive' or 'to struggle'. It is fully integrated into everyday Hindi and is the most common conversational term for 'effort', existing alongside Sanskrit equivalents like 'प्रयास' (prayās).

कौन.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit कः पुनः (kaḥ punaḥ, 'who then?'), contracted via Prakrit कवण (kavaṇa) to कौन.

rootFamily.gloss: someone; anyone; any (before singular count noun)

क्या.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit किम् (kim, 'what?'), via Prakrit किअ / काइं, from PIE *kʷís.

क्या-क्या.etymology: Distributive reduplication of क्या ('what?'), a hallmark of Hindi question syntax asking for an itemized list.

rootFamily.gloss: one each; one by one; every single

क्यों.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit किउँ (kiũ, 'how? why?'), from Sanskrit किम् पुनः.

क्योंकि.etymology: Compound of क्यों ('why') + कि ('that'), formed on the model of Persian چونکه (čūn-ki).

rootFamily.gloss: that (introducing a clause); or (in quick spoken questions)

क्रम.etymology: A tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit क्रम (krama, 'step, stride, regular order, succession'), derived from the verbal root क्रम् (kram-, 'to step, stride, proceed'). From the physical image of one footstep following another evenly, क्रम came to signify systematic sequence, serial order, and arrangement. In Hindi it is an invariable consonant-final masculine noun.

rootFamily.gloss: number (room number, phone number, shoe size)

क्रीम.etymology: Borrowed from English 'cream' into modern Hindi culinary and colour vocabulary. English 'cream' derives from Old French cresme, blending Late Latin crāma ('cream') and Christian Latin chrīsma ('anointing oil', from Greek χρῖσμα). In Hindi it is treated as a feminine noun and is frequently used attributively with रंग ('colour') to describe off-white paper or fabric.

क्लर्क.etymology: Borrowed from English clerk, which passed via Old English cleric / clerc and Late Latin clēricus ('clergyman, scholar') from Ancient Greek κληρικός (klērikós, 'belonging to the clergy', from κλῆρος klêros 'lot, heritage'). Because medieval European clergy were virtually the only literate record-keepers, 'cleric' evolved in English into 'secretary, office clerk'. In Indian administrative Hindi, क्लर्क is an invariant masculine noun.

क्लास.etymology: Borrowed from English class ('school group, lesson, railway carriage grade'), adapted via seventeenth-century French classe from Classical Latin classis ('division of Roman citizens, fleet, school group').

history.meaning: civic division -> group of students, lesson

क्लास.notes: Feminine in everyday Hindi (मेरी पियानो क्लास, 'my piano class'), influenced by feminine कक्षा (kakṣā, 'classroom, class').

क्लिक.etymology: Borrowed into modern Hindi from English 'click', originally an imitative/onomatopoeic word recorded in English from the late sixteenth century. English 'click' is closely related to Dutch klikken and German klicken, echoing a sharp metallic or mechanical snap. In contemporary Hindi, it denotes both mechanical locking sounds and digital or photographic clicks.

क्लिपबोर्ड.etymology: Adopted directly from English clipboard, a twentieth-century compound joining clip (from Old English clyppan 'to clasp, embrace') with board (from Old English bord 'plank, flat surface'). Originally devised as a portable writing pad in warehouses, clinics, and kitchens for taking notes while standing, it quickly became universal in offices. Through English workplace and administrative terminology, it entered modern Hindi unchanged as an invariant masculine noun.

खंभा.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𙀕𙀩𙀓 (khamha), from Sanskrit स्तम्भ (stambha, “pillar, post”).

खट-खट.etymology: Native Indo-Aryan echoic/onomatopoeic reduplication खट-खट imitating sharp knocking against wood or metal.

खटखटाना.etymology: Denominative verb formed in Hindi from the reduplicative onomatopoeia खट-खट (khaṭ-khaṭ, 'knocking, rapping, tapping sound on wood'), mirroring Prakrit खट्ट-खट्ट (khaṭṭa-khaṭṭa). Reduplicated C1aC2-C1aC2-ānā verbs are a signature pattern in Indo-Aryan for conveying repeated percussive actions such as knocking, rattling (खड़खड़ाना), and tapping (थपथपाना). It takes दरवाज़ा ('door') as its typical direct object.

खट्टा.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀔𑀝𑁆𑀝 (khaṭṭa). It is related to Sanskrit खट्ट (khaṭṭa, 'sour'), possibly of Dravidian or Austroasiatic origin.

खट्टापन.etymology: Formed by combining खट्टा (khaṭṭā, “sour”) + पन (-pan, “-ness”), derived from Sanskrit.

खड़खड़ाहट.etymology: Derived from the expressive reduplicative verb खड़खड़ाना (khaṛkhaṛānā, 'to rattle, clatter') by adding the productive feminine abstract suffix -आहट (-āhaṭ, marking sensations, noises, or states). The onomatopoeic base खड़-खड़ (khaṛ-khaṛ) imitates hard objects knocking loosely against one another, such as wooden slats, dry leaves, or carriage wheels. All nouns formed with -आहट take feminine gender in Hindi.

खड़ा.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit खड्ड / खड (khaḍa, 'erect, standing upright'), related to Sanskrit स्तब्ध.

rootFamily.gloss: to stop; to wait; to stay overnight (at an inn)

खड़े-खड़े.etymology: Hindi खड़े-खड़े (khaṛe-khaṛe) is an adverbial reduplication of the oblique/plural form of the adjective खड़ा (khaṛā, 'standing, upright'). The base खड़ा descends from Middle Indo-Aryan खड / खडअ (khaḍa / khaḍaa, 'erect, standing'), widely connected by Indo-Aryanists to an expressive root *खड्- / *खट्ट- or Sanskrit *खट (*khaṭa) denoting firmness or upright posture. Reduplicating the oblique form in -ए (-e) is a hallmark of Hindi adverbial syntax, expressing continuous posture ('while standing') or effortless speed ('right on the spot').

खत्म.etymology: Hindi खत्म (xatm, formally ख़त्म) is a borrowing from Classical Persian ختم (xatm, 'seal, end, conclusion'), taken from Arabic خَتْم (xatm, 'sealing, finishing, completion'). In Arabic, the root خ-ت-م originally meant 'to impress a wax or clay seal' on a document or vessel, naturally extending to 'closing, finishing, and bringing to an end'. In Hindustani, खत्म functions primarily as a predicate adjective with होना ('to finish, run out') and करना ('to conclude'). It is among the highest-frequency verbs-and-adjectives in spoken Hindi.

खनक.etymology: An expressive onomatopoeic Indo-Aryan noun paired with the verb खनकना (khanaknā, 'to clink, jingle, ring'), formed on the imitative root खन-खन (khan-khan) representing the crisp sound of metal, glass, or porcelain striking lightly, with the sound-verb suffix -क (-k). Parallel imitative formations in Sanskrit include खणखणायते (khaṇakhaṇāyate, 'tinkles, clinks'). In Hindi it is a feminine noun.

खरोंच.etymology: Of uncertain origin, possibly onomatopoeic or derived from a regional Prakrit root for scratching.

ख़ज़ाना.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian خزانه (xazāna), derived from Arabic خِزَانَة (ḵizāna), meaning treasury, vault, or storehouse. The root خ-ز-ن (ḵ-z-n) means to store or hoard.

ख़त्म.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic خَتْم (ḵatm, 'sealing, conclusion, completion'), via Classical Persian ختم.

ख़बर.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian خبر (xabar) from Arabic خَبَر (ḵabar, 'news, report, message').

ख़याल.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian خیال (khayāl, 'thought, imagination, idea') from Arabic خَيَال (khayāl, 'image, apparition, imagination, thought'), derived from the root خ-ي-ل (kh-y-l, 'to imagine, suppose'). In Hindustani it became one of the most versatile everyday nouns for 'thought, opinion, care, or attention', and also names a major genre of Hindustani classical vocal music. It is masculine.

ख़राब.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic خَرَاب (ḵarāb, 'ruined, desolate, broken'), via Classical Persian خراب.

ख़रीददार.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian خریدار (xarīdār, 'buyer, customer'), from خرید ('purchase') + agentive -دار.

ख़रीदना.etymology: Denominative verb from Classical Persian خرید (xarīd, 'purchase; bought'), past stem of خریدن (xarīdan, 'to buy'), cognate with Sanskrit क्रीणाति (krīṇāti).

ख़र्च.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian خرج (kharj, 'expenditure, outlay', often pronounced kharch in Persianate South Asia) from Arabic خَرْج (kharj, 'output, expense, tax'), derived from the root خ-ر-ج (kh-r-j, 'to go out'). Just as English 'expense' literally means 'paying out', Arabic kharj meant money going out. In Hindi the devoiced final consonant gives ख़र्च (kharch) as a masculine noun.

ख़र्चा.etymology: Borrowed into Hindustani via Classical Persian 'خرچه' (xarča, 'expenditure, outlay'), from Arabic 'خَرْج' (ḵarj, 'what goes out, expenditure, tax', derived from the verb 'ḵaraja', 'to go out') with the Persian/Hindi '-आ' ending. It declines as a regular masculine '-आ' noun ('ख़र्चा / ख़र्चे / ख़र्चों') alongside the shorter doublet 'ख़र्च'.

ख़स्ता.etymology: Hindi ख़स्ता (xastā) is borrowed from Classical Persian خسته (xasta, 'wounded, broken, exhausted; crisp or crumbly'). Originally the past participle of the Persian verb خستن (xastan, 'to wound, break'), the word referred to anything broken or fragile. In Indo-Persian and North Indian culinary usage, the sense of 'easily broken or crumbling' specialized positively to denote flaky, melt-in-the-mouth pastries and fried snacks. Hindi preserves both the culinary sense and the figurative sense of 'dilapidated' in phrases like ख़स्ता हाल.

ख़ाली.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic خَالٍ / خَالِي (ḵālī, 'empty, vacant, free'), via Classical Persian خالی.

ख़ास.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic خَاصّ (ḵāṣṣ, 'special, private, select'), via Classical Persian خاص.

ख़ुद.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian خود (xwad / xud, 'self, oneself'), cognate with Sanskrit स्व (sva) and English self.

rootFamily.gloss: one's own (my, your, his, her, our, their)

ख़ुशबू.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian خوشبو (xušbū, 'fragrant; fragrance'), from خوش (xuš, 'sweet, pleasant') + بو (bū, 'scent').

ख़ुशी.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian خوشی (xušī, 'happiness, gladness'), from خوش (xuš, 'happy, pleasant') + -ई.

rootFamily.gloss: peace of mind; cosy calm; tranquillity

ख़ुशी-ख़ुशी.etymology: Adverbial reduplication of ख़ुशी (xušī, 'happiness, pleasure', from Classical Persian خوشی).

ख़ून.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian خون (xūn, 'blood'), from Middle Persian xōn.

ख़ूब.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian خوب (xūb, 'good, fair, well, plentiful'), cognate with Sanskrit सु-.

ख़ूबसूरती.etymology: Derived in Persian/Hindustani from the adjective 'ख़ूबसूरत' ('beautiful', compounded from Persian 'خوب' xūb 'good, fair' + Arabic 'صُورَة' ṣūra 'form, face, appearance') + the abstract feminine suffix '-ई' (-ī). In Hindi it is an uncountable feminine noun, very frequently used adverbially in 'ख़ूबसूरती से' ('beautifully, gracefully').

ख़्याल.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian خیال (xayāl) from Arabic خَيَال (ḵayāl, 'imagination, thought, care').

rootFamily.gloss: mind; heart; mood / inclination (मन करना 'to feel like')

खाना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit खादति (khādati, 'chews, eats'), via Prakrit खाइ (khāi).

खामोश.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian خاموش (xāmōš, 'silent, mute, extinguished'), attested earlier in Middle Persian as xāmōš. Its Persian root connects with the idea of dying down or extinguishing (as of fire or speech), leading naturally to 'noiseless, silent'. In Hindi-Urdu (written खामोश or with nukta ख़ामोश), it is an invariable adjective prized in both everyday speech and poetic expression.

खाली.etymology: Hindi खाली (xālī, formally ख़ाली) is borrowed from Classical Persian خالی (xālī, 'empty, vacant, free'), taken from Arabic خَالٍ (xālin), the active participle of خَلَا (xalā, 'to be empty, be alone, pass away'). Entering Hindustani through daily speech and Persianate literature, it completely supplanted many older terms in casual Hindi for empty vessels, vacant rooms, and free time. In Devanagari it is written either ख़ाली with a nuqta or simply खाली. Its common antonym is भरा ('full').

खासकर.etymology: Hindi खासकर (xāskar, formally ख़ासकर) is a hybrid compound adverb formed by joining the Perso-Arabic adjective ख़ास (xās, 'special, particular') with the Hindi conjunctive element -कर (-kar, originally 'having done'). The base ख़ास was borrowed via Classical Persian خاص (xāss) from Arabic خَاصّ (xāṣṣ, 'private, special, distinct'). Attaching -कर to an adjective in the sense of 'especially' parallels native formations like विशेषकर and मुख्यकर. In modern Hindi prose and conversation, it is one of the most frequent adverbs for highlighting an example or exception.

खिंचना.etymology: Intransitive passive-sense stem corresponding to the transitive verb खींचना (khīnchnā, 'to pull, draw'), displaying the regular Indo-Aryan shortening of the stem vowel (ई -> इ) to mark intransitivity. The base खींचना likely derives from Middle Indo-Aryan *khinc- / *kheñc- (compare Prakrit खंचइ / खेंचइ, 'pulls, drags'), possibly connected to Sanskrit कर्षति (karṣati, 'drags') via regional Prakrit developments.

खिड़की.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan खडक्किआ (khaḍakkiā, 'small side door, shuttered opening'), of early Indic vernacular origin.

खिलना.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan *khillaï / Prakrit खिल्लइ ('opens up, blossoms, expands'), possibly related to Sanskrit स्फल् / खुलति (khulati) or a regional Indo-Aryan root *khil- ('to open, burst into bloom'). From botanical blossoming, the verb naturally extended in Hindi to joyful facial expressions and luminous musical notes blooming into clarity, especially in the compound खिल उठना.

खिलाड़ी.etymology: Derived within Indo-Aryan from खेल (khela, 'sport, play', Sanskrit खेलति khelati) + agentive suffix -आड़ी (-āṛī).

rootFamily.gloss: fast; heavy (rain); strong/sharp (salt, spice, sun, sound)

खिसकना.etymology: Inherited Indo-Aryan motion verb खिसकना ('to slip, shift aside').

rootFamily.gloss: to tilt; to incline; to bow
to step back; to move aside

खिसकाना.etymology: Transitive/causative verb formed with -आ (-ā-) from the intransitive stem खिसकना (khisaknā, 'to slip away, budge, slide'), which derives from Middle Indo-Aryan *khisakka- / *khasakka- (compare Prakrit खसइ, 'slips, gives way'). Its ultimate root is connected with Sanskrit स्कन्दति / स्खलति ('slips, stumbles') or an expressive Indo-Aryan motion root *khas-. In modern Hindi it specifically means shifting something smoothly across a surface.

rootFamily.gloss: to remove; to move aside; to clear away
to put; to place; to keep

खींचना.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan *kheñcaï / *khīñcaï ('pulls, draws'), parallel to Prakrit खेंचइ and connected regionally with Sanskrit कर्षति (karṣati, 'draws, pulls') or an Indo-Aryan expressive stem *khinc-. Nasalization and lengthening of the root vowel yielded Hindi खींचना (khīnchnā). It covers pulling cords, drawing lines, and even taking photographs (तस्वीर खींचना).

rootFamily.gloss: to hold; to catch; to grasp

खुजली.etymology: Inherited via Middle Indo-Aryan *khujjalī / Prakrit खुज्जइ (khujjaï, 'itches') from Sanskrit खर्जू (kharjū, 'itching, scratch') or खर्जूली (kharjūlī), related to कण्डू (kaṇḍū) and खर्जति (kharjati, 'scratches, creaks'). The cluster -rj- assimilated to -jj- in Prakrit and palatalized further into -j- before the suffix -lī in New Indo-Aryan. It is an everyday feminine noun for physical itching or figurative impatience.

खुद.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian خود (xwud, 'self, own'). Traces back to Middle Persian and is cognate with Old Persian and Avestan equivalents.

खुदना.etymology: Intransitive/passive inherited from Sanskrit क्षुद्यते / खनति, via Prakrit खुद्दइ ('is dug, is carved').

rootFamily.gloss: to carve; to sculpt; to whittle

खुलना.etymology: Inherited Middle Indo-Aryan intransitive खुलइ (khullaï, 'opens, comes untied'), paired with transitive खोलना.

rootFamily.gloss: to open; to unlock; to unwrap

खुला.etymology: Perfective participial adjective of the intransitive verb खुलना (khulnā, 'to open, become untied, clear up'), tracing via Prakrit खुल्लइ (khullaï, 'is loosened/opened') to Middle Indo-Aryan *khull-. Turner connects this stem to Sanskrit स्खलति / क्षुल्- or regional Indo-Aryan *khuḍ- ('to untie, release'). Unlike invariable Persian adjectives, खुला inflects completely for gender and number (खुला / खुली / खुले) and means both physically unshut and candid or spacious.

खुश.etymology: Hindi खुश (xuś, formally ख़ुश) is borrowed from Classical Persian خوش (xwaš / xuš, 'pleasant, sweet, glad, happy'), continuing Middle Persian xwaš ('good, pleasant, agreeable'). Originally describing anything agreeable to the senses or mind, the Persian adjective narrowed in Hindustani primarily to emotional gladness and personal contentment. In modern Hindi, खुश is among the most common adjectives in everyday speech, generating the abstract noun खुशी ('happiness') and numerous compounds like खुशखबरी and खुशबू.

खूँटी.etymology: Feminine diminutive of खूँटा (khūnṭā, 'wooden stake, peg'), inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan *khuṇṭa / Prakrit खुंट (khuṇṭa, 'peg, stump, corner'). Related to Sanskrit कुण्ट / खुण्ट- (a regional Indo-Aryan stem denoting a projecting point or post), the noun developed nasalization and compensatory lengthening in Hindi to give खूँटी (khūnṭī). Today it refers to small wall pegs and key hooks.

खेप.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit क्षेप (kṣepa, 'throw, cast, dispatch, load'), derived from क्षिप् (kṣip-, 'to throw, send'). In Prakrit खेप्प / खेव (kheppa / kheva), the initial cluster kṣ- regularly became kh-, yielding Hindi खेप (khep) with feminine gender shift. From 'a single dispatch or load sent out', it naturally evolved to mean a batch of baking or a consignment trip.

खेलना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit खेलति (khelati, 'plays, sports, sways'), via Prakrit खेलइ (khelaï). The Sanskrit root खेल् (khel-, 'to move to and fro, play') also produced the noun खेल (khel, 'game, sport'). Preserving its consonant-final stem, it gave modern Hindi खेलना (khelnā), the standard verb for playing games or sports (while musical instruments use बजाना).

खोखला.etymology: Hindi खोखला (khokhlā) is an inherited New Indo-Aryan adjective connected with Middle Indo-Aryan *खोक्ख / *खोखल्ल (*khokkhalla, 'hollow, empty inside'), parallel to Punjabi खोखला, Marathi खोकला/पोकळ, and Gujarati खोखलुं. Its repeated velar aspirate ख्-ख (kh-kh) exemplifies expressive Indo-Aryan phonology evoking a resonant empty cavity (compare खोल 'shell, casing' and खोह 'cave'). With its regular -आ ending, it inflects as खोखला / खोखली / खोखले. Today it applies vividly both to hollow tree trunks or stones and to hollow, insincere promises.

खोजना.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀔𑁄𑀚𑁆𑀚𑀤𑀺 (khojjadi), which is connected to a desi (indigenous non-Sanskritic) root or possibly from Sanskrit क्षोद (kṣoda). It evolved into the primary verb for searching or discovering in modern Hindi.

खोदना.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀔𑁄𑀤𑀤𑀺 (khodadi). This derives from Sanskrit क्षोदति (kṣodati, 'to stamp, pound').

खोना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit क्षोभयति / क्षपयति (kṣapayati, 'destroys, loses, wastes'), via Prakrit खोएइ (khoeï).

rootFamily.gloss: to be found; to get/receive (with को); to meet (with से)
to look for; to search for

खोया-पाया.etymology: Compound of perfective participles खोया ('lost', from खोना) + पाया ('found', from पाना).

rootFamily.gloss: to be found; to get/receive (with को); to meet (with से)

खोल.etymology: Inherited via Prakrit खोल्ल (kholla, 'hollow shell, husk, covering') from Sanskrit खोल्ल / खोलक (kholaka, 'helmet, shell, covering') or a regional Indo-Aryan stem *khol- ('hollow case, sheath'). In Hindi domestic usage it designates removable covers such as pillowcases and book jackets, while in baking and culinary contexts it naturally translates pastry shells and tart crusts. It functions as a masculine invariant noun in direct plural.

खोलना.etymology: Inherited transitive verb from Prakrit खोलेइ (kholeï, 'opens, unties'), paired with खुलना.

rootFamily.gloss: to open (by itself / intransitively); to come open

खौलना.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan *khavala- / *khola- ('bubbling, boiling'), related to Sanskrit क्ष्वेलति / क्वथति or an expressive Indo-Aryan stem *khaula- denoting the bubbling sound and motion of boiling liquid (compare Prakrit खवलइ / खोल्लइ). Contraction of -ava- to -au- yielded Hindi खौलना (khaulnā). Its participle खौलता हुआ is idiomatically used for anything piping or scalding hot.

गंध.etymology: Learned borrowing (tatsama) from Sanskrit गन्ध (gandha, 'smell, odour, fragrance'), which has a long history in South Asian aesthetics, perfumery, and chemistry. Cognate with Avestan gainti- ('foul smell'), it continues an Indo-Iranian stem *gandʰ-, though its deeper Proto-Indo-European origin remains debated. In Hindi the noun is feminine and serves as the base of compounds such as सुगंध ('fragrance') and दुर्गंध ('stench').

गज़ब.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian غضب (ghazab, 'wrath, fury, something overwhelming') from Arabic غَضَب (ghaḍab, 'anger, wrath'), from the root غ-ض-ب (gh-ḍ-b). In South Asian Persian and Hindustani, 'wrath' underwent dramatic semantic amelioration via exclamations of awe ('what an overwhelming thing!'), coming to mean 'marvel, wonder, awesome'. Note the voiced uvular-derived ज़ in Hindi.

गड़ना.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit. Related to Sanskrit 'gaḍṭ' or similar substrate words associated with digging or penetrating.

गड़बड़.etymology: Expressive Indo-Aryan reduplicative formation गड़बड़ ('tumult, muddle, confusion').

गड़बड़ी.etymology: Derived with the feminine nominalizing suffix -ई (-ī) from the expressive echo-word गड़बड़ (gaṛbaṛ, 'confusion, jumble, disorder'). Such reduplicated ablaut compounds in Indo-Aryan (compare तड़फड़, हड़बड़) imitate clattering, tumbled objects or chaotic activity. गड़बड़ी specifically names a discrete mistake, mix-up, or muddle.

गड्ढा.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit *𑀕𑀟𑁆𑀟 (*gaḍḍa), ultimately from Sanskrit गर्त (garta, "hole, cave, grave"). Over time, the Middle Indo-Aryan development led to the assimilation of the consonant cluster and the emergence of retroflex sounds. The aspiration is a later development typical of New Indo-Aryan phonological shifts. It shares a common etymological root with words for trenches in several other regional languages of the subcontinent.

गढ़ना.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𙀓𙀢𙀕 (gaḍhai), from Sanskrit घटते (ghaṭate, “to form, shape”).

गत्ता.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan गत्त / ग्रन्थ ('bound layers, thick board'), related to pasted paper layers.

गद्दी.etymology: Inherited via Prakrit गद्दिआ (gaddiā) from late Sanskrit / Middle Indo-Aryan *गर्दिका / गद्दा (gaddā, 'mattress, pad'), related to *गद्द् ('soft stuffed pad'). The feminine diminutive suffix -ई distinguishes a smaller seat cushion or bolster-throne (गद्दी) from a full mattress (गद्दा). Historically, गद्दी also acquired the prestigious sense of a merchant's cushioned seat of authority or a royal throne.

गमला.etymology: Borrowed into Hindustani from Portuguese gamela ('wooden trough, wide earthen tub or basin'), which entered Indian coastal and garden usage in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Portuguese gamela ultimately derives from Latin camella ('goblet, shallow dish'). Adapted to the Hindi masculine -आ declension as गमला (gamlā), it became the universal North Indian word for a flowerpot.

गरम.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian گرم (garm, 'warm, hot'), from PIE *gʷʰermós (cognate with Sanskrit घर्म and English warm).

गरमागरम.etymology: Hindi गरमागरम (garmāgaram) is an expressive reduplicative compound built on the Persian loanword गरम (garam, 'hot, warm') linked with the intensifying vowel -आ- (-ā-). The base गरम comes from Classical Persian گرم (garm, 'warm, hot'), cognate with Sanskrit घर्म (gharma, 'heat') and English 'warm'. Expressive -आ- reduplication is a vibrant word-formation device in Persian and Hindi-Urdu, seen also in धड़ाधड़ and हाथोंहाथ, conveying immediacy and intensity. In Hindi, गरमागरम vividly describes food served straight off the stove or lively breaking news.

गरमी.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian گرمی (garmī, 'warmth, heat'), from گرم (garm, 'warm, hot', cognate with Sanskrit घर्म gharma).

rootFamily.gloss: winter; cold weather (often plural सर्दियों में 'in winter')

गरिमा.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing गरिमा (garimā, 'weight, dignity, venerable worth'), from गुरु (guru, 'heavy, weighty').

गर्म.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian گرم (garm, 'warm, hot'), continuing Middle Persian garm and Proto-Iranian *garmáh. Ultimately it derives from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰermós ('warm'), making it a direct cognate of Sanskrit घर्म (gharma, 'heat, warmth'), Greek θερμός (thermós), Latin formus, and English warm. Both the Persianate spelling गर्म and the epenthetic variant गरम (garam) are current in standard Hindi.

गर्मी.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian گرمی (garmī, 'warmth, heat, summer'), formed from the adjective گرم (garm, 'warm, hot') with the abstract suffix -ی (-ī). The Persian adjective گرم continues Old Persian *garma- and Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰermós, making it directly cognate with Sanskrit घर्म (gharma, 'heat') and English 'warm'. In Hindi it inflects as a feminine -ई noun, with the plural regularly naming the summer season.

rootFamily.gloss: winter; cold weather (often plural सर्दियों में 'in winter')

गर्व.etymology: Learned borrowing (tatsama) from Sanskrit गर्व (garva, 'pride, arrogance, self-esteem'), related to गर्वित (garvita, 'proud') and possibly connected to गुरु (guru, 'heavy, weighty, dignified') from Proto-Indo-European *gʷréh₂us. That semantic link from 'weight, gravity' to 'self-importance or dignity' parallels Latin gravis and English gravity. While Sanskrit texts sometimes treated गर्व as haughty pride, in modern Hindi it most often expresses positive, warm pride in achievement or family (पर गर्व होना).

गलती.etymology: Hindi गलती (galtī, formally ग़लती) is borrowed from Classical Persian غلطی (ġalatī, 'error, mistake'), an abstract noun derived from Arabic غَلَط (ġalaṭ, 'error, slip, mistake') with the Persian suffix -ی (-ī). In Arabic, the root غ-ل-ط denotes slipping or erring in speech, calculation, or judgment. Entering Hindustani through administration, schooling, and everyday conversation, the noun became thoroughly naturalized as the primary word for any mistake, large or small. In Devanagari it appears both with and without the nuqta under ग.

गला.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit गल (gala, 'throat, neck'), cognate with Latin gula ('gullet, throat') and English 'gullet'. Through Prakrit गल (gala) and New Indo-Aryan thematic lengthening to -आ, it became Hindi गला (galā). In everyday speech it denotes both the physical throat/neck and the singing or speaking voice.

rootFamily.gloss: to speak; to say; to talk

गलाना.etymology: The causative form of the intransitive verb गलना (galnā, "to melt, decay"). It descends from the Sanskrit root गल् (gal, "to drip, drop, vanish"). Through Middle Indo-Aryan, the term came to broadly encompass phase transitions induced by heat or moisture, such as the dissolving of solids in liquids or the tenderization of food during extensive cooking.

गली.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan गल्ली (gallī, 'narrow lane, alley').

गल्ला.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian غله / گله (ġalla, 'grain store; shopkeeper's money-box') from Arabic غَلَّة (ḡalla, 'proceeds, takings').

गहरा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit गभीर (gabhīra, 'deep, profound, dense'), via Prakrit गहीर (gahīra).

rootFamily.gloss: light (in weight, flavour, sound, or brightness); gentle

ग़लत.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic غَلَط (ḡalaṭ, 'error, mistake'), via Classical Persian غلط (ġalat, 'wrong').

ग़लती.etymology: Formed with abstract suffix -ई from ग़लत ('wrong'), borrowed via Classical Persian غلط (ġalat) from Arabic غَلَط (ḡalaṭ, 'error, slip').

गाँठ.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit ग्रन्थि (granthi, 'knot, joint, bundle'), derived from ग्रन्थ् (granth-, 'to tie, string together'). Through Prakrit गंठि (gaṇṭhi), loss of initial r- in the cluster gr- and simplification of the nasal-stop cluster with compensatory vowel lengthening yielded Hindi गाँठ (gānṭh). It retains the literal sense of a tied knot as well as joints or bundles.

गाइड.etymology: Borrowed from English guide, from Old French guide.

गाजर.etymology: Inherited via Prakrit गज्जर (gajjara) from Sanskrit गर्जर (garjara, 'carrot, turnip-like root'), which also entered Classical Persian as گزر (gazar) and Arabic as جَزَر (jazar) via ancient Iranian-Indic agricultural exchange. Sanskrit -rj- assimilated to -jj- in Prakrit and simplified with compensatory vowel lengthening in Hindi (garjara > gajjara > gājar). Unlike most vegetables that are masculine or mixed, गाजर is consistently feminine in standard Hindi.

गाड़ी.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit गड्डी (gaḍḍī, 'cart, wheeled vehicle'), from early Indic *गड्ड (*gaḍḍa).

गाढ़ा.etymology: Hindi गाढ़ा (gāṛhā) is an inherited tadbhava adjective descending from Sanskrit गाढ (gāḍha, 'firmly pressed, tight, dense, deep') through Prakrit गाढ (gāḍha). The Sanskrit past participle गाढ comes from the root गाह् (gāh-, 'to plunge, dive deep'), with dental -tá fusing with the voiced aspirate to produce a retroflex voiced aspirate ḍh. In New Indo-Aryan, the intervocalic retroflex ḍh developed into the flapped retroflex ṛh, and the masculine nominative ending -आ was added. Its sense shifted smoothly from physical compactness and depth to thick liquids and rich colors.

गाना.etymology: Nominalized from the infinitive of the verb गाना (gānā, 'to sing'), which descends via Prakrit गाइ (gāi) from Sanskrit गायति (gāyati, 'sings'), from the root गै / गा (gai / gā, 'to sing', Proto-Indo-European *gēy- / *gōy-). In Hindi, the -ना (-nā) infinitive regularly doubles as a masculine -आ ending countable noun denoting a musical composition or song.

गायब.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian غایب (ghāyib, 'absent, hidden, vanished') from Arabic غَائِب (ghāʾib, 'absent, unseen, invisible'), the active participle of غَابَ (ghāba, 'to be absent, set, disappear'). Entering Hindustani through administrative and conversational Persianate register, it shifted toward 'missing or mysteriously vanished'. In Hindi it is invariable.

rootFamily.gloss: to be found; to get/receive (with को); to meet (with से)
to look; to seem; to be visible

गार्डन.etymology: Adopted from English garden, which entered Middle English from Anglo-Norman gardin ('enclosed yard or orchard'), an Old Northern French variant of Central Old French jardin. The Romance term originated from Frankish *gardō ('enclosure, yard'), itself from Proto-Germanic *gardô and Proto-Indo-European *gʰórdʰos ('enclosure, fenced space'). In Hindi it is treated as an invariant consonant-final masculine noun, commonly used in urban residential and hospitality contexts.

गाल.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit गल्ल (galla, "cheek"), which itself may have roots in earlier Dravidian or Munda substrata, as it appears alongside the more formal Sanskrit 'kapola'. Passed through Prakrit *galla directly into Old and Modern Hindi. It represents the standard, everyday anatomical term for the fleshy side of the face in modern Indo-Aryan languages.

गिनती.etymology: Hindi गिनती (gintī) is an inherited feminine action noun formed from the verb गिनना (ginnā, 'to count') with the abstract suffix -ती (-tī, from Sanskrit -ति -ti). The verb गिनना descends via Prakrit गणइ / गिणइ (gaṇaï / giṇaï) from Sanskrit गणयति (gaṇayati, 'counts, reckons, calculates', from गण 'group, number'). Raising of the first vowel a to i in Prakrit गिण- carried directly into Hindi गिन- and its derivative गिनती. Today गिनती means both the act of counting and elementary arithmetic or tallying.

गिनना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit गणयति (gaṇayati, 'counts, reckons, numbers'), via Prakrit गणेइ (gaṇeï).

rootFamily.gloss: account; tally; standard (के हिसाब से 'by the standard of / for')
number (room number, phone number, shoe size)

गिरना.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan गिरइ (giraï, 'falls, drops').

गिलास.etymology: Borrowed from English glass with an epenthetic short i breaking the initial cluster gl-.

गीत.etymology: A tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit गीत (gīta, 'sung, song, chant'), the past passive participle of गै (gai-, 'to sing', whence also गान gāna and गायक gāyaka). Used across Sanskrit poetry, drama, and music theory (including the Bhagavadgītā), it entered Hindi as a clean consonant-final masculine noun alongside the native tadbhava गाना (gānā).

गीला.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit गिल्ल (gilla, 'wet, moist, soft'), related to Sanskrit क्लिन्न / गिल.

गुज़रना.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian گذشتن / گذر (guzar, 'passing, crossing') + Hindi -ना.

rootFamily.gloss: to go; (as light verb) marks transition or completion

गुटका.etymology: Derived from the Sanskrit word गुटिका (guṭikā), meaning a small pill, pearl, or globule. In Hindi, it came to refer to small, portable items, including pocket-sized religious booklets and, more recently, small packets of chewing tobacco.

गुड.etymology: Borrowed into conversational Hindi and Hinglish from English 'good', most prominently in set greetings such as गुड मॉर्निंग ('good morning') and गुड नाइट ('good night'). English 'good' descends from Old English gōd and Proto-Germanic *gōdaz ('fitting, adequate, good'), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰedʰ- ('to unite, fit, be associated'). When used before Hindi or English nouns, गुड remains an invariable adjective.

गुत्थी.etymology: Traces back to Sanskrit ग्रन्थि (granthi, "knot, tie"). The journey through Prakrit saw the assimilation of the consonant cluster into heavily aspirated and geminated stops, leading to words like *guttha. In modern Hindi, it is frequently used metaphorically to describe a perplexing mystery, a psychological complex, or a difficult puzzle that requires untangling.

गुनगुना.etymology: An expressive reduplicated Indo-Aryan adjective (also echoed in गुनगुनाना 'to hum softly'), formed on an imitative stem गुण-/गुन- denoting soft, mild, or gentle sensation without harshness. Just as 'humming' is a soft, low-intensity sound, गुनगुना describes mild, pleasant heat—neither scalding nor cold. It inflects like a regular -आ adjective in Hindi.

rootFamily.gloss: light (in weight, flavour, sound, or brightness); gentle

गुनगुनाना.etymology: Hindi गुनगुनाना (gungunānā) is a reduplicative expressive verb built on the imitative syllable गुन- (gun-, evoking a low buzzing, murmuring, or humming resonance). Expressive reduplicated stems of the CVC-CVC-आना type are highly productive in Hindi (compare भुनभुनाना 'to grumble' and खनखनाना 'to clink'), tracing back to Prakrit mimetic formations like गुंगुणइ. It may also echo Classical Persian غنغنه (ġanġana, 'nasal humming'). In everyday Hindi, गुनगुनाना vividly conveys humming a melody softly to oneself.

गुप्त.etymology: A learned tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit गुप्त (gupta, 'protected, guarded, concealed, secret'), the past passive participle of the root गुप् (gup, 'to guard, protect, hide'). In classical Sanskrit, the primary meaning 'well-guarded' naturally shifted toward 'kept out of sight, hidden, secret'. It remains invariable in Hindi and is widely used in both formal registers and everyday storytelling.

गुरु.etymology: A tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit गुरु (guru, 'heavy, weighty, venerable, spiritual teacher, preceptor'), cognate with Greek βαρύς (barýs, 'heavy') and Latin gravis ('heavy, serious'). From 'weighty in wisdom and authority', the adjective became the classic South Asian noun for a revered teacher or master. It remains an invariable -उ masculine noun in Hindi.

गुरुवार.etymology: A Sanskritic calendrical compound of गुरु (guru, 'Jupiter, preceptor of the gods Bṛhaspati') and वार (vāra, 'day of the week, turn'). In classical Indian astronomy, Bṛhaspati (Jupiter) is the planet presiding over the fifth day of the seven-day week, matching Latin Iovis diēs ('Jove's day', French jeudi) and Germanic 'Thor's day'. Hindi uses गुरुवार as a masculine noun.

गुस्सा.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian غصه (ġussa) from Arabic غُصَّة (ḡuṣṣa, 'choking grief, distress, anger').

गूँज.etymology: Derived from Hindi गूँजना ('to echo, hum, reverberate'), inherited from Sanskrit गुञ्जति (guñjati, 'hums, buzzes').

गूँजना.etymology: Inherited through Prakrit गुंजइ (guñjaï) from Sanskrit गुञ्जति (guñjati, 'hums, buzzes, murmurs resonantly'), an expressive nasalized root related to गूंज ('echo, hum'). As in other nasalized Sanskrit clusters like -ñj-, the Prakrit consonant group simplified in Hindi with compensatory lengthening and nasalization of the preceding vowel (guñj- > gū̃j-). It serves across Hindi for both deep musical resonance and echoing voices.

गूँथना.etymology: Inherited via Prakrit गुंथइ / गुंफइ (gunthaï) from Sanskrit गुम्फति / ग्रथ्नाति (gumphati / grathnāti, 'strings together, ties, interweaves, kneads'), from the root ग्रन्थ् (granth, 'to tie, fasten, arrange'). From the core sense of working, pressing, and binding strands together, Hindi evolved both गूँथना ('to braid hair / string a garland') and the everyday kitchen sense 'to knead flour and water into cohesive dough'. Both गूँथना and गूँधना are standard spellings.

गेट.etymology: Borrowed from English gate, from Old English geat.

गेस्ट.etymology: Borrowed into Hindi hospitality vocabulary from English 'guest', complementing native मेहमान (mehmān) and अतिथि (atithi). English 'guest' comes from Old Norse gestr and Proto-Germanic *gastiz ('stranger, guest'), descending from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis ('stranger, guest, host'). Remarkably, it is directly cognate via the same Indo-European root with Latin hostis ('stranger, enemy') and English 'host'.

गेस्टहाउस.etymology: Borrowed from English guesthouse, compound of guest (from Old Norse gestr, Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis 'stranger, guest') + house (from Old English hūs 'dwelling').
गेस्टहाउस.notes: Masculine in Hindi (हमारा गेस्टहाउस), following the masculine gender of घर ('house, home').

गोल.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit गोल (gola, 'ball, globe, sphere, round').

गोला.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit गोल (gola, 'ball, globe, sphere') / गोलक (golaka, 'little ball'), via Prakrit गोल (gola) with masculine -आ enlargement in New Indo-Aryan. Related to the adjective गोल ('round'), the noun refers to any three-dimensional spherical object, from paper lantern globes and balls of thread to celestial spheres. It inflects as a regular -आ masculine noun.

गोलाई.etymology: Derived in Hindi from the adjective गोल (gol, 'round', from Sanskrit गोल) by adding the abstract feminine suffix -आई (-āī, from Middle Indo-Aryan *-āikā / *-āī). Just as चौड़ा gives चौड़ाई ('width') and लंबा gives लंबाई ('length'), गोल yields गोलाई ('roundness, curvature'). It is treated as a feminine noun.

गौरैया.etymology: Derived from गौर (gaur, 'fair, white') + the diminutive suffix -ऐया (-aiyā). 'gaur' comes from Sanskrit गौर (gaura).

ग्यारह.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit एकादश (ekādaśa, 'eleven'), via Prakrit एगारह (egāraha).

ग्राउंड.etymology: Borrowed into modern Hindi from English 'ground', prominently in architectural compounds like ग्राउंड फ्लोर ('ground floor') and खेल का ग्राउंड ('sports ground'). English 'ground' descends from Old English grund ('bottom, foundation, earth, surface') and Proto-Germanic *grunduz ('deep place, bottom'). In Hindi, it functions as a masculine countable noun.

ग्राम.etymology: The word 'ग्राम' (grām) represents two distinct etymologies that converged homophonically in modern Hindi. The first meaning, 'village', is a direct loan (tatsama) from Sanskrit 'ग्राम' (grāma, meaning 'village' or 'community'). The second meaning, a unit of weight, is a phonetically adapted loan from the English word 'gram', which itself stems from French 'gramme' and Late Latin 'gramma'.

ग्राहक.etymology: Hindi ग्राहक (grāhak) is a learned tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit ग्राहक (grāhaka, 'one who grasps, receives, or buys'). It is an agent noun formed with the suffix -अक (-aka) on the strengthened verbal root ग्रह् (grah-, 'to seize, take, receive'), cognate with English 'grab'. While in Sanskrit philosophy ग्राहक also meant 'perceiver' (contrasted with ग्राह्य 'perceived'), in commercial and modern Hindi usage it specialized to 'buyer, client, or regular customer'. Its inherited colloquial counterpart in older Indo-Aryan is गाहक.

ग्लास.etymology: Borrowed into Hindi during the British era from English 'glass' (with an epenthetic/adapted spelling ग्लास or गिलास gilās), specifically denoting a drinking tumbler. English 'glass' comes from Old English glæs and Proto-Germanic *glasą ('glass, amber'), derived from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰel- ('to shine, gleam'). While native काँच (kā̃ch) or शीशा (shīshā) denotes glass as a material, ग्लास/गिलास denotes the vessel.

घंटा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit घण्टा (ghaṇṭā, 'bell; hour struck on a bell'), via Prakrit घंटा (ghaṇṭā).

घंटाघर.etymology: Compound of घंटा (ghanṭā, 'bell, hour', from Sanskrit घण्टा) + घर (ghar, 'house').

rootFamily.gloss: to ring; to chime; to strike (the hour)
to ring (a bell); to play (a musical instrument)

घड़ियाल.etymology: Derived from घड़ी (ghaṛī, 'water-clock, hour, watch', from Sanskrit घटिका ghaṭikā 'small water-jar used to measure time') with the suffix -आल (-āl). Traditionally, a घड़ियाल was the brass plate or gong struck to announce the passing of each घड़ी (24-minute or hourly interval). Its homonym meaning 'gharial' comes separately from the snout resembling an earthen घड़ा ('pot').

घड़ी.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit घटिका (ghaṭikā, 'water-jar time-measure, period of twenty-four minutes, clock'), via Prakrit घडिआ (ghaḍiā).

घड़ीसाज़.etymology: A classic Indo-Persian compound uniting native Hindi घड़ी (ghaṛī, 'clock, watch, hour', from Sanskrit घटी ghaṭī 'water-clock jar') with the Classical Persian agentive suffix -ساز (-sāz, 'maker, builder', present stem of ساختن sāxtan 'to make'). Coined in South Asia when mechanical timepieces spread alongside Persianate craft titles, it parallels compounds like जीनसाज़ ('saddler') and रंगसाज़ ('dyer'). It is an invariable masculine noun.

घबराना.etymology: Expressive North Indian verb घबराना ('to be agitated, confused, anxious').

घबराहट.etymology: Derived from Hindi घबराना (ghabrānā, 'to be flustered, panic') + abstract suffix -आहट (-āhaṭ).

rootFamily.gloss: to feel nervous; to panic; to get flustered

घर.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit गृह (gṛha, 'house, dwelling'), via Prakrit घर (ghara) with metathesis.

घिसना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit घृष्यति / घर्षति (gharṣati, 'rubs, grinds'), via Prakrit घिसइ.

rootFamily.gloss: to polish; to shine; to brighten

घुटना.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit घुट्ट (ghuṭṭa, 'ankle, knee joint').

घुमाना.etymology: Causative of घूमना ('to turn, stroll'), from Middle Indo-Aryan घुम्मइ.

rootFamily.gloss: to turn; to bend; to be folded

घुमाव.etymology: Verbal noun in -आव from घुमाना ('to turn, spin'), causative of घूमना ('to revolve').

rootFamily.gloss: to turn; to rotate; to spin

घुलना-मिलना.etymology: Idiomatic Hindi compound verb pairing घुलना ('to dissolve, blend in', Sanskrit घूर्णते) + मिलना ('to meet, mix').

rootFamily.gloss: to be found; to get/receive (with को); to meet (with से)

घूँट.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit घुट्ट (ghuṭṭa, 'draught, swallow, sip').

घूमना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit घूर्णति (ghūrṇati, 'rolls, revolves, whirls, wavers'), via Prakrit घुम्मइ (ghummaï). Simplification of the geminate nasal -mm- with compensatory lengthening of the preceding vowel produced the Hindi stem घूम- (ghūm-) and infinitive घूमना (ghūmnā). From physical spinning and turning, it broadened naturally to strolling and touring around.

rootFamily.gloss: to turn; to bend; to be folded
to walk; to go; to move; to come along

घूरना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit घूर्णति (ghūrṇati, 'rolls, turns the eyes'), via Prakrit घुरइ / घूरइ.

rootFamily.gloss: to look; to see; to check; (after -कर) to try out

घोल.etymology: Deverbal masculine noun from Hindi घोलना (gholnā, 'to dissolve, stir into liquid, mix'), which traces back to Sanskrit घूर्ण / घोलयति (gholayati, 'stirs up, mixes together', attested in classical medical and culinary texts) via Prakrit घोलइ (gholaï). Used equally in baking for cake batter and in chemistry or painting for solutions, it stays masculine in Hindi.

घोलना.etymology: Transitive partner of intransitive घुलना (ghulnā, 'to dissolve, melt into'), derived via Prakrit घोलइ (gholaï) from Sanskrit घूर्णति / घोलयति (gholayati, 'stirs around, mixes, agitates'). Turners' Comparative Dictionary connects the Middle Indo-Aryan stem *ghōl- with expressive Indo-Aryan roots meaning 'to churn, swirl, or rock'. In modern Hindi it specifically designates blending or dissolving substances into a fluid medium.

चंपा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चम्पक (campaka, Magnolia champaca, prized golden-blossomed fragrant tree).

चक्कर.etymology: Inherited (semi-tatsama) from Sanskrit चक्र (cakra, 'wheel, circle, turn'), from PIE *kʷékʷlos ('wheel').

चखना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चक्षति (cakṣati) / चषति (caṣati, 'eats, tastes') or Middle Indo-Aryan *चक्खइ (*cakkhaï, 'tastes', compare Prakrit चक्खइ, 'tastes, relishes'). Simplification of the geminate -kkh- gave the Hindi stem चख- (chakh-) and infinitive चखना (chakhnā). It specifically means sampling food or drink to check its flavour.

rootFamily.gloss: sweet; pleasant (of voice, music, or scent)

चचेरा.etymology: Formed from चाचा (cācā, 'father's younger brother') + kinship suffix -एरा (-erā).

चढ़ना.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan चड्ढइ (caḍḍhaï, 'mounts, climbs').

rootFamily.gloss: to come down; to get off (a train); to descend
floor / storey of a building; destination

चढ़ाई.etymology: The noun 'चढ़ाई' (caṛhāī) is formed by combining the verbal root 'चढ़-' (caṛh-, from the verb 'चढ़ना', meaning 'to climb') with the feminine nominalizing suffix '-आई' (-āī). The root 'चढ़-' traces back to the Prakrit word 'चढइ' (caḍhai) and ultimately to the Sanskrit root 'चट्' (caṭ, to go or mount). The secondary meaning 'invasion' arose metaphorically from the idea of mounting a campaign or climbing up to a fort.

चढ़ाना.etymology: Causative form of the verb चढ़ना (caṛhnā, 'to climb, to ascend'). It derives from Prakrit 𑀘𑀟𑀇 (caḍaï), which has uncertain, likely Dravidian or Munda (substratum) origins. The causative 'caṛhānā' expanded metaphorically from 'making something climb' to 'offering to deities' and 'applying a layer'.

चतुर.etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit 'catura', meaning swift, dexterous, or clever. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-Aryan roots, potentially related to quick movement.

चपटा.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan *cappaṭṭa / Prakrit चप्पट्ट (cappaṭṭa, 'flat, flattened, squashed'), formed from an expressive Indo-Aryan root *capp- ('to press flat, flatten'; compare Sanskrit चिपिट cipiṭa, 'flat-nosed, flattened'). Loss of gemination yielded the Hindi -आ adjective चपटा (chapṭā). It contrasts with गोल ('round') and उभरा ('raised').

चबाना.etymology: The verb 'चबाना' (cabānā) descends from the Prakrit verb 'चब्बइ' (cabbaï), which meant 'to chew'. This Prakrit root is a natural phonetic evolution of the Sanskrit root 'चर्व्' (carv), seen in the Sanskrit verb 'चर्वति' (carvati, he chews). The historical transformation of the cluster 'rv' to a geminate 'bb' and later to a single 'b' is a standard feature of Indo-Aryan phonetic development.

चमकदार.etymology: Hybrid Indo-Persian adjective formed in Hindi-Urdu by attaching the productive Classical Persian agentive-possessive suffix -دار (-dār, 'holding, possessing', from Persian dāštan 'to have') to the native noun चमक (camak, 'brightness, sheen, sparkle'). The native stem चमक derives from the expressive Indo-Aryan root चम- ('flash, gleam'). Like all -दार compounds in Hindi, चमकदार is grammatically invariable.

चमकना.etymology: Derived in Indo-Aryan from an expressive root चम- (cham-, denoting sudden flash or glitter, compare Sanskrit चमत्कार 'astonishment, marvel') extended with the verbal suffix -क (-k-), parallel to Prakrit चमक्कइ (chamakkaï, 'flashes, sparkles'). The same root gives the feminine noun चमक ('shine, lustre') and the causative verb चमकाना ('to polish').

rootFamily.gloss: to polish; to shine; to brighten

चमकाना.etymology: Causative of चमकना ('to shine, sparkle'), formed with -आ- (-ā-).

चमचमाता.etymology: Imperfective participial adjective formed from the expressive denominative verb चमचमाना (camcamānā, 'to shine brightly, glitter'), itself built on the reduplicated mimetic stem चम-चम (cam-cam) related to चमकना ('to shine, flash'). Reduplication intensifies the visual sense of repeated, lively flashes of light on polished metal, leather, or glass. Inflecting like all -ता participles, it agrees in gender and number with its noun.

चमचा.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian چمچه (chamcha, 'ladle, large spoon'), derived from चम् (cham-, related to Persian چمیدن 'to scoop/bend' or Middle Persian *čamčak) with the diminutive suffix -چه (-cha). Entering Hindustani through Mughal and urban kitchenware vocabulary, it adapted smoothly to the masculine -आ declension as चमचा (chamchā), alongside the shorter variant चम्मच.

चमड़ा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चर्मन् (carman, 'skin, hide, leather') + extension -ड, via Prakrit चम्मड (cammaḍa).

चमत्कार.etymology: A tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit चमत्कार (camatkāra, 'astonishment, poetic wonder, spectacle, miracle'), formed from the exclamation चमत् (camat, expressing sudden wonder) and कार (kāra, 'making', from कृ 'to do/make'). In classical Sanskrit poetics it signified the flash of aesthetic delight, before widening in Hindi to mean any astonishing marvel or miracle.

चम्मच.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चमस (camasa, 'ladle, drinking vessel, spoon') or via Persian چمچه (čamča, itself related to Indo-Iranian *čamasa-).

चलन.etymology: A verbal noun derived from चलना (chalnā, 'to walk, move, be current') and corresponding to Sanskrit चलन (calana, 'moving, walking, currency', from चल् 'to move'). Just as 'current' in English comes from 'running/flowing', चलन evolved from 'movement/circulation' to mean 'what is currently practised, prevailing custom, or fashion'. It is masculine in Hindi.

rootFamily.gloss: to walk; to go; to move; to come along

चलना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चलति (calati, 'moves, walks, stirs'), via Prakrit चलइ (calaï).

rootFamily.gloss: to go; (as light verb) marks transition or completion

चलाना.etymology: Causative of चलना ('to walk, move'), from Sanskrit चालयति (cālayati, 'sets in motion').

rootFamily.gloss: to walk; to go; to move; to come along

चश्मा.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian چشمه (čašma, 'eyeglass; spring of water'), from چشم (čašm, 'eye', cognate with Sanskrit चक्षुस् cakṣus).

rootFamily.gloss: to look; to see; to check; (after -कर) to try out

चहकना.etymology: Echoic/onomatopoeic Indo-Aryan verb चहकना ('to warble, chirp brightly').

चाँद.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चन्द्र (candra, 'moon, shining, bright'), related to चन्दति ('shines') and Latin candēre ('to glow, shine white'). Through Prakrit चन्द (canda), loss of the medial nasal consonant with compensatory lengthening and nasalization of the vowel yielded Hindi चाँद (chānd). It is one of the most poetic and everyday nouns in Hindi.

चाँदी.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चन्द्रिका (candrikā, 'moonlight; bright silver'), from चन्द्र ('moon'), via Prakrit चंदिआ (candiā).

चाकू.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian چاقو (čāqū, “knife”). Originally from Turkic.

चाचा.etymology: Inherited or formed as a nursery/affectionate kinship term in Indo-Aryan (compare Prakrit चच्च / चच्चा, and Sanskrit तात tāta 'father/dear one' alongside regional reduplicated *cāccā-). Like दादा ('paternal grandfather') and मामा ('maternal uncle'), चाचा preserves its final -आ without inflecting to -ए in the direct plural or oblique singular. It denotes specifically the father's younger brother.

चादर.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian چادر (čādar, 'sheet, cloth wrap, tent'), from Middle Persian čādur.

चाबी.etymology: Borrowed from Portuguese chave ('key'), ultimately from Latin clāvis ('key').

चाय.etymology: Borrowed via Persian چای (čāy) from Sinitic 茶 (chá, 'tea'), diffused overland along Asian trade routes.

चाय-पानी.etymology: Idiomatic Hindi dvandva compound pairing चाय ('tea', from Persian/Chinese) + पानी ('water', from Sanskrit पानीय pānīya) to mean 'light refreshments and hospitality'.

चायदानी.etymology: Compound of चाय (chāy, 'tea') + Persian suffix -दानी (-dānī, 'small vessel, holder').

चार.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चत्वारि (catvāri, 'four'), via Prakrit चत्तारि (cattāri), from PIE *kʷetwóres.

चारकोल.etymology: Borrowed from English charcoal. Ultimately of uncertain origin in English, possibly derived from char (to turn to coal) and coal. The term entered Hindi during the British colonial period to refer specifically to drawing charcoal or processed carbon, distinguishing it from native words like koyalā.

चारों.etymology: Formed in Hindi-Urdu by attaching the collective plural suffix -ओं (-õ) to the cardinal numeral चार (cār, 'four'), which descends via Prakrit चत्तारो (cattāro) from Sanskrit चत्वारः (catvāraḥ, 'four', PIE *kʷetwóres). Adding -ओं creates a definite totality ('all four together'), a systematic morphological device seen in दोनों ('both'), तीनों ('all three'), and पाँचों ('all five'). चारों is invariable and precedes plural nouns.

चाल.etymology: From Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀘𑀸𑀮 (cāla). Ultimately from Sanskrit चाल (cāla, 'moving, motion').

चालीस.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चत्वारिंशत् (catvāriṃśat, 'forty'), via Prakrit चत्तालीसा (cattālīsā).

चालू.etymology: Derived from the Hindi verbal stem चल- / चाल- (from संस्कृत चल् 'to move, go') by adding the expressive/agentive suffix -ऊ (-ū, as in कमाऊ 'earning' or बिकाऊ 'for sale'). Literally 'moving, current, in operation', चालू came to denote switches turned on, running machines, and ongoing operations. It remains completely invariable in Hindi.

rootFamily.gloss: to walk; to go; to move; to come along

चाहना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चक्षते / उत्साहते or Prakrit चाहइ (cāhaï, 'looks for, wishes, desires').

cognates.meaning: impersonal 'is needed' from the same verb

rootFamily.gloss: is needed; is wanted; should (with infinitive)
mind; heart; mood / inclination (मन करना 'to feel like')

चाहिए.etymology: Grammaticalised old passive/precative form of चाहना ('is desired -> is needed, ought').

rootFamily.gloss: to want; to wish (माफ़ी चाहता/चाहती हूँ 'I apologise')
to; for; definite direct-object marker; at (times of day)

चाहे.etymology: Derived from the subjunctive or optative form of the verb चाहना (cāhnā, 'to wish, to desire'), from Sanskrit चहति (cahati). Literally meaning 'may it be desired', it grammaticalized into a conjunction meaning 'whether' or 'even if'. This represents a common linguistic shift from expressing volition to introducing concessions.

चिंता.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing चिन्ता (cintā, 'thought, care, anxiety'), from root चिन्त् ('to think, reflect').

चिकना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चिक्कण (cikkaṇa, 'smooth, glossy, unctuous, slippery'), attested in classical Sanskrit medical and poetic texts. Through Prakrit चिक्कण (cikkaṇa), simplification of the geminate -kk- and syncope of the medial vowel -a- produced Hindi चिकना (chiknā). It applies both to silky-smooth surfaces and greasy or glossy textures.

चिट.etymology: A native Indo-Aryan noun (compare Hindi चिट्ठी 'letter, note' and Prakrit चिट्ठ / *ciṭṭha-, 'written slip'), further reinforced in urban Indian usage by Anglo-Indian 'chit' ('short note, voucher, signed slip'). The English word 'chit' itself was borrowed directly from Hindustani चिट / चिट्ठी during the seventeenth century. In Hindi it is a feminine consonant-final noun.

rootFamily.gloss: slip of paper; short written note; chit

चिट्ठी.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit चिट्ठिआ (ciṭṭhiā, 'written slip, note'), source of Anglo-Indian English chit.

चिड़िया.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit चडिआ (caḍiā, 'small bird, sparrow'), from Sanskrit चटका (caṭakā).

चित्र.etymology: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit चित्र (citra, 'bright, variegated; picture, sketch').

चित्रकारी.etymology: Formed from a combination of the Sanskrit-derived noun चित्र (citra), meaning 'picture' or 'art', and the Persian suffix ـकारी (-kārī), meaning 'doing' or 'making'. This is a hybrid formation typical of Hindustani, combining classical Indo-Aryan roots with Perso-Arabic derivational morphology.

चिपकना.etymology: Expressive Middle Indo-Aryan verb चिप्पकइ ('adheres, clings closely').

rootFamily.gloss: to be tied; to be fastened

चिपचिपा.etymology: Reduplicative expressive adjective formed from the Hindi onomatopoeic stem चिप- (cip-, 'sticking, adhering', seen also in चिपकना 'to stick' and चिपचिपाहट 'stickiness'). New Indo-Aryan languages richly deploy reduplicated C1VC2-C1VC2-ā formations to convey tactile and sensory impressions. As an -आ stem adjective, it inflects regularly for gender and number (चिपचिपा, चिपचिपी, चिपचिपे).

चिमटी.etymology: Feminine diminutive of Hindi चिमटा (chimṭā, 'tongs, pincers'), derived from the verb चिमटना / चिपटना ('to cling, pinch, clasp together', related to Middle Indo-Aryan *cimp- / *cimm- 'to press, squeeze'). Just as चिमटा denotes large hearth tongs, the feminine diminutive चिमटी (chimṭī) denotes any small spring-clip, pinch-grip, clothespin, or pair of tweezers.

चिल्लाना.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan चिल्लइ (cillaï, 'cries out, shrieks').

चिह्न.etymology: A learned tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit चिह्न (cihna, 'mark, sign, emblem, badge, symptom'). In classical Sanskrit it denoted any identifying token, royal insignia, or landmark. Modern Hindi preserves the literary spelling ह्न (though commonly pronounced with metathesis as 'chinh' in speech) and treats it as a masculine noun.

चीं.etymology: Hindi चीं (cī̃) is an expressive onomatopoeic noun imitating a thin, high-pitched squeak, creak, or bird's chirp. Such monosyllabic nasalized sound-symbolic forms are pervasive across New Indo-Aryan languages (compare Bengali चीं-चीं and Punjabi चीं) and trace back to similar Prakrit mimetic particles. In Hindi, it frequently appears reduplicated as चीं-चीं for sparrows or rusty hinges, as well as in the colloquial idiom चीं बोलना or चीं न करना ('not to utter a squeak of protest'). Its nasalized long vowel vividly mimics a sustained high squeal.

चीज़.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian چیز (čīz, 'thing'), from Middle Persian tis / čīz.

चीनी.etymology: Literally 'Chinese (white refined sugar)', from चीन ('China') + -ई, referring historically to fine white crystalline sugar associated with Chinese trade.

rootFamily.gloss: sweet; pleasant (of voice, music, or scent)

चुकना.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit चुक्कइ (cukkaï, 'comes to an end, is settled, finishes').

rootFamily.gloss: to go; (as light verb) marks transition or completion
to take; to buy; light verb for inward/self-benefiting action
to give; to let (after -ने); light verb marking outward/completed action

चुटकी.etymology: Inherited via Middle Indo-Aryan *चुट्टकी / चुट्टिआ (*cuṭṭakī) from an expressive Indo-Aryan stem *cuṭ- ('to pinch, nip, snap', compare Sanskrit चोटयति coṭayati 'cuts/nips' and Hindi चोंट/चुटकुला). The sound-symbolic crispness of चुट- mirrors the sudden flick between thumb and forefinger—giving both 'a finger-snap' and the culinary measure 'a pinch of salt or spice'. It inflects as a regular feminine -ई noun.

चुनना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चिनोति (cinoti, 'gathers, selects'), via Prakrit चुणइ (cuṇaï).

चुपके.etymology: Hindi चुपके (cupke) is an inherited adverbial form derived from the expressive stem चुप (cup, 'silent, quiet') with the Middle/New Indo-Aryan adverbial suffix -के (-ke, related to -क-/-कर). The base चुप traces to Prakrit चुप्प / चुप्पि (cuppa, 'silent, still'), widely recognized as a sound-symbolic labial gesture imitating closed lips and hushed silence. In Hindi, चुपके routinely pairs with the postposition से (चुपके से, 'quietly, secretly') or doubles as चुपके-चुपके. It contrasts with ज़ोर से ('loudly') and खुलेआम ('openly').

चुपचाप.etymology: Expressive reduplicative compound built on चुप (cup, 'silent, quiet').

चूकना.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit '*cukkati'. From Sanskrit 'cyavate' (moves away, falls, fails), from root 'cyu' (to move).

चूड़ी.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चूडिका / चूडा (cūḍā, 'bracelet, ring, crest'), via Prakrit चूडी (cūḍī).

चूना.etymology: From Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀘𑀼𑀡𑁆𑀡 (cuṇṇa). Ultimately derived from Sanskrit चूर्ण (cūrṇa, 'powder, dust').

चूल्हा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चुल्लि / चुल्ली (culli / cullī, 'hearth, fireplace, stove'), via Prakrit चुल्ल (culla) / *चुल्ह (*culha). Aspiration of the geminate -ll- and lengthening of the root vowel gave Hindi चूल्हा (chūlhā) with masculine -आ ending. From village mud hearths to contemporary gas stoves, it remains the core domestic term for a cooking burner.

चेक.etymology: Borrowed into modern Hindi from English 'check', used overwhelmingly in the conjunct verb चेक करना ('to verify, inspect, examine') as well as for bank checks. English 'check' entered from Old French eschec ('check in chess'), ultimately from Classical Persian شاه (shāh, 'king', used as a warning in chess: shāh māt 'the king is helpless'). From chess, the term evolved through 'restraint, control, verification against a list' to general inspection.

चेक-इन.etymology: Borrowed from English check-in, nominalisation of the phrasal verb check in ('to verify and register one's arrival at a hotel desk or station'; English check itself derives via Old French eschec from Persian šāh 'king' in chess).

history.meaning: arrival registration at a hotel or terminal

चेक-इन.notes: Masculine noun in Hindi; turns into an active verb with करना (चेक-इन करना, 'to check in').

चेतावनी.etymology: Derived from the verb चेताना (cetānā, 'to warn, to make aware'). It ultimately stems from the Sanskrit root चित् (cit, 'to perceive, to know').

चेन.etymology: Borrowed from English chain, semantically extended in Indian English and Hindi to slide fasteners (zippers).

history.meaning: linked metal series; zipper (South Asian usage)

चेयर.etymology: Borrowed into modern urban Hindi from English 'chair', used alongside older Arabic-derived कुर्सी (kursī). English 'chair' comes via Old French chaiere from Latin cathedra ('seat, armchair'), borrowed from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra, 'seat'), from κατά (katá, 'down') and ἕδρα (hédra, 'seat', cognate with Sanskrit सदस् sadas). In Hindi, चेयर often adopts feminine agreement by semantic association with कुर्सी.

चेहरा.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian چهره (čihra, 'face, countenance, visage'), from Middle Persian čihrak.

चॉक.etymology: Borrowed into Hindi during the British school and trade era from English 'chalk', alongside native खड़िया (khaṛiyā). English 'chalk' descends from Old English cealc ('chalk, lime'), an early Germanic borrowing from Latin calx (genitive calcis, 'limestone, pebble'), related to Greek χάλιξ (khálix, 'small stone'). In Hindi, it is treated as an uncountable material noun, commonly feminine or masculine depending on regional usage.

चॉपिंग.etymology: Hindi चॉपिंग (cŏpiṅg) is a modern borrowing from English 'chopping', the present participle and gerund of 'to chop'. English 'chop' appeared in Middle English as choppen ('to strike, cut into pieces'), likely of expressive or Middle Dutch/Low German origin. In contemporary Hindi, चॉपिंग enters chiefly as a kitchen borrowing in fixed collocations such as चॉपिंग बोर्ड ('chopping board'). The borrowed English vowel /ɒ/ is rendered with the Devanagari candra-o (ऑ) to reflect the rounded open back sound.

चौक.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चतुष्क (catuṣka, 'four-way courtyard or square'), via Prakrit चउक्क (caükka).

चौकोर.etymology: A native Hindi compound of चौ- (chau-, 'four', from Sanskrit चतुर् catur) and कोर (kor, 'edge, corner, side', from Middle Indo-Aryan कोरा / Sanskrit कोटि 'edge, point'). Literally 'having four corners or edges', it functions as an invariable adjective meaning 'square' or 'quadrangular', parallel to चौकोना.

चौखट.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit. From Sanskrit 'catuṣkāṣṭha', meaning 'four pieces of wood', from 'catur' (four) and 'kāṣṭha' (wood).

चौड़ा.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit चउड (caüḍa, 'broad, flat, wide'), linked to चतुर ('four-sided, square-spread').

rootFamily.gloss: big; large; elder; very (in expressions like बड़े शौक़ से)

चौड़ाई.etymology: Derived within Hindi from चौड़ा (chauṛā, 'wide') + abstract noun suffix -आई (-āī).

चौथा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चतुर्थ (caturtha, 'fourth'), formed from चतुर् (catur, 'four') with the ancient ordinal suffix -थ (-tha, cognate with English '-th' in 'fourth'). Through Prakrit चउत्थ (caüttha), contraction of -aü- into the diphthong -au- and simplification of -tth- yielded Hindi चौथा (chauthā). It inflects regularly for gender and case.

चौथाई.etymology: Abstract fractional noun built in Hindi from the ordinal चौथा (cauthā, 'fourth') + suffix -आई (-āī), descending via Prakrit चउत्थ (cauttha) from Sanskrit चतुर्थ (caturtha, 'fourth', from चतुर catur 'four' and PIE *kʷetwóres). Adding -आई converts the ordinal 'fourth' into the substantive fraction 'a fourth part, quarter', paralleling तिहाई ('one-third'). In recipes and measurements, चौथाई is feminine.

चौदह.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चतुर्दश (caturdaśa, 'fourteen'), via Prakrit चउद्दह (caüddaha).

चौबीस.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit चतुर्विंशति (caturviṃśati, 'twenty-four'), composed of चतुर् (catur, 'four') and विंशति (viṃśati, 'twenty'). Via Prakrit चउवीस / चउब्बीस (caüvīsa / caübbīsa), the vowel hiatus -aü- contracted to -au- and medial -vv- became -b-, yielding Hindi चौबीस (chaubīs). Like all Hindi numerals, it does not inflect.

छज्जा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit छद्य (chadya, 'covering, roof, overhang') or छदिस् (chadis, 'roof, thatch', from छद् 'to cover'), via Prakrit छज्ज (chajja, 'eaves, projecting balcony'). Retaining the palatal geminate -jj- and adding the masculine -आ ending, it became Hindi छज्जा (chhajjā). In Jaipur havelis, it refers specifically to overhanging stone eaves or upper courtyard balconies.

छड़.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan छड (chaḍa) / *छडि (*chaḍi), likely connected to Sanskrit यष्टि (yaṣṭi, 'staff, rod') or शलाका / छटा ('long thin stick, rod') via regional Indo-Aryan *chaḍa- denoting a straight rod or shaft. Its consonant-final form छड़ (chhaṛ) denotes thicker structural rods, dowels, or spacer bars, whereas the -ई form छड़ी denotes a cane or slender stick.

छड़ी.etymology: Feminine diminutive of छड़ (chhaṛ, 'rod, staff'), continuing Prakrit छडी (chaḍī, 'cane, switch, wand') and related to Sanskrit चटी / शलाका ('slender stick'). In everyday Hindi, छड़ी is the primary word for a gentleman's walking stick or cane as well as a slender wooden dowel.

छत.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit छत्त्र (chattra, 'parasol, covering, shelter'), via Prakrit छत्त (chatta).

छपना.etymology: Intransitive stem derived in Indo-Aryan alongside the transitive verb छापना (chhāpnā, 'to stamp, print'), connected to Sanskrit छप् / क्षप् or Prakrit छप्पइ (chhappaï, 'presses, stamps'). Originally referring to block-printing textiles with carved wooden stamps—a craft famous in Jaipur—it naturally extended to modern printing presses and newspapers. Short vowel -अ- marks the intransitive form.

छपाक.etymology: An expressive onomatopoeic formation in Hindi imitating the sudden slap and burst of water when a flat or heavy object hits a pool or basin, formed from the imitative base छप- (chhap-, compare छप-छप 'splashing') and the abrupt sound-ending -आक (-āk, as in धमाक 'bang' and तड़ाक 'crack'). It is used both as an interjection and a sound noun.

छल्ला.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit छल्ल (challa, 'ring, loop, bark').

छह.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit षष् (ṣaṣ, 'six'), via Prakrit छ (cha), from PIE *swéḱs.

छाँव.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit छाया (chāyā, 'shade, shadow, reflection', cognate with Greek σκιά skiā). Through Prakrit छाआ / छाँह (chāā / chāṁha, with spontaneous nasalization and glide development -h-/-v-), the word evolved into Hindi छाँव (chhānv) alongside poetic छाँह. While छाया remained in formal Hindi, छाँव became the warm, everyday spoken word for shade under a tree.

छात्र.etymology: A tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit छात्र (chātra, 'pupil, disciple, student'), derived from छत्र (chattra, 'umbrella, shelter', from छद् 'to cover/protect') with vriddhi strengthening of the first vowel. Traditionally, a pupil was one who covered or sheltered the faults of his preceptor or sat under the teacher's sheltering protection. In modern Hindi it is the standard masculine noun for a student.

छानना.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 'chaṇṇa', from Sanskrit 'channati'. Connected to the root 'chad' (to cover).

छाया.etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit छाया (chāyā, “shadow, shade, reflection”).

छायादार.etymology: A classic Perso-Sanskrit hybrid adjective combining Sanskrit-derived छाया (chāyā, 'shade') with the Persian productive suffix -दार (-dār, 'having, holding', from داشتن 'to have/hold', cognate with Sanskrit धर्). Literally 'shade-bearing', छायादार functions as an invariable adjective across Hindi prose and everyday speech to describe leafy trees and cool courtyards.

छिड़कना.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan छिट्टक्कइ ('scatters drops, sprinkles').

छिपना.etymology: Inherited Indo-Aryan intransitive verb छिपना ('to be covered, hide').

छिपाना.etymology: Transitive/causative of छिपना ('to hide'), formed with -आ- (-ā-).

rootFamily.gloss: slip of paper; short written note; chit

छिलका.etymology: Derived in Hindi from the verbal stem छील- / छिल- (chhīlnā, 'to peel, pare, scrape'), which descends from Sanskrit छल्ल (challa, 'bark, skin, peel') or शल्क (śalka, 'scale, bark, chip') via Prakrit छल्लि / छिल्ल (challi / chilla). Extended with the diminutive-noun suffix -का (-kā), it became the standard masculine noun छिलका (chhilkā) for fruit peels, rinds, and husks.

छीलन.etymology: The noun 'छीलन' (chīlan) is derived from the Hindi verb 'छीलना' (chīlnā), meaning 'to peel' or 'to scrape'. The verb itself traces back to the Sanskrit root 'क्षुर' (kṣura) or 'क्षिप्' (kṣip), combined with Indo-Aryan phonetic developments in Prakrit. The suffix '-अन' (-an) is added to the verbal root to form a noun denoting the product or result of the action, hence 'that which is peeled off' or 'shavings'.

छुट्टा.etymology: Formed from the same Middle Indo-Aryan stem छुट्ट (chuṭṭa, 'free, loose, detached', related to छूटना 'to come loose') as छुट्टी, with the masculine adjectival/nominal suffix -आ (-ā). Literally meaning 'loose, untied, separate', छुट्टा functioned first as an adjective for untethered or individual items. In commercial Hindi, the plural छुट्टे (chhuṭṭe) came to signify small coins and loose change broken down from larger currency notes.

छुट्टी.etymology: Derived from छूटना (chūṭnā, “to be left, let go”), from Sanskrit छुट्यति (chuṭyati, “to break, cut”).

छूट.etymology: Deverbal feminine noun from छूटना (chūṭnā, 'to be released, remitted'), from Sanskrit छुट् / क्षुट् via Prakrit छुट्टइ.

छूटना.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀙𑀼𑀝𑁆𑀝𑀤𑀺 (chuṭṭadi), from Sanskrit क्षुट्यते (kṣuṭyate, 'to be split, broken'). It serves as the intransitive counterpart to छोड़ना (choṛnā).

छूना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit छुपति (chupati, 'touches'), via Prakrit छुवइ (chuvaï).

छेड़ना.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit छेडइ (cheḍaï, 'touches, stirs, teases').

rootFamily.gloss: to make laugh; to cheer up

छेद.etymology: Learned/semi-learned borrowing from Sanskrit छेद (cheda, 'cut, slit, perforation, hole'), from छिद् ('to pierce').

छोटा.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit छुट्ट / छोट्ट (choṭṭa, 'small, short, slender').

rootFamily.gloss: big; large; elder; very (in expressions like बड़े शौक़ से)
less; little; fewer; कम से कम 'at least'
a little; some; a few (in plural)

छोड़ना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit छोरयति / क्षोडयति ('releases, lets go, leaves'), via Prakrit छोडेइ (choḍeï).

rootFamily.gloss: to put; to place; to keep

जँचना.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan जच्चइ ('is tested, proves fitting, looks becoming').

history.meaning: to be tested; to look becoming

जंगल.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit जङ्गल (jaṅgala, 'arid, rough, uncultivated terrain, wasteland or scrubland'), via Prakrit जंगल (jaṅgala). Paradoxically, in ancient Sanskrit medical and geographical texts जङ्गल denoted dry, sparsely vegetated ground rather than dense tropical rainforest. Over centuries in Hindi-Urdu it came to mean any thick woods or forest, and in the eighteenth century British colonial usage borrowed the word into English as jungle.

जंगला.etymology: Derived from Persian جنگلا (jangalā, 'grating, lattice'), which is a variation or diminutive of 'jangal' (wood, thicket). The term historically referred to a wooden lattice or fence resembling intertwined branches. In modern Hindi, it designates window grilles or protective metal/wood railings.

जंगली.etymology: Derived from जंगल (jaṅgal, 'forest, wilderness') combined with the adjectival suffix -ई (-ī). It traces back to Sanskrit जङ्गल (jaṅgala, 'arid, sterile, desert').

जग.etymology: Borrowed in this household sense from early modern and modern English jug ('deep spouted vessel with a handle for pouring water or milk', attested in sixteenth-century English, likely a familiar transfer from the pet name Jug for Joan/Judith).
जग.notes: Unrelated to its native homograph जग ('the world', inherited from Sanskrit जगत् jagat); पानी का जग means 'a pitcher of water'.

जगमगाना.etymology: An onomatopoeic formation representing the flickering or sparkling of light.

जगह.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian جایگاه (jāygāh, 'place, station'), shortened in spoken Hindustani to जगह.

जगाना.etymology: Causative verb derived from जागना (jāgnā, 'to be awake, wake up'), with regular stem-vowel shortening (ā > a before -आना). जागना descends via Prakrit जग्गइ (jaggaï) from Sanskrit जाग्रति / जागर्ति (jāgarti, 'keeps watch, wakes', from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ger- 'to wake', cognate with Greek ἐγείρω egeírō). Thus जगाना preserves one of the oldest Indo-European verbal roots for waking someone from sleep.

जज़्बात.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian جذبات (jazbāt, 'feelings, emotions') from Arabic جَذَبَات (jaḏabāt), the feminine sound plural of جَذْبَة (jaḏba, 'impulse, attraction, emotion', from the root ج-ذ-ب j-ḏ-b 'to draw, attract'). In Hindustani, the Arabic plural form was lexicalized as a masculine plural-only noun meaning 'feelings, sentiment, emotions', pairing with the adjective जज़्बाती.

जज़्बाती.etymology: Formed in Hindustani from the Arabic-Persian loanword जज़्बात (jazbāt, 'emotions, feelings') by attaching the adjectival suffix -ई (-ī). Literally 'pertaining to emotions', it describes both emotionally sensitive people and sentimental gestures or situations. Like other -ई adjectives, it is completely invariable in Hindi.

जड़ना.etymology: Derived from the noun जड़ (jaṛ, 'root, base'). In modern Hindi, it means to fix firmly, as in embedding jewels or delivering a solid strike.

जड़ी.etymology: Derived from जड़ (jaṛ, 'root'), which continues Prakrit जडा (jaḍā) and Sanskrit जटा (jaṭā, 'fibrous root, matted braid'). With the feminine diminutive suffix -ई (-ī), जड़ी specifically came to mean a medicinal or aromatic rootlet and, especially in the dvandva compound जड़ी-बूटी (jaṛī-būṭī), culinary and Ayurvedic herbs. Its meaning reflects traditional Indian medicine and cooking, where roots and leafy sprigs are grouped together.

जड़ी-बूटी.etymology: A compound of जड़ी (jaṛī, 'medicinal root') and बूटी (būṭī, 'herb, plant'). Both words ultimately stem from Sanskrit, reflecting traditional Indian medicinal practices.

जब.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit यदा (yadā, 'when [relative]'), via Prakrit जइया / जब्ब.

rootFamily.gloss: then; at that time; तब तक 'until then'
just then; at that very moment; that explains why

जबकि.etymology: A compound conjunction formed in Hindi by joining the relative temporal adverb जब (jab, 'when', from Sanskrit यदा yadā via Prakrit जह / जब्ब) with the subordinating complementizer कि (ki, 'that', from Persian که). Literally 'when that', the pair developed a strong contrastive sense equivalent to English 'whereas' or 'while'.

rootFamily.gloss: when (in a statement or time clause, never a question!)

जमा.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic جَمْع (jamʿ, 'gathering, sum, deposit'), via Classical Persian جمع (jam').

जयपुर.etymology: Sanskrit compound जयपुर (Jayapura, 'City of Jai / Victory'), named after its founder Sawai Jai Singh II (1727).
