Just as Latin trānscrībere meant 'writing across', Arabic naql shifted from 'moving across' to 'copying text or imitating'. In Hindi it is feminine.

नक़्शा.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic نَقْشَة (naqša, 'drawing, design, map'), via Classical Persian نقشه (naqša).

नक़्शाकार.etymology: A hybrid compound of Arabic-derived 'naqśā' (map, plan, drawing) and the Persian suffix '-kār' (doer, maker). Literally 'map-maker'.

नक़्शानवीस.etymology: A classical Perso-Arabic compound formed in Hindustani from नक़्शा (naqshā, 'map, plan, sketch', from Arabic نَقْشَة naqsha 'drawing, engraving') and the Persian agentive suffix -नवीस (-navīs, 'writer, drafter', present stem of Classical Persian نوشتن navishtan 'to write'). Literally 'map-drafter', it denotes a professional cartographer or draftsman.

नक़्शानवीसी.etymology: A compound of Arabic origin نَقْشَة (naqša, 'map' or 'drawing') via Persian, and the Persian suffix ـنویسی (-navīsī, 'writing' or 'drafting') from the verb نوشتن (neveštan, 'to write'). It refers to the profession or act of cartography and map-making.

नक्काशीदार.etymology: From नक्काशी (nakkāśī, 'carving') + Persian suffix -दार (-dār, 'possessing'). The root 'nakkāśī' comes from Arabic نَقَّاش (naqqāš).

नक्शा.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian نقشه (naqša, 'sketch, map, design, plan'), from Arabic نَقْشَة (naqša, 'engraving, painting, pattern'), derived from the triliteral root ن ق ش (n-q-š, 'to engrave, carve, paint, variegate'). Originally denoting an engraved design or miniature drawing, the word broadened in Indo-Persian administrative and architectural usage to mean a building blueprint, map, or spatial plan. In Hindi it inflects regularly as a masculine -आ noun.

नक्शानवीस.etymology: Hindi नक्शानवीस (naqśānavīs) is a Perso-Arabic occupational compound formed from नक़्शा (naqśā, 'map, chart, blueprint') and नवीस (navīs, 'writer, draftsman, clerk'). The first part comes via Classical Persian نقشه (naqša, 'sketch, map') from Arabic نَقْش (naqš, 'engraving, drawing, design'), while the second part is the present stem of Classical Persian نوشتن (nivištan, 'to write'). Comparable to चिट्ठीनवीस and अर्ज़ीनवीस, the compound literally means 'map-drawer'. In modern Hindi it evokes skilled traditional cartography and architectural drafting.

नज़र.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic نَظَر (naẓar, 'sight, look, glance'), via Classical Persian نظر.

rootFamily.gloss: to look; to see; to check; (after -कर) to try out

नज़ारा.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian نظاره (nazāra) from Arabic نَظَارَة (naẓāra, 'looking, spectacle, view'), from root ن-ظ-ر ('to look').

rootFamily.gloss: to look; to see; to check; (after -कर) to try out

नदी.etymology: Inherited/borrowed from Sanskrit नदी (nadī, 'river, flowing stream').

नन्हा.etymology: Inherited affectionate Indo-Aryan adjective नन्हा ('tiny, tender, very young'), via Prakrit णण्ह.

नमक.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian نمک (namak, 'salt'), from Middle Persian namak.

नमकीन.etymology: Derived from नमक ('salt', from Persian نمک namak) + Persian suffix -ईन (-īn, 'characterised by').

rootFamily.gloss: sweet; pleasant (of voice, music, or scent)

नमस्ते.etymology: Learned Sanskrit greeting नमस्ते (namas te, literally 'a bow to you'), from नमस् ('bow, reverence') + ते ('to you').

नमी.etymology: Derived from the Persian adjective نم (nam, "moist, damp"), which shares Indo-Iranian roots with similar Sanskrit concepts. The abstract noun forming suffix -ī (-ई) was added in Persian and retained in Hindustani to create 'namī' (dampness). It is the most common colloquial and semi-formal term for humidity or wetness in modern Hindi.

नया.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit नव (nava) / नवक (navaka, 'new, fresh, young'), via Prakrit णवअ (ṇavaa), from PIE *néwos.

rootFamily.gloss: old (of things, places, memories, or friendships)

नरम.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian نرم (narm, 'soft, gentle, tender'), from Middle Persian narm.

rootFamily.gloss: light (in weight, flavour, sound, or brightness); gentle

नल.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit नल (nala, 'hollow reed, tube, water pipe').

नहाना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit स्नाति (snāti, 'bathes, washes'), via Prakrit ण्हाइ (ṇhāi).

नहीं.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit न हि (na hi, 'surely not') or नास्ति ('is not'), fused in Prakrit णहिं (ṇahiṃ).

rootFamily.gloss: don't! (negative marker used ONLY with imperatives)
not (with subjunctive, infinitive, or न ... न 'neither ... nor')

ना.etymology: Inherited from Indo-Aryan न / ना used clause-finally as an inviting tag question ('is it not?').

rootFamily.gloss: just; a little; kindly (polite request softener)
not (with subjunctive, infinitive, or न ... न 'neither ... nor')

नाइन.etymology: Borrowed into modern urban Hindi and Hinglish from the English cardinal number 'nine', frequently heard in room numbers, times, and phone digits alongside native नौ (nau). English 'nine' descends from Old English nigon and Proto-Germanic *newun, directly cognate with Sanskrit नवन् (navan, 'nine') and Latin novem from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Thus English 'nine' and Hindi नौ share the exact same Indo-European ancestor.

नाक.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit नक्र / नासिका (nāsikā, 'nose'), via Prakrit णक्क (ṇakka).

नाज़ुक.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian نازک (nāzuk, 'delicate, slender, fragile, subtle'), continuing Middle Persian nāzuk ('tender, fine, delicate') from an Iranian root *nāz- ('tender, graceful'). Entering Hindustani through poetic, artistic, and everyday domestic speech, नाज़ुक serves as an invariable adjective for anything fragile, fine-textured, or sensitive.

rootFamily.gloss: light (in weight, flavour, sound, or brightness); gentle

नाटक.etymology: A tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit नाटक (nāṭaka, 'drama, play, actor'), derived from नट् (naṭ-, 'to dance, act, perform', itself a Prakritization of नृत् nṛt- 'to dance'). In classical Indian aesthetics (Nāṭyaśāstra), नाटक is the premier dramatic genre. In everyday Hindi it means both theatrical drama and 'put-on pretence'.

नानबाई.etymology: From Persian نان‌بای (nân-bây), from نان (nân, 'bread') + بائی (bây, 'baker'). It refers to traditional bakers of Indian flatbreads.

नाप.etymology: Deverbal noun from नापना (nāpnā, 'to measure'), inherited from Sanskrit ज्ञापयति / मापयति (māpayati, 'causes to measure') via Prakrit मापेइ / नापेइ.

rootFamily.gloss: number (room number, phone number, shoe size)

नापना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit ज्ञापयति / मापयति (māpayati, 'measures out'), via Prakrit मावइ / नापइ.

नाम.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit नामन् (nāman, 'name') via Prakrit नाम (nāma), reinforced by Persian نام (nām); from PIE *h₁nómn̥.

नाराज़.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian ناراض (nārāz, 'displeased'), from نا- (nā-, 'not') + راضی (rāzī, 'pleased').

नाल.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian نعل (naʿl, 'horseshoe, sandal, sole') from Arabic نَعْل (naʿl, 'sandal, shoe, horseshoe'), from the root ن-ع-ل (n-ʿ-l, 'to shoe a horse, wear sandals'). In Persian and Hindustani, نعل specialized for the U-shaped iron shoe nailed to a horse's hoof, adapting in Hindi without the Arabic glottal stop as feminine नाल (nāl).

नाव.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit नौ / नावा (nau / nāvā, 'boat, ship', from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us, directly cognate with Greek ναῦς naûs and Latin nāvis). Through Prakrit नावा (nāvā), loss of the final vowel yielded Hindi नाव (nāv), retaining its feminine grammatical gender. It is one of the oldest maritime words in Indo-European.

नाविक.etymology: A tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit नाविक (nāvika, 'sailor, helmsman, pilot, pertaining to ships'), formed by vriddhi strengthening from नौ (nau, 'ship, boat') with the relational suffix -इक (-ika). Literally 'pertaining to a boat' or 'one who works a boat', it functions in Hindi both as an invariable masculine noun for a mariner and attributively ('nautical').

नाश्ता.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian ناشتا (nāštā, 'fasting; morning meal breaking the fast').

निकलना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit निष्क्रमति / निष्कलति (niṣkalati, 'goes out, issues forth'), via Prakrit निक्कलइ (nikkalaï).

rootFamily.gloss: to go; (as light verb) marks transition or completion

निकालना.etymology: Transitive/causative counterpart of निकलना (nikalnā, 'to come out, emerge'), formed by lengthening the stem vowel (अ -> आ). Both verbs trace back to Sanskrit निष्कालयति (niṣkālayati, 'drives out, expels') / निष्क्रामति via Prakrit निक्कालइ / णिक्कलइ (nikkālaï / ṇikkalaï). In everyday Hindi, निकालना covers taking out items, unpacking bags, and solving problems.

rootFamily.gloss: to come out; to leave; to emerge
to pour; to put in; to add
to open; to unlock; to unwrap

निखारना.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit, stemming from the Sanskrit root नि- (ni-, "down, into") combined with a derivative of क्षार् (kṣār, "to wash, flow, cleanse"). Over centuries, the phonetic transition from kṣ to kh occurred, yielding the Middle Indo-Aryan base. The causative suffix -ā was appended to create a transitive verb signifying the act of purifying, brightening, or bringing something to its full aesthetic potential.

निगम.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing निगम (nigama, 'guild, market town, corporate body').

निचला.etymology: Derived in Hindi from the adverb and postposition नीचे (nīche, 'below, beneath') by shortening the initial vowel and attaching the positional adjective suffix -ला (-lā, parallel to पिछला 'back/previous' from पीछे and अगला 'next/front' from आगे). Its base नीचे continues Sanskrit नीचैः (nīcaiḥ, 'low, below'). It inflects regularly for gender and number.

rootFamily.gloss: less; little; fewer; कम से कम 'at least'

निजी.etymology: Formed from Sanskrit निज (nija, 'one's own, innate') + Hindi suffix -ई (-ī).

rootFamily.gloss: one's own (my, your, his, her, our, their)

निडर.etymology: Inherited prefixal formation नि- (from Sanskrit निर्-, 'without') + डर ('fear').

निभाना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit निर्वाहयति (nirvāhayati, 'carries through, accomplishes'), via Prakrit निब्बहइ.

rootFamily.gloss: with; together with (के साथ); together (एक साथ)

निमंत्रण.etymology: A tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit निमन्त्रण (nimantraṇa, 'calling in, inviting, invitation'), formed from the prefix नि- (ni-, 'in, down') and मन्त्रण (mantraṇa, 'counseling, addressing', from मन्त्र् 'to speak solemnly, summon'). Originally denoting a respectful summons to a feast or ceremony, it serves in modern Hindi as the standard formal noun for an invitation.

नियम.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing नियम (niyama, 'restraint, rule, fixed observance'), from नि- + यम् ('to hold, regulate').

निरीक्षक.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing निरीक्षक (nirīkṣaka, 'observer, examiner, inspector'), from निर्- + ईक्ष्.

निरीक्षण.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing निरीक्षण (nirīkṣaṇa, 'careful examination, inspection').

निर्णायक.etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit निर्णायक (nirṇāyaka), derived from the root निर्- (nir-, 'out') + नी (nī, 'to lead') with the agentive suffix -अक (-aka). It originally meant 'one who leads to a conclusion' and is used in modern Hindi for 'decisive' or a 'judge'.

निर्देश.etymology: The noun 'निर्देश' (nirdeś) is a direct borrowing (tatsama) from classical Sanskrit 'निर्देश' (nirdeśa). It is derived from the prefix 'निर्-' (nir-, meaning 'out' or 'clearly') and the verbal root 'दिश्' (diś, meaning 'to point out' or 'to direct'). In modern Hindi, it is heavily used in formal, technical, and official contexts to signify guidelines, instructions, or directives.

निवाला.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian نواله (nawāla, 'mouthful, morsel of food').

निशान.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian نشان (nišān, 'mark, sign, emblem'), from Middle Persian nišān.

निशानी.etymology: Formed from Persian نشان (nišān) + -ई (-ī), Classical Persian نشانی (nišānī, 'souvenir, token').

नींद.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit निद्रा (nidrā, 'sleep'), via Prakrit निद्दा (niddā) with spontaneous nasalisation.

नींबू.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit निम्बू / निम्बूक (nimbūka, 'lime, lemon').

नीचा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit नीच (nīca, 'low, situated below'), via Prakrit णीच (ṇīca).

rootFamily.gloss: upstairs; above; on top of (के ऊपर)

नीचे.etymology: Oblique locative of नीचा ('low'), inherited from Sanskrit नीचैस् (nīcais, 'below, downward').

rootFamily.gloss: upstairs; above; on top of (के ऊपर)

नीम.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit निम्ब (nimba, 'neem tree'), via Prakrit निंब (nimba).

rootFamily.gloss: small leaf; herb leaf; tea leaf

नीला.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit नील (nīla, 'dark blue, indigo'), source of Persian نیل and English aniline / lilac.

cognates.meaning: ultimately from Sanskrit नील via Persian and Arabic

नुकीला.etymology: An Indo-Persian hybrid adjective. It combines the Persian loanword नोक (nok, 'point, tip') with the native Hindi adjectival suffix -ईला (-īlā, 'possessing the quality of'). This morphological blending demonstrates the deep integration of Persian vocabulary into native Hindi grammatical structures.

ने.etymology: Inherited from Apabhramsha instrumental-agentive postposition ने / णें, replacing older Sanskrit instrumental endings.

rootFamily.gloss: to; for; definite direct-object marker; at (times of day)

नैपकिन.etymology: Borrowed from English napkin, diminutive of Old French nappe ('tablecloth').

नोक.etymology: Borrowed from Persian نوک (nok, 'point, tip, beak'). It was assimilated into Hindi to describe the pointed end of sharp objects like pens, needles, or swords. Its phonetic simplicity and utility made it a ubiquitous term in the vernacular, replacing many older Indo-Aryan equivalents.

नोट.etymology: Borrowed from English note, passing through Old French note ('mark, letter, musical tone') from Latin nota ('mark, sign, written character'). The Latin noun relates to nōscere ('to know'), descending from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃- ('to know', cognate with Sanskrit ज्ञा jñā and Hindi जानना). In modern Hindi, नोट serves as an invariant masculine noun across office memos, paper currency, and music.

नोटपैड.etymology: Borrowed into modern Indian office and café Hindi from the English compound 'notepad'. It combines 'note' (from Latin nota, 'written mark or memo') with 'pad' (sixteenth-century English 'cushion, bundle of paper sheets glued at one edge', of uncertain origin). In Hindi, it functions as a masculine countable noun.

नोटबुक.etymology: Borrowed from English 'notebook' through modern schooling, architecture, and office stationery in South Asia. English 'notebook' compounds 'note' (from Old French note and Latin nota 'mark, sign') and 'book' (Old English bōc). In Hindi it adopts feminine grammatical gender by analogy with किताब ('book') and कॉपी ('copybook').

history.meaning: bound book of blank pages for notes

नोटिस.etymology: Borrowed from English notice, from Old French notice / Latin nōtitia.

नोट्स.etymology: Borrowed from English notes (plural of note, from Latin nota).

नौ.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit नव (nava, 'nine'), via Prakrit णव (ṇava), from PIE *h₁néwn̥.

नौकरी.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian نوکری (nawkarī, 'service, employment'), from نوکر (nawkar, 'servant, employee').

नौजवान.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian نوجوان (naw-jawān, 'young person'). It is a compound of نو (naw, 'new') and جوان (jawān, 'young').

नौवाँ.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit नवम (navama, 'ninth'), reshaped in Hindi from नौ + ordinal suffix -वाँ.

पंक्ति.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing पङ्क्ति (paṅkti, 'row, line, series of five'), from पञ्चन् ('five').

पंखा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पक्षक (pakṣaka, 'wing, side, fan', diminutive of पक्ष pakṣa 'wing, feather'), via Prakrit पक्ख (pakkha) with spontaneous nasalization (*पंखा *paṅkhā) and masculine -आ ending. Because traditional hand-fans were shaped like bird wings or made from feathers and palm leaves, 'wing' evolved into the standard Hindi noun for any fan (also borrowed into English as 'punkah').

पंचर.etymology: Borrowed from English puncture, from Late Latin pūnctūra ('a pricking').

पंद्रह.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पञ्चदश (pañcadaśa, 'fifteen'), via Prakrit पण्णरह (paṇṇaraha).

rootFamily.gloss: a quarter past; plus a quarter (+¼)

पकड़ना.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan पक्कडइ (pakkaḍaï, 'seizes, grips').

rootFamily.gloss: to hand over; to pass (something into someone's hand)
to put; to place; to keep

पकड़ाना.etymology: Causative of पकड़ना ('to hold, grasp'), meaning 'to place in someone's grip, hand over'.

rootFamily.gloss: to hold; to catch; to grasp
to give; to let (after -ने); light verb marking outward/completed action

पकना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पचति / पच्यते (pacati / pacyate, 'cooks, bakes, ripens', from पच् pac-, cognate with Greek πέσσω, Latin coquere, and English 'cook') or directly the participial stem पक्व (pakva, 'cooked, ripe'). Through Prakrit पक्कइ (pakkaï), simplification of -kk- yielded the Hindi stem पक- (pak-) and infinitive पकना (paknā).

पका.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पक्व (pakva, 'cooked, baked, mature, ripe', past passive participle of पच् 'to cook, ripen') via Prakrit पक्क (pakka). While the geminate form gave पक्का (pakkā, 'solid, permanent, well-baked'), the single-consonant variant पका (pakā) aligned with the verb पकना and specialized for ripe fruit and cooked dishes. It inflects regularly for gender and number.

पकाना.etymology: Causative inherited from Sanskrit पचति / पाचयति (pācayati, 'cooks, bakes, ripens').

cognates.meaning: distant PIE *pekʷ- ('to cook, ripen') cognate via Latin coquō

पक्का.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पक्व (pakva, 'cooked, ripe, fired brick, mature, solid'), via Prakrit पक्क (pakka).

पक्षी.etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit पक्षिन् (pakṣin, “winged, bird”), from पक्ष (pakṣa, “wing”).

पचास.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पञ्चाशत् (pañcāśat, 'fifty'), via Prakrit पंचासा (pañcāsā).

पच्चीस.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पञ्चविंशति (pañcaviṃśati, 'twenty-five'), via Prakrit पच्चीसइ (paccīsaï).

पटरी.etymology: Feminine diminutive of पटरा / पाट (paṭrā / pāṭ, 'plank, flat wooden strip'), inherited from Sanskrit पट्ट / पट्टिका (paṭṭa / paṭṭikā, 'flat slab, plank, strip') via Prakrit पट्ट / पट्टी (paṭṭa / paṭṭī) with the diminutive suffix -री (-rī). Originally denoting a narrow wooden strip or roadside footpath, it naturally extended in the railway era to steel rail tracks.

पटिया.etymology: A diminutive or dialectal form of the noun पट्टा (paṭṭā) or पट्टी (paṭṭī), tracing back to Sanskrit पट्ट (paṭṭa, "slab, tablet, board"). The -iyā suffix is employed to specify a distinct flat, hard surface, typically used in rural or construction contexts to describe stone or wooden platforms spanning small gaps or used for seating.

पट्टा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पट्ट (paṭṭa, 'tablet, copperplate charter, lease document').

पट्टिका.etymology: A tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit पट्टिका (paṭṭikā, 'small flat plate, tablet, strip, document'), feminine diminutive of पट्ट (paṭṭa, 'flat slab, metal plate, royal charter'). While its tadbhava descendant पट्टी means a narrow strip or bandage, learned पट्टिका was retained in formal Hindi for commemorative metal or stone plaques and nameplates.

पट्टी.etymology: Feminine diminutive of पट्टा, from Sanskrit पट्टिका (paṭṭikā, 'narrow plate, ribbon, strip').

पड़ना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पतति (patati, 'falls, alights'), via Prakrit पडइ (paḍaï).

rootFamily.gloss: is needed; is wanted; should (with infinitive)

पड़ोस.etymology: Inherited as a tadbhava noun through Prakrit पडोवस / पडिवेस (paḍivesa) from Sanskrit प्रतिवेश (prativeśa, 'neighbouring house, neighbourhood'), compounded from प्रति- (prati-, 'near, beside') and वेश (veśa, 'dwelling, house', from विश् viś 'to enter, settle', cognate with Latin vīcus and Greek οἶκος oîkos). Through Middle Indo-Aryan sound changes, -ti- retroflexed before v to -ḍ- (yielding paṛ-) and -veśa rounded to -os.

पड़ोसी.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit प्रतिवेशिन् (prativeśin, 'living nearby, neighbour'), via Prakrit पडिवेसिअ.

पढ़ना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पठति (paṭhati, 'reads aloud, recites, studies'), via Prakrit पढइ (paḍhaï).

पतझड़.etymology: A transparent native Hindi compound noun formed from पत (pat, reduced from पत्ता pattā / Sanskrit पत्र pattra 'leaf') and झड़ (jhaṛ, stem of झड़ना jhaṛnā 'to shed, drop, fall', from Prakrit झडइ jhaḍaï). Literally meaning 'leaf-fall', पतझड़ parallels English 'fall' in naming the autumn season after the shedding of tree foliage. In Hindi, it is a masculine singular noun for the post-monsoon/autumn season.

पतला.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit प्रतनु / पत्रल ('thin, slender'), via Prakrit पत्तल (pattala).

पता.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पत्रक / प्रत्यय ('token, trace, whereabouts'), giving Middle/Early Hindi पता ('trace, address, awareness').

पति-पत्नी.etymology: Sanskrit dvandva compound पति-पत्नी: पति (pati, 'husband, master', PIE *pótis) + पत्नी (patnī, 'wife', PIE *pótnih₂).

पतीला.etymology: Hindi पतीला (patīlā) is a North Indian domestic utensil noun whose origin connects with Middle Indo-Aryan *पत्तल्ल / *पतील- or an early Indo-Aryan derivative of पात्र (pātra, 'vessel, receptacle') with a diminutive/utensil suffix -ईल-आ. Some lexicographers also compare it with Perso-Arabic पातिला or regional Prakrit pot terms denoting wide-mouthed metal vessels. In Hindi, the masculine पतीला designates a large, straight-sided cooking pot, contrasting with the smaller feminine पतीली. It is an indispensable word in Indian kitchens.

पत्ता.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पत्र (patra, 'leaf, wing, page'), via Prakrit पत्त (patta).

पत्ती.etymology: Diminutive in -ई from पत्ता ('leaf'), inherited from Sanskrit पत्र (patra, 'leaf, wing, page') via Prakrit पत्त (patta).

पत्थर.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit प्रस्तर (prastara, 'flat stone, rock slab'), via Prakrit पत्थर (patthara).

पदक.etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit पदक (padaka, “ornament of the neck, coin, medal”).

पनीर.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian پنیر (panīr, 'cheese'), from Middle Persian panīr.

पन्ना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पर्ण (parṇa, 'leaf, betel leaf, written leaf/page'), via Prakrit पण्ण (paṇṇa).

पब्लिक.etymology: Borrowed into modern Hindi civic and everyday speech from English 'public', used both as an invariable adjective and as a collective feminine noun meaning 'the general public'. English 'public' came via Old French public from Latin pūblicus ('of the people, belonging to the state'), altered from Old Latin poplicus under the influence of pūbēs ('adult population'), related to populus ('people'). It complements the Sanskritic adjective सार्वजनिक (sārvajanik).

पर.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit उपरि (upari, 'above, upon') for 'on', and परम् (param, 'further, however') for 'but', merged in Prakrit परि / पर.

rootFamily.gloss: upstairs; above; on top of (के ऊपर)

परख.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit परीक्षा (parīkṣā, 'examination, test'), via Prakrit परिक्खा (parikkhā).

परखना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit परीक्षते (parīkṣate, 'looks around carefully, examines, tests', from परि- 'around' + ईक्ष् 'to see'). Through Prakrit परिक्खइ (parikkhaï), lowering of the vowel and loss of gemination produced the Hindi verb परखना (parakhnā) alongside the feminine noun परख ('assay, test, discernment'). It is the everyday tadbhava counterpart of learned परीक्षा करना.

rootFamily.gloss: to look; to see; to check; (after -कर) to try out

परछाईं.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit. Derived from Sanskrit 'praticchāyā', combining 'prati' (towards) and 'chāyā' (shadow).

परत.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पर्पट / परत ('thin layer, crust, fold').

परमानेंट.etymology: Borrowed into modern Hindi from English 'permanent', coexisting with Sanskritic स्थायी (sthāyī) and Persian-derived पक्का (pakkā). English 'permanent' derives via Old French permanent from Latin permanēns, the present participle of permanēre ('to stay to the end, endure'), from per- ('through') and manēre ('to remain', cognate with Greek μένω ménō). In Hindi, it serves as an invariable adjective.

परिवार.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing परिवार (parivāra, 'surrounding circle, household, family').

परीक्षण.etymology: Borrowed directly from Sanskrit परीक्षण (parīkṣaṇa, 'testing, examining, trial').

परेशान.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian پریشان (parēšān, 'scattered, dishevelled, distressed').

परेशानी.etymology: From Classical Persian پریشانی (parēšānī, 'distress, trouble'), from پریشان (parēšān, 'scattered, troubled') + -ई.

परोसना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit परिवेषयति (pariveṣayati, 'waits upon, serves food around'), via Prakrit परिवेसइ.

पर्ची.etymology: Diminutive in -ई from पर्चा, borrowed from Classical Persian پرچه (parča, 'piece of cloth or paper, slip').

पर्दा.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian پرده (parda, 'curtain, screen, veil'), from Middle Persian pardag.

rootFamily.gloss: cloth; piece of fabric; clothes (in plural कपड़े)

पल.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पल (pala, 'a tiny measure of time, one-sixtieth of a ghaṭikā; twenty-four seconds').

पलंग.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पर्यङ्क (paryaṅka, 'bed, couch, litter'), via Prakrit पल्लंक (pallaṅka).

cognates.meaning: via Portuguese from the same Sanskrit word

पलटना.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀧𑀮𑀝𑁆𑀝𑀇 (palaṭṭaï), potentially from Sanskrit पर्यस्त (paryasta, 'overturned') or a deshi (regional) root. It expresses a physical or metaphorical reversal of state. The term is highly versatile, describing everything from flipping a page to overturning a regime.

पलना.etymology: The intransitive counterpart of transitive पालना (pālnā, 'to nourish, rear, keep'), inherited through Prakrit पलइ / पालइ from Sanskrit पालयति (pālayati, 'protects, guards, nourishes'), the causative of पा (pā, 'to protect', Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- 'to shepherd, guard'). Following Hindi's systematic vowel-length alternation, short-vowel पलना means 'to be nourished, grow up', while long-vowel पालना means 'to raise or rear'. It frequently appears in the rhyming echo pair पलना-बढ़ना ('to grow up').

पल्ला.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पल्लव (pallava, 'sprout, shoot, lappet, skirt-hem') or पटल (paṭala, 'covering, leaf, shutter'), via Prakrit पल्ल / पल्लव (palla / pallava, 'hem, flap, panel'). With masculine -आ enlargement in Hindi, पल्ला (pallā) came to denote a hinged flap, door leaf, window shutter, or balance pan.

पश्चिम.etymology: A pure Tatsama (direct borrowing) from Sanskrit पश्चिम (paścima, 'hinder, western, later'). Ancient Indian geographical orientation faced east toward the rising sun, making the west the 'hinder' or 'back' direction. It remains the formal and standard word for the western cardinal direction in Hindi.

पसंद.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian پسند (pasand, 'approval, choice, pleasing'), from Middle Persian pasand.

rootFamily.gloss: mind; heart; mood / inclination (मन करना 'to feel like')

पसंदीदा.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian پسندیده (pasandīda, 'chosen, approved, favourite'), past participle of پسندیدن ('to approve, like').

पहचानना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit प्रत्यभिजानाति (pratyabhijānāti, 'recognises'), via Prakrit पच्चभिजाणइ.

पहनना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit परिदधाति / पिनह्यति (pinahyati, 'ties on, puts on attire'), via Prakrit पइण्हइ.

rootFamily.gloss: cloth; piece of fabric; clothes (in plural कपड़े)

पहला.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit पहिल / पडमिल्ल (pahila, 'first, foremost'), from Sanskrit प्रथम (prathama).

पहले.etymology: Oblique/adverbial form of पहला ('first'), inherited from Prakrit पहिले ('at first, earlier').

पहिया.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit प्रधि (pradhi, 'wheel rim'), via Prakrit पहिअ (pahia).

rootFamily.gloss: to turn; to rotate; to spin

पहुँचना.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit पहुच्चइ (pahuccaï, 'reaches, arrives, suffices'), from Sanskrit प्रभूयते.

rootFamily.gloss: to come down; to get off (a train); to descend

पाँच.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पञ्च (pañca, 'five'), via Prakrit पंच (pañca), from PIE *pénkʷe.

पाँचों.etymology: Hindi पाँचों (pā̃cõ) is the collective/definite plural form of the cardinal numeral पाँच (pā̃c, 'five'), formed by attaching the plural oblique ending -ओं (-õ) to indicate 'all five together'. The base पाँच is an inherited tadbhava numeral descending from Sanskrit पञ्च (pañca, 'five') via Prakrit पंच (paṃca). In the shift from Middle to New Indo-Aryan, the nasal consonant before the palatal affricate resolved into nasalization with compensatory lengthening of the preceding vowel (paṃca > pā̃c). The collective suffix -ओं is likewise used in दोनों, तीनों, and चारों.

पाइप.etymology: Borrowed from English pipe, from Old English pīpe.

history.meaning: hollow tube for water or steam

पाउच.etymology: Borrowed into modern Hindi retail and everyday speech from English 'pouch'. English 'pouch' entered from Old North French pouche ('bag, sack, pocket'), variant of Old French poche, of Frankish/Germanic origin (compare English 'poke' and 'pocket'). In Hindi, पाउच takes masculine gender and refers to small zippered cases or sealed packaging packets.

पाना.etymology: Regional/technical Indo-Aryan workshop noun पाना (pānā, 'grip-spanner, wrench'), related to पाणि ('hand, grip').

पानी.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पानीय (pānīya, 'drinkable; water'), gerundive of पा (pā, 'to drink'), via Prakrit पाणीअ (pāṇīa).

पाबंदी.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian پابندی (pābandī, 'adherence, punctuality, restriction').

पाया.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀧𑀸𑀤 (pāda), from Sanskrit पाद (pāda, 'foot, leg'). In modern usage, it specifically refers to the legs of furniture like beds or chairs.

पार.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पार (pāra, 'further bank, opposite shore, across'), from PIE *per- ('to cross over').

पारिवारिक.etymology: Learned Sanskrit vriddhi derivative पारिवारिक (pārivārika, 'relating to family'), from परिवार + -इक.

पार्सले.etymology: Hindi पार्सले (pārsle) is a direct modern loanword from English 'parsley', adopted through international cookbooks and urban culinary vocabulary. English 'parsley' comes from Old French peresil and Late Latin petrosilium, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πετροσέλινον (petrosélinon, literally 'rock-celery', from πέτρα 'rock' and σέλινον 'celery'). Because parsley is not native to traditional North Indian cuisine, Hindi uses the transliterated English name directly. It is typically differentiated from native धनिया ('coriander/cilantro').

पाल.etymology: Hindi पाल (pāl) descends from Sanskrit पट्ट (paṭṭa) or प्रावार (prāvāra, covering, cloth, mantle) via Prakrit पवाल / पाल, referring to a stretched sheet of woven cloth. In maritime and riverine North Indian usage, the word specialized for a boat's canvas sail and protective awnings. The semantic link between an enclosing cloth sheet and a wind-catching sail is preserved across Indo-Aryan nautical vocabulary.

पालिका.etymology: पालिका (pālikā) is a learned borrowing (tatsama) from Sanskrit पालिका (pālikā), the feminine agentive noun derived from the root पाल् (pāl, 'to protect, guard, govern'). In Classical Sanskrit it meant a female guardian or caretaker, and in modern Hindi administrative terminology it was adopted in compounds like नगर पालिका ('municipality') and कार्यपालिका ('executive branch'). Its transparent derivational suffix -इका marks feminine institutional nouns.

पास.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पार्श्वे (pārśve, 'at the side of, beside, near'), via Prakrit पस्से (passe).

rootFamily.gloss: with; together with (के साथ); together (एक साथ)

पिघलना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit प्रगलति (pragalati, 'drips, melts away'), via Prakrit पग्घलइ (pagghalaï).

पिछला.etymology: Derived from पीछे ('behind, after') + adjectival suffix -ला, ultimately from Sanskrit पश्चात (paścāt).

rootFamily.gloss: old (of things, places, memories, or friendships)

पिन.etymology: Borrowed from English pin, descending from Old English pinn ('peg, bolt, nail'), which either developed from Proto-Germanic *pinnô or was an early Germanic borrowing from Latin pinna ('feather, wing, pointed tip'). Through sewing, stationery, and machinery, English pin entered everyday Hindi usage seamlessly. In Hindi it regularly takes feminine grammatical gender, matching native सुई ('needle').

पियानो.etymology: Borrowed via English piano from Italian pianoforte ('soft-loud').

rootFamily.gloss: to ring (a bell); to play (a musical instrument)

पिलाना.etymology: पिलाना (pilānā) is the regular Hindi causative verb formed from पीना (pīnā, 'to drink'), which itself descends from Sanskrit पिबति (pibati, 'drinks') via Prakrit पिअइ (piai). When forming the causative in -आना, the long stem vowel of पी- shortens to पि-, and an epenthetic -ल्- is inserted between the vowel-final root and the causative suffix. This -ल्- insertion is a hallmark of Hindi vowel-final causative stems such as दिलाना and सिलाना.

cognates.meaning: to cause to drink; to serve a drink

पिसना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पिनष्टि / पिष्यते (piṣyate, 'is ground, crushed'), via Prakrit पिसइ.

पिसा.etymology: The past participle of the intransitive verb पिसना (pisnā, "to be ground"), descending from Sanskrit पिष्ट (piṣṭa, "crushed, ground"). The root is √पिष् (piṣ, "to crush"). In modern Hindi, it functions primarily as an adjective describing powdered spices and grains, while metaphorically denoting a state of severe suffering or exploitation under pressure.

पीछे.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पश्चात् (paścāt, 'behind, after, in the rear'), via Prakrit पच्छा -> पाछे / पीछे.

rootFamily.gloss: ahead; forward; further on; in front (के आगे)

पीठ.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 'piṭṭha'. From Sanskrit 'pṛṣṭha', meaning back, rear, or hind part.

पीतल.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पित्तल (pittala, 'brass, bell-metal'), via Prakrit पित्तल (pittala).

पीना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पिबति (pibati, 'drinks'), via Prakrit पिअइ (piaï), from PIE *peh₃- ('to drink').

पीला.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पीतल / पीत (pīta, 'yellow, golden'), via Prakrit पीअल (pīala).

पुआल.etymology: पुआल (puāl) derives from Sanskrit पलाल (palāla, 'straw, stalk') through Prakrit पुलाल / पुआल (pulāla / puāla). The intervocalic -ल- weakened and dropped in Middle Indo-Aryan, yielding the hiatus vowel sequence -उआ- preserved in modern Hindi. Related rustic words across North India denote rice or wheat straw used in weaving hats, mats, and animal bedding.

पुकारना.etymology: पुकारना (pukārnā) traces back to a Prakrit expressive verbal base पुक्कारइ (pukkārai, 'cries out, shouts'), related to Sanskrit फुत्कार / पुत्कार (onomatopoeic cries or calls). The initial geminate -क्क- simplified to single -क- with compensatory adjustments in Hindi, producing the modern stem पुकार-. Its core sense encompasses shouting to draw attention, summoning someone, and addressing a person by a specific title.

rootFamily.gloss: to call; to invite; to summon

पुड़िया.etymology: पुड़िया (puṛiyā) is a diminutive feminine noun from Sanskrit पुटिका (puṭikā, 'small fold, pocket, packet'), derived from पुट (puṭa, 'fold, cavity'). Via Prakrit पुडिआ (puḍiā), intervocalic -ट- voiced and flapped to -ड़- in Hindi. Traditional Indian pharmacies and spice shops have long used folded paper पुड़िया sachets to measure single doses or small quantities.

history.meaning: small fold; leaf or paper packet

rootFamily.gloss: small leaf; herb leaf; tea leaf

पुदीना.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian پودینه / پودنه (pūdīna / pūdna, 'mint, pennyroyal'), from Middle Persian pūdag.

rootFamily.gloss: small leaf; herb leaf; tea leaf

पुराना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पुराण (purāṇa, 'ancient, belonging to former times'), via Prakrit पुराण (purāṇa).

पुल.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian پل (pul, 'bridge'), from Middle Persian puhl, cognate with Avestan pərətu-.

rootFamily.gloss: across; beyond (के पार); पार करना 'to cross'

पुश्तैनी.etymology: Formed from Classical Persian پشت (pušt, 'back, generation, lineage') + Indo-Persian suffix -ऐनी.

पुस्तकालय.etymology: Learned Sanskrit compound पुस्तकालय (pustakālaya, 'house of books'), from पुस्तक + आलय.

पूछना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पृच्छति (pṛcchati, 'asks, questions'), via Prakrit पुच्छइ (pucchaï), from PIE *preḱ- ('to ask').

rootFamily.gloss: to tell; to explain; to let someone know

पूरा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पूरक / पूर्ण (pūrṇa, 'filled, complete'), via Prakrit पूरअ (pūraa), from PIE *pleh₁- ('to fill').

पूर्व.etymology: A direct tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit पूर्व (pūrva, "in front, before, eastern"). In ancient Indo-Aryan cosmology and geography, facing the rising sun (the east) was the primary orientation, hence the word means both "front/eastern" and "earlier/previous" in time. It is a cognate with Old Persian 𐎱𐎽𐎢𐎺 (paruva) and shares a deep Indo-European root related to "before" or "first".

पेंच.etymology: Hindi पेंच (pẽc, also पेच) is borrowed from Classical Persian پیچ (pēč, 'twist, curl, screw, complication'), derived from the present stem of پیچیدن (pēčīdan, 'to twist, wind, coil'). Entering Hindustani through craftsmanship, mechanics, and wrestling terminology, the word gained a spontaneous nasalization in spoken Hindi (पेंच alongside पेच). Because a screw turns in a spiral thread, the Persian word for 'twist' naturally named threaded metal screws as well as figurative knots or legal snags. It also generates the compound पेचकस ('screwdriver', literally 'screw-tightener').

पेंट.etymology: Borrowed from English paint, via Old French peindre from Latin pingere.

पेंसिल.etymology: Borrowed from English pencil, from Old French pincel and Latin pēnicillum ('fine brush').

पेच.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian پیچ (pēč, 'twist, coil, screw'), verbal noun stem of پیچیدن (pēčīdan, 'to twist').

पेचकस.etymology: Hybrid Persian–Hindi compound पेचकस: Persian پیچ (pēč, 'screw') + Hindi stem कस (from कसना kasnā, 'to tighten', Sanskrit कषति).

पेड़.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan पेड्ड / पिण्ड ('trunk, clump, tree'), connected to Sanskrit पिण्ड (piṇḍa, 'mass, trunk').

rootFamily.gloss: small leaf; herb leaf; tea leaf

पेन.etymology: Borrowed from English pen, from Old French penne and Latin penna ('feather quill').

पेपर.etymology: Borrowed from English paper, which comes from Latin papyrus. The word has been fully integrated into Hindi vocabulary, particularly in the contexts of academic examinations and printed newspapers.

पेशकश.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian پیشکش (peshkash, 'present, tribute, offering brought before a superior or host'), compounded from پیش (pesh, 'in front, before', cognate with Sanskrit प्राञ्च्) and کش (kash, present stem of کشیدن kashīdan 'to draw, bring, pull'). Historically used in Mughal court culture for a formal gift or tribute presented to a ruler, it broadened in modern Hindi to mean any polite offer or proposal.

पेस्ट्री.etymology: पेस्ट्री (pesṭrī) is a direct borrowing from English 'pastry', which entered English from Old French 'pastee' / 'paste' and ultimately Late Latin 'pāsta' ('dough'). Adopted into urban Indian bakery and café vocabulary, it regularly takes feminine grammatical gender in Hindi by analogy with native -ई nouns like मिठाई and रोटी.

पैंतीस.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पञ्चत्रिंशत् (pañcatriṃśat, 'thirty-five'), via Prakrit पणतीसा.

पैक.etymology: Hindi पैक (paik) is a modern borrowing from English 'pack' (both the verb 'to pack' and its participial sense 'packed'), naturalized into everyday Hindi travel, retail, and food-delivery usage. English 'pack' entered Middle English from Middle Dutch/Low German pak ('bundle, bale'), originally of Germanic trade origin. In Hindi, the English syllable maps to पैक and enters the productive light-verb frame पैक करना ('to pack up') and पैक होना ('to get packed'). Note that it is distinct from the unrelated noun पैग ('peg/drink').

पैकेट.etymology: Borrowed from English packet, diminutive of pack via Anglo-Norman.

rootFamily.gloss: cloth bag; tote bag; shopping sack

पैडल.etymology: Adopted from English pedal, which was borrowed from French pédale and Italian pedale, going back to Latin pedālis ('pertaining to the foot'), an adjective from pēs, pedis ('foot', cognate with Sanskrit पद् pad and Hindi पैर). Both French and Italian applied the Latin adjective specifically to the foot-operated levers of organs, harpsichords, and looms before English adopted it for musical instruments and bicycles. As pianos, bicycles, and treadle sewing machines spread across India in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, पैडल entered Hindi directly as a masculine consonant-final noun.

पैदल.etymology: पैदल (paidal) derives from Sanskrit पदाति (padāti) or पादतल (pādatala, 'sole of the foot') via Middle Indo-Aryan पयदल / पैदल, literally 'by foot'. In Old and Modern Hindi it solidified as an invariable adverb meaning 'on foot' and an attributive modifier for foot soldiers or hikers. The initial diphthong ऐ reflects contraction across the dropped intervocalic consonant.

rootFamily.gloss: to walk; to go; to move; to come along

पैनल.etymology: Hindi पैनल (painal) is a borrowing from English 'panel', used in Hindi for wooden wall sections, solar panels, electrical boards, and advisory committees. English 'panel' goes back via Old French panel ('piece of cloth or parchment, flat compartment') to Vulgar Latin *pannellus, a diminutive of Latin pannus ('cloth, rag, piece'). In Devanagari, the English vowel /æ/ is rendered with ऐ (ai), matching स्टैंड and कैप्सूल. It is widely naturalized in carpentry, electronics, and institutional vocabulary.

पैमाना.etymology: पैमाना (paimānā) is a borrowing from Classical Persian پیمانه (paymāna, 'measure, measuring cup, scale'), derived from the Persian verb پیمودن (paymūdan, 'to measure'). Entering Hindustani through Mughal administration, carpentry, and architecture, it came to denote a physical ruler as well as an abstract yardstick or standard. In Hindi it regularly inflects like native -आ masculine nouns.

पैर.etymology: Inherited via Prakrit पयर / पअर (payara) from Sanskrit पद + -र or पद्र / पद (pada, 'foot, step')—specifically traced in Turner's Comparative Dictionary to Sanskrit *पदर / पद् (pad, 'foot') or पद् + चर (pādacara). Sanskrit पद् descends directly from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds ('foot'), making पैर cognate with Latin pēs, Ancient Greek πούς (poús), and English foot. In modern Hindi it is the everyday masculine noun for 'foot' and colloquially 'leg'.

पैराग्राफ़.etymology: Borrowed from English paragraph, ultimately from Greek parágraphos ('side-stroke marking a section').

history.meaning: distinct section of a written text

पैसा.etymology: Early Modern Hindi पैसा (paisā, 'copper quarter-anna coin; money'), traditionally connected to Sanskrit पदांश (padāṃśa, 'quarter part').

पॉप.etymology: Borrowed into modern Hindi from English 'pop', an imitative/onomatopoeic word recorded in Middle English (around 1400) for a sudden sharp explosive sound like a cork or bubble bursting. Like English 'pop', it also extends in contemporary Indian usage to pop music and carbonated drinks. In mechanical or narrative Hindi, it captures a crisp snapping release.

पॉलिश.etymology: पॉलिश (polish) was borrowed from English 'polish', itself derived via Old French 'poliss-', stem of 'polir', from Latin 'polīre' ('to smooth, polish'). In Indian everyday Hindi it covers shoe polish, metal polish, and wood varnish, and combines easily with करना ('to polish'). It is uniformly assigned feminine gender.

पोंछना.etymology: पोंछना (ponchhnā) descends from Sanskrit प्रोञ्छति (proñchhati, 'wipes off, rubs clean'), a compound of प्र- and उञ्छ् ('to gather, sweep, wipe'), through Prakrit पुंछइ (puñchhai). The initial cluster प्र- simplified to प- while the nasalized palatal cluster -ञ्छ- yielded nasalized -छ- in Hindi. Its core meaning of wiping moisture or dust off a surface has remained unchanged for over two millennia.

पोटली.etymology: The noun 'पोटली' (poṭlī) is a diminutive form of the word 'पोटा' (poṭā) or 'पोट' (poṭ). It is derived from Middle Indo-Aryan, possibly related to the Sanskrit word 'पुट' (puṭa), which means a fold, pocket, or small envelope. The diminutive feminine suffix '-ली' (-lī) designates its small size. It traditionally refers to a small cloth bundle tied with a knot.

पोता.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पौत्र (pautra, 'son's son, grandson'), via Prakrit पोत्त (potta).

पोस्टकार्ड.etymology: Borrowed from British and Indian English postcard (attested from 1870 when postal administrations introduced open correspondence cards), combining post ('mail service', via French poste and Italian posta < Latin posita 'relay station') + card (via French carte < Latin charta).

history.meaning: open card sent through the post without an envelope

पोस्टकार्ड.notes: Masculine in Hindi; deeply familiar across India both for picture postcards and India Post's classic buff-yellow inland postal card.

पोस्टर.etymology: पोस्टर (posṭar) is an English loanword from 'poster', originally meaning a placard posted on a wall or post, from the verb 'to post' (Latin 'postis', doorpost or pillar). It entered modern Hindi through print media, theatre, and municipal notices. Like most consonant-final English borrowings denoting flat objects, it is masculine and invariable in the direct plural.

पौधा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पोतक (potaka, 'young shoot, sapling, young one'), via Prakrit पोअ / पौध.

rootFamily.gloss: small leaf; herb leaf; tea leaf

पौने.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पादोन (pādona, 'less by a quarter'), from पाद ('quarter') + ऊन ('deficient, less').

rootFamily.gloss: a quarter past; plus a quarter (+¼)
half past; plus a half (with numbers 3 and above)

प्याज़.etymology: Hindi प्याज़ (pyāz) is a borrowing from Classical Persian پیاز (piyāz, 'onion'), which continues Middle Persian piyāz and Old Iranian words for bulbous plants. The word spread from Persian into numerous languages across South and Central Asia, including Punjabi, Bengali, and Turkish (as piyaz). In Hindi, the initial cluster py- preserves the Persian vocalization, while the final z is written with a nuqta (ज़). It replaced earlier Sanskritic पलाण्डु in everyday North Indian speech.

प्यार.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit प्रियकार (priyakāra, 'showing kindness, affection'), via Prakrit पिआआर.

प्यारा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit प्रियकार / प्रिय (priya, 'beloved, dear'), via Prakrit पिआर (piāra).

rootFamily.gloss: sweet; pleasant (of voice, music, or scent)

प्याला.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian پیاله (piyāla, 'cup, goblet, bowl'), ultimately from Ancient Greek φιάλη (phiálē, 'broad shallow bowl').

प्याली.etymology: प्याली (pyālī) is the feminine diminutive of प्याला (pyālā, 'cup, goblet'), borrowed from Classical Persian پیاله (piyāla, 'cup, bowl'), which traces back to Middle Persian and Greek 'phiálē' ('shallow bowl'). In Hindi, the feminine suffix -ई creates the smaller, everyday domestic sense of a teacup or small bowl for tea, curd, or chutney. It is a staple word in North Indian hospitality.

प्रताप.etymology: From Sanskrit प्रताप (pratāpa, 'glowing heat, majesty, valour'), from प्र- + ताप ('warmth').

rootFamily.gloss: Mohan (warm, slightly absent-minded owner of Aangan Haveli)
Kavya (young woman managing reception at Aangan Haveli)

प्रतिनिधि.etymology: Hindi प्रतिनिधि (pratinidhi) is a learned Sanskrit tatsama compound formed from प्रति- (prati-, 'in return, in place of, facing') and निधि (nidhi, 'deposit, placing down, likeness'). Literally 'one placed in someone's stead' or 'an image/substitute', the Sanskrit term designated a proxy in ritual and governance. The element निधि derives from नि- ('down') plus धा ('to put, place'). In modern Hindi political, legal, and institutional prose, प्रतिनिधि is the standard word for a representative or delegate.

प्रतिशत.etymology: A modern Sanskritic compound (tatsama) coined as a calque on European 'percent' from Sanskrit 'प्रति' (prati, 'for each, per') + 'शत' (śata, 'hundred'). Sanskrit 'प्रति' is cognate with Greek 'prós', while 'शत' descends from Proto-Indo-European '*ḱm̥tóm', making it directly cognate with Latin 'centum' and English 'hundred'. Thus 'प्रतिशत' mirrors the literal structure of Latin 'per centum' ('by the hundred') using native Indo-Aryan roots.

प्रयोगशाला.etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit. A compound of प्रयोग (prayoga, 'experiment, practice') + शाला (śālā, 'room, hall').

प्रशिक्षु.etymology: Hindi प्रशिक्षु (praśikṣu) is a formal Sanskrit-based coinage created for modern technical, vocational, and administrative Hindi from प्र- (pra-, intensive prefix 'forth, thorough') and शिक्षु (śikṣu, 'desirous of learning, learner'). The root शिक्ष् (śikṣ-, 'to wish to be able, learn, study') is itself an old desiderative formation of शक् ('to be able'). Adopted in official Hindi lexicons during the twentieth century to translate 'trainee' or 'apprentice', प्रशिक्षु supplies a standardized counterpart to traditional Persianate शागिर्द. It remains invariable between singular and direct plural.

प्रिय.etymology: Hindi प्रिय (priya) is a tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit प्रिय (priya, 'dear, beloved, pleasing, favorite'). The Sanskrit adjective descends directly from Proto-Indo-European *priHós ('dear, beloved'), making it a direct cognate of Old English frēo ('free, dear'), English 'friend', and German frei. Within Indo-Aryan, the same root gave rise to प्रेम ('love') and प्रीति ('affection'). In modern Hindi, प्रिय retains a warm, slightly elevated register ideal for addressing friends in letters and naming cherished places or objects.

प्रेशर.etymology: Borrowed from English pressure, via Old French from Latin pressūra.

प्रोफ़ेसर.etymology: प्रोफ़ेसर (profesar) is borrowed from English 'professor', which derives from Latin 'professor' ('one who professes an art or science'), from 'profitērī' ('to declare publicly'). Introduced into India with nineteenth-century colleges and universities, it is used across Hindi both as an academic title and as a respectful term of reference for senior scholars.

प्लान.etymology: Borrowed from English 'plan', which entered English in the late seventeenth century from French 'plan' ('ground plan, flat drawing'). The French word derives from Latin 'plānus' ('flat, level'), reflecting how architectural floor plans drawn on a flat surface broadened in sense to mean any structured scheme or intention. In everyday Hindi, 'प्लान' is masculine and commonly pairs with 'बनाना' ('to make') or 'बदलना' ('to change').

प्लास्टिक.etymology: प्लास्टिक (plāsṭik) comes from English 'plastic', derived via Latin 'plasticus' from Ancient Greek 'plastikós' ('capable of being moulded'), from 'plássein' ('to mould, shape'). Adopted globally in the twentieth century for synthetic polymers, it entered Hindi unchanged in meaning as a masculine material noun.

प्लीज़.etymology: Borrowed from English 'please', shortened from the polite formula 'if you please' (literally 'if it pleases you'). English 'please' comes through Anglo-Norman and Old French 'plaisir' from Latin 'placēre' ('to please, be agreeable'). In conversational Hindi, 'प्लीज़' serves as an invariable polite request particle alongside native 'कृपया' and 'ज़रा'.

प्ले.etymology: Borrowed from English 'play' in the specific technological sense of audio or media playback. English 'play' goes back to Old English 'plega' ('brisk movement, game, exercise'), of West Germanic origin. In contemporary Hindi, 'प्ले' is used as an invariable masculine loanword in phrases such as 'प्ले बटन' and 'प्ले करना' ('to play a recording').

प्लेट.etymology: प्लेट (pleṭ) is a borrowing from English 'plate', from Old French 'plate' ('thin sheet of metal') and Medieval Latin 'platta', rooted in Ancient Greek 'platýs' ('flat, broad'). Because it rhymes with and functions alongside native feminine tableware terms like तश्तरी and थाली, Hindi consistently assigns it feminine gender with the plural प्लेटें.

प्लेटफ़ॉर्म.etymology: Borrowed from English platform, from French plate-forme ('flat form').

फँसना.etymology: फँसना (phansnā) stems from Sanskrit स्पर्श (sparśa) or a Middle Indo-Aryan expressive root फंस- (phansa-, 'to stick fast, be snared'), possibly connected with Sanskrit पाश (pāśa, 'noose, snare') with aspiration transfer. Its nasalized vowel -अँ- reflects the older nasal cluster. In modern Hindi it forms a productive pair with the transitive verb फँसाना ('to trap, entangle').

cognates.meaning: to get stuck; to be trapped

rootFamily.gloss: to tuck in; to wedge; to slip (a note into a handle)

फँसाना.etymology: Causative of फँसना ('to be caught/wedged'), from Prakrit फंसइ.

rootFamily.gloss: slip of paper; short written note; chit
to put; to place; to keep

फटना.etymology: फटना (phaṭnā) derives from Sanskrit स्फटति (sphaṭati, 'bursts, splits open') via Prakrit फट्टइ (phaṭṭai). The initial sibilant cluster स्फ- simplified to aspirated फ- in Prakrit, and the geminate -ट्ट- shortened to single -ट- in Hindi. It retains the intransitive sense of splitting, bursting, or ripping on its own.

फल.etymology: From Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀨𑀮 (phala). Ultimately derived from Sanskrit फल (phala, 'fruit, result, consequence').

फ़र्नीचर.etymology: Borrowed from English 'furniture', via Old French 'fourniture' ('equipment, supply, furnishings'), derived from 'fournir' ('to furnish, provide', ultimately of Germanic origin cognate with Old High German 'frummen', 'to forward, provide'). Like English 'furniture', Hindi 'फ़र्नीचर' is a collective, uncountable masculine noun.

फ़र्श.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian فرش (farš) from Arabic فَرْش (farš, 'spreading out; carpet, paved floor').

rootFamily.gloss: woven cotton rug; flat-weave floor mat

फ़व्वारा.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic فَوَّارَة (fawwāra, 'jet of water, fountain'), via Classical Persian فواره.

फ़ाउंटेन.etymology: फ़ाउंटेन (fāunṭen) is borrowed from English 'fountain', from Old French 'fontaine' and Late Latin 'fontāna' ('spring of water'). In Hindi, while a courtyard water fountain is usually called फ़व्वारा, the English loanword फ़ाउंटेन became firmly established for stationery items like फ़ाउंटेन पेन ('fountain pen') and फ़ाउंटेन स्याही ('fountain-pen ink').

फ़िलहाल.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic فِي الْحَال (fī l-ḥāl, literally 'in the present state / at the moment'), via Persian فی‌الحال.

rootFamily.gloss: right now; just now; still / yet
then; at that time; तब तक 'until then'

फ़ुटपाथ.etymology: Hindi फ़ुटपाथ (fuṭpāth) is the nuqta-marked orthographical form of फुटपाथ, borrowed directly from English 'footpath'. The English compound joins 'foot' (from Old English fōt, cognate with Sanskrit पद्) and 'path' (from Old English pæþ), originally naming a narrow walking trail before generalizing to paved urban walkways. Adding the subscript dot (nuqta) under फ indicates the labiodental fricative /f/ in standard educated Hindi pronunciation. Today it serves as the ubiquitous word for a street-side pedestrian pavement.

फ़ेल्ट.etymology: Borrowed from English felt, continuing Old English felt ('compressed woollen cloth') and Proto-Germanic *feltaz ('beaten or compacted material'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pel- ('to beat, push, drive'). Its name reflects the ancient manufacturing process of pounding wet wool fibres together rather than weaving them. In Hindi technical and musical terminology, फ़ेल्ट is an uncountable masculine noun.

फ़ैशन.etymology: फ़ैशन (faishan) comes from English 'fashion', derived via Old French 'façon' ('make, form, manner') from Latin 'factiō' ('a making, doing'). Entering urban Hindi during the colonial and modern eras, it covers clothing styles, social trends, and popular customs, taking masculine gender.

फ़ैसला.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic فَيْصَلَة (fayṣala, 'settlement, judgement, decision'), via Classical Persian فیصله.

rootFamily.gloss: settled; arranged; decided (तय करना 'to plan, arrange')

फ़ोटो.etymology: Borrowed from English 'photo', a nineteenth-century clipping of 'photograph' (coined by Sir John Herschel in 1839 from Ancient Greek 'φῶς, φωτός' phōs/phōtós 'light' + 'γραφή' graphḗ 'drawing, writing', literally 'light-drawing'). In Hindi, 'फ़ोटो' is frequently treated as an invariable feminine noun (by analogy with Perso-Arabic 'तस्वीर'), though masculine agreement also occurs colloquially.

फ़ोन.etymology: Borrowed from English phone, clipped from telephone (Greek τῆλε 'far' + φωνή 'voice').

rootFamily.gloss: number (room number, phone number, shoe size)

फ़ोल्डर.etymology: Borrowed from English folder, an agentive/instrumental noun formed from the verb fold (Old English fealdan, Proto-Germanic *falþaną, PIE *pel- 'to fold') + -er. Originally naming a folded sheet of stiff paper or cardboard used to hold loose documents together, it later extended to graphical computing icons as well. In Hindi office usage it is an invariant masculine noun.

फ़ोल्डिंग.etymology: Hindi फ़ोल्डिंग (folḍiṅg) is a direct borrowing from English 'folding', the participial adjective from 'to fold'. English 'fold' continues Old English fealdan ('to fold, bend double') from Proto-Germanic *falþaną, cognate with Sanskrit पुट (puṭa, 'fold, pocket') and Greek -plásios. In Hindi, फ़ोल्डिंग enters predominantly as an invariable attributive modifier for collapsible furniture and equipment such as फ़ोल्डिंग कुर्सी and फ़ोल्डिंग बिस्तर. The nuqta under फ marks the borrowed English /f/ sound.

फ़्यूज़.etymology: Hindi फ़्यूज़ (fyūz) is a modern technical loanword from English 'fuse', introduced alongside domestic electrical wiring. English 'fuse' (in the electrical sense, named because an overloaded wire melts) comes from Latin fūsus, the past participle of fundere ('to pour, melt, cast'), cognate with English 'foundry' and Greek chéō. In Hindi, the English initial /f/ is marked with a nuqta (फ़), and the word pairs idiomatically with the native verb उड़ना ('to fly/blow') in फ़्यूज़ उड़ना ('to blow a fuse').

फ़्रिज.etymology: Borrowed from English fridge, colloquial shortening of refrigerator.

फ़्रेंच.etymology: Borrowed from English French ('of or relating to France'), descending from Old English Frencisc and Proto-Germanic *frankiskaz ('of the Franks').

history.meaning: pertaining to France or its language

फ़्रेंच.notes: Invariable adjective in spoken Hindi (फ़्रेंच विंडो, फ़्रेंच टोस्ट), coexisting with literary फ़्रांसीसी.

फ़्रेम.etymology: फ़्रेम (frem) is borrowed from English 'frame', which originates from Old English 'framian' ('to profit, construct, build'). In Hindi it is universally used for picture frames, eyeglass frames, and structural borders, carrying masculine grammatical gender and taking -ओं only in the oblique plural.

फ़्लोर.etymology: Borrowed from English 'floor', descending from Old English 'flōr' ('floor, ground, storey') and Proto-Germanic '*flōruz', ultimately from Proto-Indo-European '*plā-ro-' ('flat surface', cognate with Latin 'plānus'). In modern Hindi, 'फ़्लोर' is a masculine noun most often used for building storeys ('फर्स्ट फ़्लोर', 'टॉप फ़्लोर') alongside Perso-Arabic 'मंज़िल'.

फाड़ना.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀨𑀟𑁆𑀟𑀇 (phaḍḍaï), derived from Sanskrit स्फटति (sphaṭati), meaning to split, burst, or rend. This native Indo-Aryan verb has evolved to mean tearing or ripping forcefully in modern Hindi.

फिर.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit फिरइ ('turns around, comes back'), used adverbially for 'again, next, then'.

rootFamily.gloss: then; at that time; तब तक 'until then'

फिसलना.etymology: Inherited Indo-Aryan verb फिसलना ('to slip, glide'), from Prakrit फिसल्लइ.

फुटपाथ.etymology: Hindi फुटपाथ (phuṭpāth) is a borrowing from English 'footpath', adopted into Hindi during the colonial expansion of paved streets and municipal roads. English 'footpath' combines 'foot' (from Old English fōt, cognate with Sanskrit पद् pad-) and 'path' (from Old English pæþ), originally denoting a track for walkers and later a paved sidewalk. In Devanagari, the word is written either फुटपाथ or with a nuqta as फ़ुटपाथ to reflect the English labiodental /f/. In Indian urban usage it specifically means the pedestrian sidewalk alongside a street.

फुलाना.etymology: Causative of फूलना ('to swell, expand'), formed with -आ- (-ā-).

rootFamily.gloss: to swell; (साँस फूलना) to be out of breath
to make laugh; to cheer up

फूल.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit फुल्ल (phulla, 'blown, blooming flower'), via Prakrit फुल्ल (phulla).

फूलदान.etymology: Hindi फूलदान (phūldān) is a classic Ganga-Jamuni hybrid compound combining the inherited Indo-Aryan noun फूल (phūl, 'flower') with the Classical Persian suffix -دان (-dān, 'container, holder'). Hindi फूल descends from Sanskrit फुल्ल (phulla, 'expanded, blossomed') via Prakrit फुल्ल (phulla), while Persian -دان continues Old Iranian *-dāna- ('receptacle', cognate with Sanskrit धान dhāna). This productive hybrid pattern appears across everyday Hindi household objects such as कूड़ेदान ('trash can') and चायदान ('teapot'). It remains the standard Hindi word for a flower vase.

फूलना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit फुल्लति (phullati, 'blooms, expands, swells').

rootFamily.gloss: to puff up; (मुँह फुलाना) to sulk, pout

फेंकना.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan फिक्कइ / फेंकइ ('flings, hurls').

rootFamily.gloss: to put; to place; to keep
to save; to protect; to spare

फेंटना.etymology: फेंटना (phenṭnā) is traced to a Middle Indo-Aryan verbal root फेंट- / फिट्ट- (pheṇṭ- / phiṭṭ-, 'to beat, strike, mix by beating'), linked to Sanskrit स्फिट् / स्फुट् or regional Prakrit culinary vocabulary. It originally meant beating or shuffling (including shuffling playing cards, ताश फेंटना) and whipping ingredients smoothly together. The nasalized vowel reflects the historical nasal+stop cluster -ण्ट-.

cognates.meaning: to beat; to whisk; to shuffle

rootFamily.gloss: to dial (a phone number); to mix; to match/compare

फैलना.etymology: फैलना (phailnā) derives from Middle Indo-Aryan फल्ल- / फइल- (phalla- / phaila-, 'to spread out, open wide'), related to Sanskrit प्रथति / स्फल् ('to expand, spread'). Through Prakrit फइलइ, the vowel sequence coalesced into the Hindi diphthong ऐ in फैल-. It denotes both physical expansion and the bleeding or smudging of ink on paper.

फैलाना.etymology: Transitive-causative counterpart of Hindi 'फैलना' ('to spread out, expand'), derived from an Indo-Aryan root meaning 'to swell, open wide, expand' (often compared with Sanskrit 'स्फार' / 'प्रथ्' through Middle Indo-Aryan expressive forms 'फेल-' / 'फल्ल-'). The '-आना' suffix regularly derives the active transitive verb 'to cause to spread' from the intransitive base.

फॉर.etymology: Transliterated directly into Devanagari from the English preposition 'for', which descends from Old English 'for' and Proto-Germanic '*fura', cognate with Latin 'prō' and Sanskrit 'प्र' (pra, 'forward, before'). In Hindi text it is not a productive native postposition; rather, it appears inside borrowed English titles, song names, and set phrases.

फोल्ड.etymology: Borrowed from English 'fold', from Old English 'feald' ('a fold, crease') and 'fealdan' ('to fold'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European '*pel-' ('to fold'). In Hindi it is very commonly used as the nominal element in conjunct verbs with 'करना' ('to fold') and 'होना' ('to fold up'), alongside native 'मोड़ना' and Perso-Arabic 'तह करना'.

फोल्डिंग.etymology: Borrowed from English 'folding', the participial adjective from the verb 'fold' (Old English 'fealdan'). In Indian English and everyday Hindi, 'फोल्डिंग' is widely used as an invariable modifier before furniture nouns such as 'कुर्सी' ('chair'), 'मेज़' ('table'), or 'पलंग' ('cot') to denote collapsible pieces.

फ्रंट.etymology: Borrowed from English front, which passed from Old French front ('forehead, front part') into Middle English and ultimately comes from Latin frōns, frontis ('forehead, brow, facade'). In hospitality, office, and architectural contexts, Hindi frequently adopts English front directly in set phrases such as फ्रंट डेस्क and फ्रंट गेट. It behaves as an uninflected modifier regardless of the gender of the noun it precedes.

फ्राइडे.etymology: Borrowed from English 'Friday', from Old English 'Frīġedæġ' ('day of Frigg'), a Germanic calque of Latin 'diēs Veneris' ('day of Venus'). Like other English day names used in bilingual urban Hindi alongside native 'शुक्रवार', 'फ्राइडे' is treated as a masculine noun.

फ्रेज़.etymology: Borrowed from English 'phrase', via Late Latin 'phrasis' from Ancient Greek 'φράσις' (phrásis, 'speech, way of speaking, expression'), derived from 'φράζω' (phrázō, 'to point out, tell, declare'). From grammar and rhetoric, the term extended in Western musicology to a self-contained melodic unit, the sense in which it is borrowed as a masculine noun in Hindi.

फ्रॉस्टेड.etymology: Borrowed from English 'frosted', the past-participial adjective from 'frost' (Old English 'forst', 'freezing cold'). In architecture and interior design it describes glass etched or sandblasted to scatter light like a coat of frost, and Hindi uses 'फ्रॉस्टेड' as an invariable loan adjective.

फ्लैट.etymology: Borrowed from English 'flat', from Old Norse 'flatr' ('level, flat'), cognate with Old High German 'flaz' and Greek 'platýs' ('broad, flat'). In Hindi it functions both as an invariable adjective/adverb for level surfaces or slightly lowered musical pitch and, in housing contexts, as a noun meaning 'apartment'.

बँटना.etymology: From Sauraseni Prakrit 𑀯𑀁𑀝𑀤𑀺 (vaṃṭadi). Ultimately from Sanskrit वण्टति (vaṇṭati, 'to divide, apportion').

बँधना.etymology: Intransitive/passive counterpart of बाँधना ('to tie'), inherited from Sanskrit बध्यते (badhyate, 'is bound') via Prakrit बंधइ.

बंडल.etymology: बंडल (banḍal) is borrowed from English 'bundle', which comes from Middle English 'bundel' and is related to Dutch 'bondel' and the verb 'bind' ('to tie'). Adopted into South Asian postal, shopkeeping, and household Hindi, it refers to both tied bundles and wrapped parcels, carrying masculine gender.

बंद.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian بند (band, 'bound, fastened, closed'), from PIE *bʰendʰ- ('to bind').

rootFamily.gloss: to open (by itself / intransitively); to come open
to open; to unlock; to unwrap
to stop (someone/something); to block; to hold back

बंदरगाह.etymology: बंदरगाह (bandargāh) is a Classical Persian compound noun بندرگاه (bandargāh), combining بندر (bandar, 'port, haven, trading city') and گاه (gāh, 'place, station'). The element bandar derives from Middle Persian and ultimately shares roots with 'band' ('embankment, mooring'). It entered Hindustani through maritime commerce along the Indian Ocean coast.

बक्सा.etymology: Early nativised borrowing from English box with Hindi masculine -आ declension (बक्सा / बक्से / बक्सों).

बगल.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian بغل (baġal, 'armpit, side, flank').

rootFamily.gloss: near (के पास); in one's possession ('to have')

बग़ल.etymology: Borrowed directly from Classical Persian بغل (bağal, "armpit, embrace, side"). The word entered the Hindustani lexicon during the medieval period of Indo-Persian contact and was fully assimilated. It retains both its literal anatomical meaning ("armpit") and its spatial extension ("side" or "adjacent position"), demonstrating a common semantic shift found in many Eurasian languages.

बग़ीचा.etymology: A diminutive form of the Persian word باغ (bāğ, "garden"), formed by attaching the Persian suffix ـچه (-če / -ca). It literally translates to 'small garden'. It became fully naturalized in Hindi during the Mughal period, reflecting the deep Persian influence on horticultural vocabulary and landscape architecture in North India.

बगीचा.etymology: बगीचा (bagīchā) is borrowed from Persian باغیچه (bāghīcha, 'little garden'), formed from باغ (bāgh, 'garden, orchard') plus the Persian diminutive suffix -چه (-cha). In Hindi the long vowel ā in the first syllable shortened to a, and Persian घ was simplified to ग in everyday speech. It regularly inflects as a masculine -आ noun (बगीचे).

बचना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit वच्यते / वञ्चति (vañcati, 'escapes, avoids'), via Prakrit वच्चइ / बच्चइ.

rootFamily.gloss: to save; to protect; to spare

history.meaning: state of being a child; childhood

बचाना.etymology: Causative/transitive in -आना formed from बचना ('to be saved, escape').

rootFamily.gloss: to be left over; to be saved; to avoid

बच्चा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit वत्सक (vatsaka, 'little calf, child'), via Prakrit वच्छअ (vacchaa).

बच्ची.etymology: Feminine counterpart of बच्चा, from Prakrit वच्छिआ (vacchiā).

बजट.etymology: Borrowed from English 'budget', which entered English from Middle French 'bougette' ('small leather pouch or bag'), a diminutive of Old French 'bouge' from Latin 'bulga' ('leather knapsack', of Gaulish Celtic origin). Because the British Chancellor of the Exchequer carried financial papers in a leather wallet, 'opening the budget' came to mean presenting a financial plan—a meaning carried directly into Hindi as a masculine noun.

बजना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit वाद्यते (vādyate, 'is sounded, rings'), via Prakrit वज्जइ (vajjaï).

rootFamily.gloss: to ring (a bell); to play (a musical instrument)

बजाना.etymology: Causative/transitive in -आना from बजना, inherited from Sanskrit वादयति (vādayati, 'causes to sound, plays music').

rootFamily.gloss: to ring; to chime; to strike (the hour)

बजाय.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian بجای (ba-jā-yi, literally 'in the place of'), from بـ ('in') + جای ('place').

rootFamily.gloss: to change; to swap; to replace

बजे.etymology: Frozen masculine plural/oblique perfective participle of बजना ('to strike, chime'): सात बजे = 'seven [hours] struck'.

rootFamily.gloss: to ring; to chime; to strike (the hour)

बटन.etymology: बटन (baṭan) is borrowed from English 'button', from Old French 'boton' ('bud, button'), related to 'bouter' ('to push out'). Upon entering Hindi, it expanded naturally from coat and shirt buttons to mechanical push-buttons and electrical switches on appliances. It is an invariable consonant-final masculine noun.

बटुआ.etymology: The noun 'बटुआ' (baṭuā) originates from the Sanskrit word 'वट' (vaṭa), which could denote a string, rope, or a woven pouch. Over time, through Middle Indo-Aryan (Prakrit) phonetic shifts, it took the form 'baṭuā' in modern Hindi. The diminutive suffix '-उआ' (-uā) was appended to emphasize its small size, establishing its current meaning as a small pouch or modern pocket-wallet.

बड़ा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit वड्र / वृद्ध (vṛddha, 'grown, large'), via Prakrit वड्ड (vaḍḍa).

बढ़ई.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit वर्धकि (vardhaki, 'carpenter, wood-cutter'), via Prakrit वड्ढइ (vaḍḍhaï).

rootFamily.gloss: to carve; to sculpt; to whittle

बढ़ना.etymology: Inherited (tadbhava) from Sanskrit 'वर्धते' (vardhate, 'grows, increases, thrives'), via Prakrit 'वड्ढइ' (vaḍḍhaï), with loss of initial 'v-'/shift to 'b-' and retroflexion of '-rdh-' to '-ḍḍh-' > '-ṛh-'. The Sanskrit root 'वृध्' (vṛdh-, 'to grow, increase') is cognate with Avestan 'varəz-'. In Hindi, 'बढ़ना' means both quantitative growth ('कीमत बढ़ना') and spatial or temporal advancement ('आगे बढ़ना').

बढ़ाना.etymology: Hindi बढ़ाना (baṛhānā) is the inherited transitive/causative verb corresponding to बढ़ना (baṛhnā, 'to grow, advance, increase'). Both trace back to Sanskrit वर्धति / वर्धयति (vardhati / vardhayati, 'grows; causes to grow, increases') via Prakrit वड्ढइ / वड्ढावेइ (vaḍḍhaï / vaḍḍhāvei). In the development into Western Hindi, initial v- shifted regularly to b-, and the Middle Indo-Aryan geminate retroflex -ḍḍh- simplified to flapped retroflex ढ़ (ṛh). Paired with the causative -आ- suffix, बढ़ाना covers extending hours, raising volume, and advancing a task.

बढ़िया.etymology: Derived from बढ़ना ('to advance, excel', from Sanskrit वर्धते vardhate) + suffix -इया.

बताना.etymology: Denominative verb from बात ('word, matter'), from Sanskrit वार्ता (vārtā) via Prakrit वत्ता.

rootFamily.gloss: to explain; to help someone understand

बत्ती.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit वर्तिका (vartikā, 'lamp-wick, taper'), via Prakrit वत्तिआ (vattiā).

बदलना.etymology: Denominative verb built on Arabic loanword बदल (badal, 'exchange, replacement').

बदलाव.etymology: Derived within Hindi from बदलना (badalnā, 'to change') + abstract suffix -आव (-āv).

rootFamily.gloss: to change; to swap; to replace

बधाई.etymology: बधाई (badhāī) descends from Sanskrit वर्धापन (vardhāpana, 'congratulation, festivity on growth or birth', from वृध् 'to grow, prosper') via Prakrit वड्ढावणा / वधाइआ (vaḍḍhāvaṇā). In Hindi, initial व- shifted to ब- and the intervocalic -ढ- simplified to -ध-, yielding बधाई. Traditionally sung or offered at weddings, births, and auspicious milestones, it is today's standard word for congratulations.

बन.etymology: Borrowed from English bun ('small soft bread roll').

बनना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit वर्ण्यते / वन्यते or Prakrit बणइ (baṇaï, 'is made, is prepared, turns out').

rootFamily.gloss: to make; to prepare; to build

बनाना.etymology: Transitive/causative in -आना formed from बनना ('to be made, become').

rootFamily.gloss: to be made; to turn out; to become

बनावट.etymology: Derived within Hindi from बनाना (banānā, 'to make, fashion') + abstract feminine suffix -आवट (-āvaṭ).

rootFamily.gloss: to make; to prepare; to build

बराबर.etymology: बराबर (barābar) is a borrowing from Classical Persian برابر (barābar, 'abreast, equal, level, opposite'), literally 'breast to breast', formed from بر (bar, 'chest, on') + آ (ā, linking vowel) + بر (bar, 'chest'). Entering Hindustani in the medieval period, it gained wide spatial, mathematical, and figurative currency for anything level, matched, or equivalent.

बर्तन.etymology: Inherited (tadbhava) from Sanskrit 'वर्तन' (vartana, 'means of livelihood, implement, utensil', or 'पत्त्र-वर्तन'), derived from 'वृत्' (vṛt-, 'to turn, exist, serve'). In Middle Indo-Aryan the sense shifted from general household implements or provisions to cooking pots and eating utensils. In modern Hindi, 'बर्तन' is masculine and serves as the standard cover term for pots, pans, and tableware.

बर्फ़.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian برف (barf, 'snow, ice'), from Middle Persian wafr.

rootFamily.gloss: winter; cold weather (often plural सर्दियों में 'in winter')

बर्बाद.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian برباد (barbād, literally 'given to the wind; ruined').

rootFamily.gloss: to save; to protect; to spare

बल.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit वल / वलि (vali, 'fold, wrinkle, twist; curve'), homophonous with Sanskrit बल (bala, 'strength').

rootFamily.gloss: to turn; to bend; to be folded

बलूत.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian 'balūt' (oak), originally from Arabic 'ballūṭ'. This is a widespread borrowing in Middle Eastern and South Asian languages.

बल्कि.etymology: बल्कि (balki) is borrowed from Classical Persian بلکه (balke, 'rather, on the contrary, nay even'), itself a compound of Persian بل (bal, from Arabic بل 'nay, rather') and the subordinating particle که (ke, 'that'). Adopted early into Hindustani prose and conversation, it serves as the primary corrective conjunction following a negated statement.

बल्ब.etymology: Borrowed from English bulb ('electric light bulb'), from Latin bulbus.

बशर्ते.etymology: Borrowed from Persian بشرطی (ba-šart-i), meaning 'on the condition of'. It is formed by combining the prefix 'ba-' (with) and the Arabic loanword 'šarṭ' (condition).

बस.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian بس (bas, 'enough, sufficient, only'), from Middle Persian bas.

rootFamily.gloss: just; a little; kindly (polite request softener)

बसंत.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 'vasanta'. A tadbhava (nativized) form of Sanskrit 'vasanta' (spring).

बहना.etymology: बहना (bahnā) descends from Sanskrit वहति (vahati, 'flows, carries, blows') through Prakrit वहइ (vahai). As in many inherited Indo-Aryan words in Hindi, initial व- shifted regularly to ब-, yielding the stem बह-. It preserves both the liquid sense of flowing and the older Vedic and Classical sense of wind moving.

बहस.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic بَحْث (baḥṯ, 'inquiry, discussion, debate'), via Classical Persian بحث (bahs).

बहीखाता.etymology: A compound of बही (bahī, 'register, diary') and खाता (khātā, 'account'). 'Bahī' comes from Sanskrit वहिका (vahikā, 'book of accounts'), while 'khātā' derives from the root verb खाना (khānā, 'to eat/consume' - metaphorically referring to consuming funds or an entry). Together, they refer to traditional merchant ledgers.

बहुत.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit बहुत्व / प्रभूत (bahu, 'much, abundant, many'), via Prakrit बहुत्त (bahutta).

rootFamily.gloss: very, very much; warm/heartfelt (in thanks and wishes)

बहुत-बहुत.etymology: Intensifying reduplication of बहुत ('very, much'), standard in warm expressions of gratitude.

बाँटना.etymology: Inherited via Prakrit वंटइ (vaṇṭaï) from Sanskrit वण्टयति / वण्टति (vaṇṭayati / vaṇṭati, 'shares out, apportions, divides'). Just as Sanskrit व- regularly shifted to ब- in core Hindi vocabulary and Prakrit -ṇṭ- lengthened the vowel with nasalization, vaṇṭ- yielded Hindi बाँटना (bā̃ṭnā) and the related noun बँटवारा ('partition, division'). It covers dividing physical portions, delegating chores, and sharing joys.

बाँधना.etymology: बाँधना (bāndhnā) derives from Sanskrit बध्नाति (badhnāti, 'binds, ties', root बन्ध्) via Prakrit बन्धइ (bandhai). In the development to Hindi, the consonant cluster -न्ध- simplified to -ध- with compensatory lengthening and nasalization of the preceding vowel, yielding बाँध-. Its forms remain central to everyday physical and figurative binding expressions.

बाएँ.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit वाम (vāma, 'left, left-hand'), via Prakrit वाम -> बायाँ/बाएँ.

rootFamily.gloss: to the right; on the right
to turn; to bend; to be folded

बाक़ी.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic بَاقٍ / بَاقِي (bāqī, 'remaining, enduring, balance'), via Classical Persian باقی.

rootFamily.gloss: to be left over; to be saved; to avoid

बाकी.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic بَاقِي (bāqī, 'remaining, lasting, everlasting'), an active participle of the root ب-ق-ي (b-q-y).

बाज़ार.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian بازار (bāzār, 'market'), from Middle Persian wāzār.

बाज़ी.etymology: बाज़ी (bāzī) is borrowed from Classical Persian بازی (bāzī, 'play, game, sport, wager'), derived from the Persian verbal stem باز- (bāz-, 'to play, lose/stake') from باختن (bākhtan). Entering Hindustani through courtly games, chess, and literature, it became embedded in idiomatic phrases such as बाज़ी जीतना and बाज़ी मारना ('to win the contest or day').

rootFamily.gloss: to win; to overcome; to beat

बाड़.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit 𑀯𑀸𑀟 (vāḍa), deriving from Sanskrit वाट (vāṭa, 'enclosure, fence'). It retains the original meaning of an enclosing structure made of wood, wire, or bushes. It is part of a larger word family related to enclosed spaces, including words like 'bāṭikā' (garden).

बात.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit वार्ता (vārtā, 'news, tidings, talk, matter'), via Prakrit वत्ता (vattā).

rootFamily.gloss: to speak; to say; to talk

बातचीत.etymology: A Hindi echo-compound formed from 'बात' ('word, speech, matter') + the rhyming/paired element 'चीत' (echoing 'चित्त' or 'चीज़'). 'बात' itself is a tadbhava inheritance from Sanskrit 'वार्ता' (vārtā, 'tidings, news, talk') via Prakrit 'वत्ता' (vattā). In Hindi, 'बातचीत' is an uncountable feminine noun meaning informal talk, dialogue, or negotiation.

बाथरूम.etymology: Borrowed from English bathroom, compound of bath (Old English bæþ, 'warm immersion washing') + room (Old English rūm, 'space, chamber').
