लाजवाब.etymology: Indo-Persian compound from Arabic لا (lā, 'no, without') + جواب (jawāb, 'answer, peer, match').

लाना.etymology: Contracted compound of ले आना ('to take and come -> bring'), from लेना + आना.

rootFamily.gloss: to take; to buy; light verb for inward/self-benefiting action
to give; to let (after -ने); light verb marking outward/completed action

लायक़.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic لَائِق (lāʾiq, "worthy, proper, fit"), the active participle of the verb لَاقَ (lāqa, "to befit, to suit"). It entered Hindi-Urdu via Persian during the medieval era. The term is heavily utilized as both an independent adjective and a postpositional marker to create adjectives of utility or worth from verbs.

लाल.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian لعل (laʿl, 'ruby, spinels, ruby-red'), via Arabic لَعْل.

लालटेन.etymology: Borrowed from English lantern via folk-phonetic adaptation लालटेन (influenced by लाल 'red, glowing').

history.meaning: lamp with a transparent protective case

लिए.etymology: Grammaticalised oblique perfective participle of लेना ('having taken -> for the sake of').

rootFamily.gloss: to; for; definite direct-object marker; at (times of day)

लिखना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit लिखति (likhati, 'scratches, draws, writes'), via Prakrit लिखइ (likhaï).

rootFamily.gloss: to have written; to file/register (a report or booking)

लिखवाना.etymology: Indirect causative in -वाना formed from लिखना ('to write').

लिखावट.etymology: Derived within Hindi from लिखाना / लिखना ('to write') + abstract feminine suffix -आवट (-āvaṭ).

लिनन.etymology: Hindi लिनन (linan) is a direct borrowing from English 'linen', introduced through textile trade and household terminology during the colonial era. English 'linen' derives from Old English līnen ('made of flax'), formed from līn ('flax')—itself an early Germanic loan or cognate of Latin līnum ('flax, thread') and Ancient Greek λίνον (línon). In Hindi, the word filled a lexical gap for woven flax fabric as distinct from native कपास/सूती ('cotton') and रेशम ('silk'). It is now standard in garment and hospitality contexts.

लिनेन.etymology: लिनेन (linen) is borrowed from English 'linen', which comes from Old English 'līnen' ('made of flax'), from Latin 'līnum' ('flax'). Adopted into South Asian hospitality and textile vocabulary for crisp woven flax cloth, napkins, and table coverings, it takes masculine grammatical gender.

rootFamily.gloss: cloth; piece of fabric; clothes (in plural कपड़े)

लिपटना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit लिप्त (lipta, 'smeared, joined, clinging') + extension -ट, via Prakrit लिप्पडइ.

लिफ़ाफ़ा.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian لفافه (lifāfa) from Arabic لِفَافَة (lifāfa, 'wrapping, covering, envelope'), from root ل-ف-ف ('to wrap').

rootFamily.gloss: slip of paper; short written note; chit

लिस्ट.etymology: Borrowed from English 'list', which entered from French 'liste' ('strip of paper, roll, catalogue'), originally from Old High German 'līsta' ('border, strip, edge'), reflecting how inventories were written on narrow strips of parchment. In Hindi, 'लिस्ट' is a feminine noun ('लिस्ट बनाना', 'लिस्ट में नाम होना') used alongside Perso-Arabic 'फ़ेहरिस्त' and Sanskritic 'सूची'.

लेकिन.etymology: Borrowed into Hindustani via Classical Persian 'لیکن' (lēkin, 'but, however') from Arabic 'لٰكِن' (lākin, 'but, yet'), an adversative conjunction formed from 'lā' + 'kanna' / related Semitic emphatic particles. Along with 'मगर' and native 'पर' or Sanskritic 'किन्तु', 'लेकिन' is the most frequent everyday adversative conjunction in Hindi.

लेटर.etymology: Borrowed from English 'letter', via Old French 'letre' from Latin 'littera' ('letter of the alphabet'; plural 'litterae', 'epistle, written document'). In modern Indian usage, 'लेटर' is a masculine noun especially common for official correspondence and typed notices alongside native 'चिट्ठी' and Perso-Arabic 'ख़त'.

लेना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit लभते / नी (labhate, 'takes, receives'), via Prakrit लेइ (leï).

rootFamily.gloss: to give; to let (after -ने); light verb marking outward/completed action
to put; to place; to keep

लेबल.etymology: Hindi लेबल (lebal) is a direct borrowing from English 'label', adopted through packaging, commerce, and archival labeling. English 'label' comes from Old French label ('ribbon, strip, tag'), likely of Frankish origin related to Old High German lappa ('flap, rag, strip', cognate with English 'lap' and 'lobe'). In Hindi, the English word retains its singular form in general reference and enters compounds with लगाना ('to affix a label'). It covers everything from jar stickers to record and clothing brands.

लेमन.etymology: Borrowed from English lemon, which came via Old French limon and Medieval Latin limo from Arabic لَيْمُون (laymūn) and Persian لیمو (līmū). Remarkably, those West Asian citrus words trace back to South and Southeast Asia—ultimately related to Sanskrit निम्बू (nimbū) and Hindi नींबू (nī̃bū), making लेमन and native नींबू distant etymological doublets reunited through global culinary trade. In Hindi café menus, लेमन is treated as masculine.

लैंप.etymology: Borrowed from English lamp, via Old French lampe from Greek λαμπάς (lampás, 'torch').

लैंपपोस्ट.etymology: Borrowed directly from English 'lamppost'. It is used primarily in urban Indian contexts for street lighting infrastructure.

लैमिनेट.etymology: Hindi लैमिनेट (laimineṭ) is a direct borrowing from English 'laminate', entering modern Hindi through furniture-making, interior architecture, and office stationery. English 'laminate' derives from Latin lāminātus, the past participle of lāmināre ('to hammer or form into thin plates'), built on lāmina ('thin plate, sheet, layer'). In Hindi, the English word serves primarily as a noun denoting synthetic layered paneling or protective plastic coating. It often contrasts with solid timber (ठोस लकड़ी) in building and carpentry descriptions.

लॉबी.etymology: Borrowed from English lobby, from Medieval Latin lobia ('covered walk, foyer').

लोकल.etymology: Borrowed from English 'local', via Old French from Late Latin 'locālis' ('pertaining to a place'), derived from Latin 'locus' ('place, spot'). In everyday Hindi, 'लोकल' is an invariable adjective used broadly for neighbourhood shops, local residents, regional produce, and commuter trains.

लोग.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit लोक (loka, 'world, realm, people, folk'), via Prakrit लोग (loga).

लोहा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit लोह (loha, 'reddish metal, copper, iron'), via Prakrit लोह (loha).

लौ.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit लोचि / प्रभा or अलात, via Prakrit लोअ ('glow, flame tongue').

rootFamily.gloss: to burn; to be lit / switched on (of a light)

लौटना.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit लोट्टइ (loṭṭaï, 'turns back, rolls back, returns').

rootFamily.gloss: to go; (as light verb) marks transition or completion

वक़्त.etymology: वक़्त (vaqt) entered Hindi via Classical Persian وقت (vaqt) from Arabic وقت (waqt, 'time, period, fixed moment'). Alongside Sanskrit-derived समय, it is one of the most frequent everyday words for time, occasion, or the right moment in spoken North Indian Hindi.

वकील.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic وَكِيل (wakīl, 'representative, legal agent, advocate'), via Classical Persian وکیل.

वजह.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian وجه (wajh) from Arabic وَجْه (wajh, 'face, aspect, manner, reason').

वनस्पति.etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit वनस्पति (vanaspati), which literally translates to 'lord of the forest'. It is a compound of वन (vana, 'forest') and पति (pati, 'lord' or 'master'). In modern Hindi, it is used scientifically and generally for vegetation and flora.

वरक़.etymology: वरक़ (varaq) entered Hindi via Classical Persian ورق (varaq) from Arabic ورق (waraq, 'leaf, foliage, sheet of paper or beaten metal'). In Jaipur's traditional craft culture—both miniature painting and artisanal mithai-making—वरक़ specifically denotes paper-thin beaten gold or silver leaf applied for luminous highlights.

वरना.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian ورنه (warna, contraction of و گر نه wa gar na, 'and if not').

वर्कशॉप.etymology: वर्कशॉप (varkshop) is borrowed from English 'workshop', a compound of 'work' and 'shop' dating from Early Modern English for a room where manual crafts or repairs are carried out. In Hindi it is commonly treated as feminine by analogy with native words like कार्यशाला and दुकान.

history.meaning: room or building for craft and repair work

वसंत.etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit 'vasanta', meaning spring. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-Iranian '*vasantás', from Proto-Indo-European '*wésr̥' (spring).

वह.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit ओह / वह (vaha, 'that one'), distal counterpart of एह ('this').

वहाँ.etymology: Distal counterpart of यहाँ ('here'), formed on the distal stem व- in Early Hindi.

वही.etymology: Emphatic demonstrative built in Hindi by fusing the distal demonstrative pronoun वह (vah, 'that, he, she') with the inclusive/emphatic particle ही (hī, 'very, indeed, only'). वह derives via Middle Indo-Aryan ओ/वो from Sanskrit असौ / अव-, while ही continues Prakrit ज्जिअ / हि and Sanskrit एव / हि ('indeed'). Together, वही pinpoints exact identity ('that exact same one'), contrasting with proximal यही ('this very one').

वहीं.etymology: Hindi वहीं (vahī̃) is a compound emphatic demonstrative adverb formed within Hindi by fusing the distal locative adverb वहाँ (vahā̃, 'there') with the emphatic particle ही (hī, 'very, just, right'). The base वहाँ derives from Middle Indo-Aryan distal pronominal forms built on *o- / *ava- ('that yonder') with a locative adverbial suffix parallel to यहाँ ('here') and कहाँ ('where'). When fused with ही, the vowels coalesce into -हीं while preserving the final nasalization of वहाँ. It conveys the precise sense of 'in that exact place' or 'then and there'.

वाक्य.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing वाक्य (vākya, 'utterance, statement, sentence'), from वाच् ('speech, voice').

cognates.meaning: PIE *wekʷ- ('to speak') cognate via Latin vōx

वादा.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic وَعْدَة (waʿda, 'promise, pledge'), via Classical Persian وعده (waʿda).

rootFamily.gloss: to fulfil; to carry through; to uphold (a role, promise, teamwork)

वापस.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian واپس (wāpas, 'back, behind, returning'), from وا ('back') + پس ('after, behind').

वायलिन.etymology: वायलिन (vāyalin) comes from English 'violin', borrowed from Italian 'violino', the diminutive of 'viola' (ultimately from Medieval Latin 'vitula', a stringed instrument). Introduced into India during the colonial era and widely integrated into both Western and Carnatic/Hindustani classical ensembles, it takes masculine gender in Hindi.

वार्निश.etymology: Hindi वार्निश (vārniś) is borrowed from English 'varnish', introduced through colonial carpentry, furniture-making, and building maintenance. English 'varnish' comes from Old French vernis and Medieval Latin vernīx ('fragrant resin'), tracing ultimately to Late Greek Βερενίκη (Bereníkē, referring to Berenice in Cyrenaica, famous for resinous amber-like trade goods). In Hindi, the word is assimilated cleanly in Devanagari as वार्निश, used with करना or लगाना ('to apply varnish'). It denotes clear protective wood finishes in contrast with colored पेंट ('paint').

वाला.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit पालक (pālaka, 'keeper, guardian, holder'), via Prakrit वालअ (vālaa), grammaticalised into an all-purpose adjectival suffix.

rootFamily.gloss: -ish; a bit (with थोड़ा/छोटा); which (in कौन सा)

वाल्ट्ज़.etymology: Borrowed via English 'waltz' from German 'Walzer' ('a gliding, turning dance in triple time'), derived from 'walzen' ('to roll, turn, revolve', from Old High German 'walzan' and Proto-Indo-European '*wel-' 'to turn, roll'). Originating in Austrian and German folk dances in the late eighteenth century, the term entered Hindi musical vocabulary for 3/4-time ballroom dances and piano pieces.

वाल्त्ज़.etymology: वाल्त्ज़ (vāltz) is borrowed via English 'waltz' from German 'Walzer' ('a revolving dance in triple time'), derived from 'walzen' ('to roll, turn, revolve'). In Hindi musical usage it refers both to the three-beat ballroom dance and to compositions written in waltz rhythm, taking masculine gender.

वाल्व.etymology: Borrowed from English valve, from Latin valva ('folding door leaf').

वास्तुकला.etymology: वास्तुकला (vāstukalā) is a Sanskritic compound (tatsama) formed from वास्तु (vāstu, 'dwelling site, building, structure', from वस् 'to dwell') and कला (kalā, 'art, craft'). Classical Indian treatises such as the Vāstu Śāstras used वास्तु for spatial design and building science, and modern Hindi coined वास्तुकला as the standard equivalent of 'architecture'.

वास्तुकार.etymology: Learned Sanskrit compound वास्तुकार (vāstukāra, 'builder, architect'), from वास्तु ('site, building') + कार ('maker').

वाह.etymology: Borrowed/shared across Indo-Iranian (Persian واه wāh / Sanskrit वाह), a natural exclamation of admiration.

rootFamily.gloss: oh!; hey!; wait a moment! (surprise or sudden realisation)

विंटर.etymology: Borrowed from English 'winter', descending from Old English 'winter' and Proto-Germanic '*wintruz' (perhaps meaning 'wet season', related to 'water' or Proto-Indo-European '*wend-' / '*wed-'). In urban Hindi it frequently appears in commercial and seasonal compounds like 'विंटर मेन्यू' or 'विंटर कलेक्शन' alongside native 'सर्दी / जाड़ा'.

विजेता.etymology: The noun 'विजेता' (vijetā) is a direct borrowing from classical Sanskrit. It is the nominative singular form of the Sanskrit agent noun 'विजितृ' (vijitṛ), meaning 'victor' or 'conqueror'. The root is 'जि' (ji, to win or conquer) combined with the prefix 'वि-' (vi-, denoting intensity or separation). It serves as the primary formal term for 'winner' in modern standard Hindi.

विदेश.etymology: Hindi विदेश (videś) is a tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit विदेश (videśa, 'another country, foreign region, abroad'). It combines the prefix वि- (vi-, 'apart, separate, distinct') with देश (deśa, 'place, region, country', from दिश् 'to point out, direct'). In classical Sanskrit, विदेश contrasted with स्वदेश ('one's own country') to denote any distant or unfamiliar territory. In contemporary Hindi, it serves as the standard polite noun for foreign countries and going abroad, alongside colloquial परदेस.

विदेशी.etymology: Hindi विदेशी (videśī) is a Sanskritic adjective formed by attaching the possessive/relational suffix -ई (-ī, Sanskrit -इन् -in) to the noun विदेश (videśa, 'foreign country'). Its components combine वि- ('apart, different, away') with देश ('country, region'), literally designating 'belonging to another land'. In modern Hindi, विदेशी works seamlessly both as an adjective ('foreign, imported') and as an animate noun ('foreigner'). It pairs symmetrically with देशी / स्वदेशी ('native, domestic').

विधि.etymology: विधि (vidhi) is a learned borrowing (tatsama) from Sanskrit विधि (vidhi, 'rule, precept, manner, prescribed method'), formed from वि- + धा ('to lay down, ordain, arrange'). From ancient ritual and grammatical rules, its sense generalized in Hindi to any step-by-step method, legal procedure, or culinary recipe.

विनम्र.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing (tatsama) विनम्र (vinamra, 'bowed, modest, courteous'), from वि- + नम्र ('bending, humble').

विभाग.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing विभाग (vibhāga, 'division, section, department'), from वि- + भज्.

विरासत.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic وِرَاثَة (wirāṯa, 'inheritance, heritage'), via Classical Persian وراثت (wirāsat).

विश्वविद्यालय.etymology: विश्वविद्यालय (vishvavidyālaya) is a modern Sanskrit-based compound coined in the nineteenth/twentieth century to translate English 'university' (from Latin 'universitas'). It combines विश्व (viśva, 'all, universe') + विद्या (vidyā, 'knowledge, learning') + आलय (ālaya, 'abode, hall'). Because आलय is masculine, the whole compound takes masculine gender.

वीकेंड.etymology: Borrowed from English 'weekend', a late-nineteenth-century compound of 'week' (Old English 'wice', 'turning, series of days') and 'end' (Old English 'ende'). As modern office schedules created a two-day rest period in South Asian cities, 'वीकेंड' entered Hindi as a masculine noun since no single native word covers Saturday and Sunday together.

वे.etymology: Plural of वह ('that; he/she'), formed in Early Hindi on the distal stem व-.

वैन.etymology: Borrowed from English 'van', a nineteenth-century shortening of 'caravan' ('covered wagon or group of travelers', from Persian 'کاروان' kārvān). In Hindi, 'वैन' is routinely assigned feminine gender by analogy with 'गाड़ी' ('vehicle, carriage') and takes regular feminine plurals 'वैनें / वैनों'.

वैसा.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit वइस (vaïsa, 'like that'), distal analogical formation alongside अइस ('like this') and जइस ('like which').

वैसे.etymology: Oblique/adverbial form of वैसा ('like that'), grammaticalised as a conversational topic-shifter ('incidentally, otherwise').

history.meaning: in that manner -> by the way

rootFamily.gloss: thus; like this; (with ही) just like that / casually

वॉइस.etymology: Borrowed from English 'voice', via Old French 'vois' from Latin 'vōx, vōcis' ('voice, sound, word'), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European '*wekʷ-' ('to speak', directly cognate with Sanskrit 'वाच्' vāc, 'speech, voice'). In modern Hindi it is feminine (matching 'आवाज़') and appears particularly in media terms like 'वॉइस नोट' and 'वॉइस ओवर'.

वॉटरकलर.etymology: The word 'वॉटरकलर' is a direct borrowing from the English word 'watercolor' and is fully integrated into the vocabulary of modern Hindi speakers.

वॉटरप्रूफ़.etymology: वॉटरप्रूफ़ (voṭarprūf) is a direct borrowing from English 'waterproof', compounding 'water' and 'proof' (Old French 'preuve', 'tested, impervious'). Widely used in Indian stationery, packaging, and outdoor gear vocabulary, it serves as an invariable modifier.

वॉल.etymology: Borrowed from English 'wall', from Old English 'weall' ('rampart, stone wall'), itself an early Germanic borrowing from Latin 'vallum' ('palisade, earthen rampart', from 'vallus', 'stake'). In Hindi, 'वॉल' is feminine (matching 'दीवार') and appears mainly in interior-design and household compounds like 'वॉल क्लॉक', 'वॉल पेपर', and 'वॉल पेंट'.

वॉल्ट्ज़.etymology: Hindi वॉल्ट्ज़ (vŏlṭz) is a borrowing from English 'waltz', which itself entered English in the late eighteenth century from German 'Walzer' ('revolving dance'). The German noun comes from the verb walzen ('to roll, turn, dance the waltz'), derived from Old High German walzan and Proto-Germanic *waltijaną. In Devanagari transcription, English /w/ is rendered with व and the rounded vowel with ऑ, preserving the final consonant cluster -ltz. In Hindi, the word appears exclusively in cultural, musical, and ballroom-dance contexts.

व्यक्ति.etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit व्यक्ति (vyakti). In Sanskrit, it meant 'manifestation' or 'appearance', eventually evolving to mean 'individual' or 'person'.

व्यवस्थित.etymology: Learned borrowing (tatsama) from Sanskrit व्यवस्थित (vyavasthita, 'arranged in order, settled, regulated'), the past passive participle of वि-अव-स्था (vi-ava-sthā, 'to place apart in order, establish'). It pairs the prefixes वि- ('apart') and अव- ('down') with the root स्था (sthā, 'to stand', PIE *steh₂-). Connected to the noun व्यवस्था ('arrangement, system'), it remains invariable in Hindi.

व्यापार.etymology: Hindi व्यापार (vyāpāra) is a direct tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit व्यापार (vyāpāra, 'occupation, activity, business, transaction'). It is composed of the prefixes वि- (vi-, 'apart, variously') and आ- (ā-, 'toward') attached to पार / पर् (from पृ 'to bring across, busy oneself'), originally meaning 'active engagement or employment'. Over time in classical and commercial Sanskrit, the term narrowed from general activity to trade, commerce, and professional livelihood. Modern Hindi uses व्यापार broadly for commerce, trade, and owning a business.

व्यावसायिक.etymology: Learned Sanskrit vriddhi derivative व्यावसायिक (vyāvasāyika, 'relating to trade or business'), from व्यवसाय + -इक.

व्हाइट.etymology: Borrowed from English 'white', descending from Old English 'hwīt' ('bright, white') and Proto-Germanic '*hwītaz', from Proto-Indo-European '*ḱweyd-' ('to shine, be white'), cognate with Sanskrit 'श्वेत' (śveta, 'white'). In Hindi, 'व्हाइट' is an invariable loan adjective used alongside Perso-Arabic 'सफ़ेद' in clothing, décor, and compounds.

श.etymology: The 30th consonant of the Devanagari syllabary. Derived from the Brahmi letter 𑀰 (śa).

शटर.etymology: Borrowed from English shutter ('hinged or rolling metal cover that shuts a shopfront or window'), agent/instrument noun from shut (Old English scyttan, 'to bolt, bar, close') + -er.

history.meaning: movable security cover for a window or shopfront

शटर.notes: In Indian towns and bazaars, शटर उठाना ('pulling up the rolling iron shutter') and शटर गिराना ('pulling down the shutter') mark opening and closing a shop for the day.

शनिवार.etymology: शनिवार (shanivār) is a Sanskrit-derived compound (tatsama) from शनि (Śani, the planet Saturn and deity associated with it) and वार (vāra, 'day of the week, turn'). Following the classical planetary weekday system shared with Greco-Roman tradition, Saturn's day corresponds directly to English 'Saturday'.

शब्द.etymology: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit शब्द (śabda, 'sound, voice, word').

शर्ट.etymology: शर्ट (sharṭ) is borrowed from English 'shirt', descending from Old English 'scyrte' ('short garment, tunic', cognate with 'skirt' from Old Norse). It largely replaced or sits alongside कमीज़ (from Arabic/Portuguese) in modern Indian Hindi and routinely takes feminine gender (plural शर्टें).

शर्त.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic شَرْط (šarṭ, 'condition, stipulation'). It entered Hindi via Persian and is widely used in both legal and everyday contexts.

शहतीर.etymology: शहतीर (shahtīr) is borrowed from Classical Persian شاهتیر (shāhtīr, 'main beam, ridge-pole'), a compound of شاه (shāh, 'king, chief, largest') and تیر (tīr, 'beam, shaft, arrow'). In traditional North Indian haveli carpentry and masonry, it denotes the primary heavy ceiling timber spanning a room or veranda.

शहद.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian شهد (šahd) from Arabic شَهْد (šahd, 'honeycomb, pure honey').

rootFamily.gloss: sweet; pleasant (of voice, music, or scent)

शहर.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian شهر (šahr, 'city, town'), from Middle Persian šahr ('land, realm, city').

शांत.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing (tatsama) शान्त (śānta, 'calmed, tranquil, still'), past participle of शम् ('to grow calm').

rootFamily.gloss: peace of mind; cosy calm; tranquillity

शांति.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing शान्ति (śānti, 'peace, calm, tranquillity'), from root शम् ('to grow calm').

rootFamily.gloss: peace of mind; cosy calm; tranquillity

शागिर्द.etymology: Hindi शागिर्द (śāgird) is a loanword from Classical Persian شاگرد (šāgird, 'pupil, apprentice, servant'). The Persian term derives from Middle Persian šāgird, historically analyzed as an Iranian compound meaning 'one who serves or attends' under a master. Entering Hindustani through guild crafts, music lineages, and Persianate education, it specifically denotes a traditional apprentice learning directly from an उस्ताद ('master'). In modern Hindi it carries a warm, traditional flavor alongside Sanskritic प्रशिक्षु ('trainee').

शानदार.etymology: Indo-Persian compound from Arabic شان (šān, 'dignity, splendour') + Persian دار (-dār, 'possessing').

शाबाश.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian شاباش (šābāš, contraction of شاد باش šād bāš, 'be joyful! bravo!').

शाबाशी.etymology: Hindi शाबाशी (śābāśī) is an abstract feminine noun derived from the exclamation शाबाश (śābāś, 'bravo, well done') with the nominalizing suffix -ई (-ī). The base शाबाश entered Hindustani from Classical Persian شاباش (šābāš), a contracted form of شاد باش (šād bāš, literally 'be happy, may you rejoice'), from شاد ('glad') and the imperative of بودن ('to be'). Passing from a celebratory cheer into an abstract noun, शाबाशी came to mean warm praise, commendation, or applause for an achievement. It pairs canonically with देना ('to praise') and मिलना ('to receive praise').

शाम.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian شام (šām, 'evening'), from Middle Persian šām.

rootFamily.gloss: evening (in polite greeting शुभ संध्या! 'Good evening!')

शामिल.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic شَامِل (šāmil, 'comprising, including, comprehensive'), via Classical Persian شامل.

rootFamily.gloss: with; together with (के साथ); together (एक साथ)

शायद.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian شاید (šāyad, 'it may be; perhaps'), 3rd sg. present of شایستن ('to be fitting, be possible').

शाही.etymology: शाही (shāhī) is borrowed from Classical Persian شاهی (shāhī, 'royal, kingly'), formed from شاه (shāh, 'king, sovereign', Old Persian 'xšāyaθiya-') plus the adjectival suffix -ई (-ī). In Rajasthani and North Indian cultural usage, it evokes regal elegance, grand hospitality, and fine craftsmanship.

rootFamily.gloss: big; large; elder; very (in expressions like बड़े शौक़ से)

शिक्षक.etymology: शिक्षक (shikshak) is a learned borrowing (tatsama) from Sanskrit शिक्षक (śikṣaka, 'teacher, instructor'), an agent noun from the desiderative root शिक्ष् (śikṣ, 'to wish to know, learn, teach', from शक् 'to be able'). In modern Hindi it functions as the primary formal and colloquial noun for a school or college teacher.

शिफ्ट.etymology: Borrowed from English 'shift', from Old English 'sciftan' ('to arrange, divide, change position') and Proto-Germanic '*skiftijaną'. In Hindi, 'शिफ्ट' serves both as a feminine noun meaning a work shift or relocation ('शिफ्ट करना / होना', 'to move house or move objects') and as a conjunct-verb complement.

शिल्प.etymology: शिल्प (shilp) is a learned borrowing (tatsama) from Sanskrit शिल्प (śilpa, 'variegated art, skill, handicraft, mechanical art'). Across South Asian cultural history, it encompasses woodworking, pottery, textile printing, and stone carving, forming compounds such as हस्तशिल्प ('handicraft') and शिल्पकार ('artisan').

शीर्षक.etymology: A pure tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit शीर्षक (śīrṣaka, "head, helmet, heading"), which is an extension of शीर्ष (śīrṣa, "head"). In modern Hindi literary and journalistic contexts, its anatomical meaning is entirely replaced by its textual application, serving exclusively as the standard term for the title of a book, article, or document.

शीशा.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian شیشه (šīša, 'glass, bottle, mirror'), from Middle Persian šīšag.

शुक्र.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian شکر (šukr) from Arabic شُكْر (šukr, 'gratitude, thanks').

cognates.meaning: everyday 'thank you' from the same Arabic root

rootFamily.gloss: God; the Lord (भगवान का शुक्र है! 'Thank goodness!')

शुक्रवार.etymology: Learned Sanskrit compound शुक्रवार (śukravāra): शुक्र ('bright; the planet Venus') + वार ('day of the week').

शुक्रिया.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic شُكْرِيَّة (šukriyya) / Classical Persian شکریه ('gratitude, thanks'), from Arabic شُكْر ('thanks').

शुद्ध.etymology: A Tatsama loan from Sanskrit शुद्ध (śuddha, 'pure, clean, cleared'), representing the past participle of the root शुध् (śudh, 'to purify'). It is extensively used in modern Hindi to describe physical purity (like milk or metals) as well as grammatical, moral, or linguistic correctness.

शुभ.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing (tatsama) शुभ (śubha, 'bright, auspicious, fortunate, good').

rootFamily.gloss: evening (in polite greeting शुभ संध्या! 'Good evening!')

शुरुआत.etymology: Formed in Hindustani from 'शुरू' (borrowed via Persian from Arabic 'شُرُوع' šurūʿ, 'beginning, entering upon') + the Arabic-Persian feminine plural/abstract ending '-आत' (-āt), reinterpreted in Hindi as a singular feminine abstract noun 'शुरुआत' ('beginning, start'). It is widely used for the opening of a season, project, or musical piece.

शुरुआती.etymology: Derived from the noun 'शुरुआत' (śuruāt, meaning beginning) with the suffix '-ī'. 'Śuruāt' comes from Arabic 'shurū' (beginning).

शुरू.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic شُرُوع (šurūʿ, 'beginning, commencement, entering upon'), via Classical Persian شروع.

शून्य.etymology: शून्य (shūnya) is a direct borrowing from Sanskrit शून्य (śūnya, 'empty, void, zero'), derived from शून (śūna, 'swollen, hollow', PIE *ḱewh₁- 'to swell, be hollow'). In ancient Indian mathematics, शून्य named the positional place-value symbol for zero. Rendered into Arabic as ṣifr, it subsequently gave rise via Medieval Latin to both English 'cipher' and 'zero'.

rootFamily.gloss: number (room number, phone number, shoe size)

शेड.etymology: Borrowed from English 'shade', from Old English 'sceadu' ('shadow, shelter from light') and Proto-Germanic '*skadwaz', cognate with Ancient Greek 'σκότος' (skótos, 'darkness'). In Hindi, 'शेड' is a masculine loanword commonly used for lampshades, colour shades/tints, and overhead awnings.

शेफ़.etymology: शेफ़ (shef) is borrowed via English 'chef' from French 'chef (de cuisine)' ('head of the kitchen'), where 'chef' continues Latin 'caput' ('head'). Adopted into modern Indian hospitality and café vocabulary, it serves both as a formal culinary title and an affectionate compliment to a talented cook.

शेल्फ़.etymology: Borrowed from English shelf, from Middle Low German schelf.

शैली.etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit शैली (śailī, “custom, habit, style, behavior”).

शॉर्टकट.etymology: शॉर्टकट (shorṭkaṭ) is borrowed from English 'shortcut', a compound of 'short' and 'cut' ('a path cut across to shorten a journey'). Widely used in contemporary urban Hindi for both quicker street routes and faster methods of doing a task, it takes masculine gender.

शॉवर.etymology: Borrowed from English shower ('overhead perforated water spray for bathing', transferred in nineteenth-century English from shower 'brief fall of rain', Old English scūr, Proto-Germanic *skūraz).
शॉवर.notes: Written with the chandrakala vowel sign ॉ (ऑ) used specifically in Devanagari to represent open rounded English vowels.

शोध.etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit 'śodha', meaning purification, correction, or search. Derived from the root 'śudh' (to purify, cleanse).

शोर.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian شور (šōr, 'tumult, outcry, commotion; saltiness').

शोरबा.etymology: Hindi शोरबा (śorbā) is borrowed from Classical Persian شوربا (šōrbā, 'broth, stew, soup'), a compound of شور (šōr, 'salty, brackish') and با (bā, 'cooked dish, gruel, stew', from Middle Persian bāg). Through Persian culinary influence at the Mughal and regional courts, شوربا entered Hindustani and spread across Eurasia as Turkish çorba, Russian шурпа, and Balkan chorba. In Hindi it denotes a thin, flavorful savory broth or light gravy. Its masculine -आ ending fits cleanly into the regular Hindi declension.

शौक़.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian شوق (šawq) from Arabic شَوْق (šawq, 'longing, eagerness, fondness').

rootFamily.gloss: mind; heart; mood / inclination (मन करना 'to feel like')

सँकरा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit संकीर्ण / संकट (saṅkaṭa, 'crowded together, contracted, narrow'), via Prakrit संकड (saṅkaḍa).

सँभलना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit सम्भृ / सम्भलति (sambhalati, 'supports oneself, recovers balance'), via Prakrit संभलइ.

rootFamily.gloss: to handle; to look after; to hold steady

सँभालना.etymology: Transitive/causative in -आना from सँभलना ('to steady oneself'), from Sanskrit सम्भारयति.

rootFamily.gloss: to be careful; to steady oneself

संकरा.etymology: Derived from Sanskrit सङ्कट (saṅkaṭa, "narrow, contracted, dangerous") through Prakrit intermediates like *sikkaḍa or directly via *saṅkara. Another theory traces it to a nasalized variant of a native Indo-Aryan root for tightening. The development reflects typical Middle Indo-Aryan lenition of medial consonants, resulting in a term widely used across modern Hindi dialects for spatial constriction.

संगीत.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing सङ्गीत (saṅgīta, 'sung together; concert, music'), from सम्- ('together') + गीत ('sung').

rootFamily.gloss: to ring (a bell); to play (a musical instrument)

संगीतकार.etymology: संगीतकार (sangītkār) is a Sanskrit-based compound (tatsama) formed from संगीत (saṅgīta, 'symphony, vocal and instrumental music', from सम्- + गीत 'sung together') and कार (kāra, 'maker, doer'). In Hindi it refers generally to any musician, instrumentalist, or composer.

संतरा.etymology: Early borrowing from Portuguese Sintra (a town near Lisbon famed for sweet oranges introduced via sixteenth-century Lusitanian trade).

history.meaning: Portuguese town famed for sweet oranges

rootFamily.gloss: sweet; pleasant (of voice, music, or scent)

संतुलित.etymology: The adjective 'संतुलित' (santulit) is a Sanskrit borrowing (tatsama) into modern Hindi. It is formed by combining the prefix 'सम्-' (sam-, meaning 'together' or 'completely') and the past participle 'तुलित' (tulita, meaning 'weighed' or 'measured'), derived from the root 'तुल्' (tul, to lift or weigh). Therefore, its literal meaning is 'properly weighed', leading to the modern meaning of 'balanced'.

संदूक.etymology: Borrowed into Hindustani via Classical Persian 'صندوق' (sandūq) from Arabic 'صُنْدُوق' (ṣundūq, 'wooden chest, coffer, trunk'), itself an early Arabic borrowing from Imperial Aramaic/Greek 'συνθήκη' or Late Latin/Greek container terms. In Hindi it is a masculine noun referring to sturdy storage trunks, tool chests, and coffers.

संदूक़ची.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian صندوقچه / Indo-Persian संदूक़ची, diminutive of Arabic صُنْدُوق (ṣundūq, 'box, chest').

संदेश.etymology: संदेश (sandesh) is a learned borrowing (tatsama) from Sanskrit सन्देश (sandeśa, 'message, news, command'), derived from सम्- + दिश् ('to point out, communicate, direct'). Classical Sanskrit poetry even featured the Sandeśakāvya ('messenger poem') genre; in modern Hindi it remains the standard word for a written or spoken message.

संध्या.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing सन्ध्या (sandhyā, 'junction of day and night; twilight, evening'), from सम्- + ध्या.

संपत्ति.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing सम्पत्ति (sampatti, 'prosperity, property, estate'), from सम्- + पद्.

संभलना.etymology: Derived via Prakrit संभलइ (sambhalaï) from Sanskrit सम्भरति (sambharati, 'gathers together, holds together, supports'), composed of सम्- (sam-, 'together') and भरति (bharati, 'bears, carries', from PIE *bʰer-). The semantic evolution moved from 'collecting oneself' to 'regaining balance, being careful'. Its conjunctive participle form संभलकर (sambhalkar) functions idiomatically as an adverbial warning meaning 'watch out!' or 'tread carefully'.

संभावित.etymology: A tatsama borrowing directly from Sanskrit सम्भावित (sambhāvita), the past passive participle of the causative form of सम्-√भू (sam-√bhū, "to come together, exist, be possible"). The word structurally means "that which has been made possible or conceived." It is extensively used in modern formal Hindi to convey probability, expectation, or theoretical likelihood.

संयोग.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing संयोग (saṃyoga, 'conjunction, coincidence'), from सम्- + युज्.

संवारना.etymology: Hindi संवारना (sãvārnā, formally सँवारना) is an inherited tadbhava verb descending from Sanskrit संवारयति (saṃvārayati) or संस्करोति / सम्वरति via Prakrit संवारइ (saṃvāraï, 'arranges, covers, prepares, adorns'). The Old Indo-Aryan prefix सम्- (sam-, 'together, well') weakened to nasalization on the first syllable, while intervocalic -vār- was retained cleanly before the infinitive suffix -ना. Throughout North Indian usage, the verb spans grooming one's hair, arranging a room neatly, and painstakingly restoring an old structure. Its intransitive counterpart is सँवरना.

सकना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit शक्नोति (śaknoti, 'is able, can'), via Prakrit सक्कइ (sakkaï).

rootFamily.gloss: is needed; is wanted; should (with infinitive)

सख़्त.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian سخت (saxt, 'hard, firm, stern'), from Middle Persian saxt.

सख्त.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian سخت (saxt, 'hard, firm, severe, difficult'), continuing Middle Persian saxt and Old Iranian *saxta- ('strong, taut, firm', from the root *sang- 'to be heavy, firm'). In Hindi-Urdu (written सख्त or with nukta सख़्त), it covers physical rigidity, severe weather, harsh words, and strict rules. As a Persian loanword, it never inflects for gender or number.

सच.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit सत्य (satya, 'true; truth'), via Prakrit सच्च (sacca).

सच-सच.etymology: A reduplicated adverbial form of the adjective/noun सच (sac, "truth"). 'Sac' itself derives from Sanskrit सत्य (satya, "true, real"), which passed through Pali and Prakrit as 'sacca'. The reduplication 'sac-sac' is a morphological feature highly characteristic of South Asian languages, used here to intensify the meaning and emphasize absolute frankness or transparency.

सचमुच.etymology: सचमुच (sachmuch) is an expressive echo-compound formed from सच (sach, 'true, truth', descending from Sanskrit सत्य via Prakrit सच्च) paired with the rhyming echo element मुच. Such jingle-compounds are highly productive in colloquial Hindi to add warmth, emphasis, or earnestness meaning 'really and truly'.

rootFamily.gloss: truth (सच में? 'Really?'; सच कहूँ तो 'To tell the truth')
completely; absolutely; (with नहीं) not at all

सच्चा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit सत्यक (satyaka, 'true, faithful'), via Prakrit सच्चअ (saccaa).

rootFamily.gloss: truth (सच में? 'Really?'; सच कहूँ तो 'To tell the truth')

सजना.etymology: सजना (sajnā) derives from Sanskrit सज्जति (sajjati, 'is ready, equips oneself, adorns') or सज्ज (sajja, 'equipped, arrayed') via Prakrit सज्जइ (sajjai). In Hindi the geminate -ज्ज- simplified to -ज-, yielding the intransitive verb सजना ('to be adorned, look lovely') alongside the transitive सजाना ('to decorate').

cognates.meaning: to be decorated; to look graceful

सजाना.etymology: A causative verb derived from सजना (sajnā, "to be adorned"), which originates from Sanskrit सज्ज (sajja, "prepared, armed, equipped"). Over time, the martial or preparatory connotations of the Old Indo-Aryan root softened into purely aesthetic ones in the vernacular, centering on the beautification and orderly arrangement of spaces and persons.

सज्जन.etymology: Learned Sanskrit compound सज्जन (sajjana, 'good person, gentleman'), from सत् ('good, true') + जन ('person').

सटाना.etymology: Causative of the verb सटना (saṭnā, 'to be close, to adhere'). This group of words derives from Sanskrit शट (śaṭa), implying closeness or joining.

सटीक.etymology: सटीक (saṭīk) traces to Sanskrit सटीक (saṭīka, 'accompanied by a commentary, exact, authentic') or Prakrit सट्ठीक (saṭṭhīka, 'quite right, exact', from स- + ठीक 'right, proper'). In modern Hindi, it means 'spot-on, precise, accurate', especially regarding measurements, timing, or phrasing.

सड़क.etymology: Inherited Indo-Aryan noun सड़क (saṛak, 'beaten road, highway'), from Prakrit सडक्क.

सधा.etymology: Perfective participle of the intransitive verb सधना (sadhnā, 'to be mastered, trained, steadied'), descending through Prakrit सद्ध (saddha) from Sanskrit साध्यते (sādhyate, 'is accomplished, mastered') and सिद्ध (siddha, 'perfected'). The Sanskrit root साध् (sādh, 'to reach the goal, achieve') relates to साधु (sādhu, 'straight, good'). Used adjectivally as सधा / सधी / सधे, it praises hands, voices, or strokes honed through long discipline.

सन.etymology: सन (san) descends from Sanskrit शण (śaṇa, 'hemp, Cannabis/Crotalaria juncea fibre') via Prakrit सण (saṇa). The palatal sibilant श- regularly became dental स- in Hindi, and retroflex -ण- flattened to -न-. Remarkably, English 'sunn (hemp)' was borrowed back from this very Indian word during colonial botanical trade.

सनरूम.etymology: Hindi सनरूम (sanrūm) is a direct modern loanword from English 'sunroom', adopted in contemporary architecture and translated fiction for glass-enclosed sunlit rooms. English 'sunroom' is a transparent twentieth-century compound of 'sun' (from Old English sunne, Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥, cognate with Sanskrit सूर्य sūrya) and 'room' (from Old English rūm, 'space, chamber'). In Hindi, the English syllables map straightforwardly into Devanagari without internal modification. It parallels other architectural English compounds now naturalized in Hindi such as बेडरूम and बाथरूम.

सपना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit स्वप्न (svapna, 'sleep, dream'), via Prakrit सिविण / सपण, from PIE *swépnos.

सपाट.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit. Derived from Sanskrit 'samapaṭṭa', meaning a flat or even surface, from 'sama' (even) + 'paṭṭa' (slab).

सप्तक.etymology: Hindi सप्तक (saptak) is a tatsama borrowing from Sanskrit सप्तक (saptaka, 'set of seven, heptad'), derived from the numeral सप्तन् (saptan, 'seven') with the collective suffix -क (-ka). Sanskrit सप्तन् descends from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥, making सप्तक directly cognate with Latin septem, Greek heptá, and English 'seven'. In classical Indian musicology, सप्तक names the complete seven-swara scale register (sa, re, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni) spanning an octave. Modern Hindi uses it for both Indian classical registers and Western octaves.

सप्ताहांत.etymology: Modern Sanskritised compound सप्ताहान्त (saptāhānta): सप्ताह ('seven-day week') + अन्त ('end').

सफ़र.etymology: सफ़र (safar) entered Hindi via Classical Persian سفر (safar) from Arabic سفر (safar, 'journey, travel, departure'). Widely naturalized across North Indian speech, music, and literature, it stands alongside Sanskritic यात्रा as the most common everyday word for a trip or journey.

सफ़ाई.etymology: Hindi सफ़ाई (safāī) is a hybrid abstract noun formed in Hindustani by attaching the native Indo-Aryan abstract suffix -आई (-āī) to the Arabic-Persian loanword साफ़ (sāf, 'clean, clear'). The base साफ़ comes from Classical Persian صاف (sāf), itself borrowed from Arabic صَافٍ (ṣāfin, 'pure, clear, unclouded'). Combining a Perso-Arabic adjective with the productive Hindi feminine suffix -आई reflects the deep morphological integration of Hindustani vocabulary. Today सफ़ाई covers physical cleaning, neatness of craft, and personal explanation.

सफ़ेद.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian سفید (safēd, 'white, bright'), cognate with Sanskrit श्वेत (śveta) and English white.

सब.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit सर्व (sarva, 'all, whole, every'), via Prakrit सब्ब (sabba), from PIE *solh₂wós.

सबसे.etymology: Compound of सब ('all') + ablative-comparative postposition से ('than'), literally 'than all'.

सब्ज़ी.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian سبزی (sabzī, 'greenery, herbs, vegetables'), from سبز (sabz, 'green').

सभी.etymology: Hindi सभी (sabhī) is an emphatic quantifier formed within Hindi by combining the inherited pronoun/determiner सब (sab, 'all') with the emphatic particle ही (hī, 'very, even, only'). The base सब descends from Sanskrit सर्व (sarva, 'all, whole, entire') via Prakrit सव्व (savva), where the cluster -rv- assimilated to -vv- and shifted to -b in Hindi. Fusing सब with ही caused internal aspiration, producing स-भ-ई (sabhī), a morphological pattern mirrored in तभी ('just then') and अभी ('right now'). It stresses collective inclusion of every member.

सभ्य.etymology: सभ्य (sabhya) is a learned borrowing (tatsama) from Sanskrit सभ्य (sabhya, 'fit for the assembly, well-bred, polite, civilized'), derived from सभा (sabhā, 'assembly, council, court'). Just as English 'civil' evolved from 'city' and 'courteous' from 'court', Sanskrit सभ्य shifted from 'belonging to the assembly' to 'courteous and civilized'.

history.meaning: fit for an assembly; well-mannered; polite

समंदर.etymology: समंदर (samandar) is a colloquial semi-tatsama development of Sanskrit समुद्र (samudra, 'gathering of waters, sea, ocean', from सम्- + उद्र 'water'), via Prakrit समुद्द / समुंदर. The intrusive nasal -अं- and epenthetic vowel -अ- broke up the final consonant cluster -द्र, yielding the warm spoken form समंदर alongside literary समुद्र.

समझ.etymology: Derived from Middle Indo-Aryan Prakrit 𑀲𑀫𑀚𑁆𑀛 (samajjhā), tracing back to Sanskrit सम्यञ्च (samyañca, 'correct, directed together'). The semantic shift progressed from 'proper alignment' to 'comprehension' and 'understanding'. In Old Hindi, it crystallized as a noun through zero-derivation from the verb 'samajhnā'. It reflects the conceptualization of knowledge as gathering and synthesizing facts.

समझदारी.etymology: Abstract noun derived in Hindi-Urdu by adding the feminine abstract suffix -ई (-ī) to the hybrid adjective समझदार (samajhdār, 'sensible, wise'). The first element समझ (samajh, 'understanding') descends via Prakrit समुज्झ (samujjha) from Sanskrit सम्बुध्यते (sambudhyate, 'awakens, understands'), while -दार (-dār) is the Classical Persian possessive suffix ('having'). Together they yield a feminine noun denoting practical judgment and tact.

समझना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit सम्बुध्यते (sambudhyate, 'awakens to, perceives, understands'), via Prakrit संबुज्झइ (sambujjhaï).

rootFamily.gloss: to explain; to help someone understand

समझाना.etymology: Causative in -आना formed from समझना ('to understand').

rootFamily.gloss: to understand; to realise; to figure out
to tell; to explain; to let someone know

समय.etymology: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit समय (samaya, 'appointed time, season, occasion'), from सम्- + इ ('to come together').

समय-सारणी.etymology: Learned Sanskrit compound समय ('time') + सारणी ('table, chart, list').

समान.etymology: Borrowed directly from Sanskrit समान (samāna, 'same, equal, similar'). It shares an Indo-European root with English 'same'.

समानांतर.etymology: समानांतर (samānāntar) is a Sanskritic compound (tatsama) formed from समान (samāna, 'equal, same') + अन्तर (antara, 'interval, distance'). Literally meaning 'having an equal interval throughout', it was adopted in modern Hindi geometry, engineering, and everyday description to correspond directly to English 'parallel'.

समीक्षा.etymology: Learned borrowing (tatsama) from Sanskrit समीक्षा (samīkṣā, 'close inspection, thorough investigation, inquiry'), built from the prefix सम्- (sam-, 'together, completely') + ईक्षा (īkṣā, 'seeing, looking', from the root ईक्ष् īkṣ 'to see, look closely', PIE *h₃ekʷ- 'eye, to see'). Classical Indian philosophy also uses समीक्षा for analytical reflection. In contemporary Hindi it serves as a formal feminine noun for official reviews and inspections.

समुद्र.etymology: Learned borrowing (tatsama) from Sanskrit समुद्र (samudra, 'ocean, sea, confluence of waters'), already prominent in the Rigveda. Morphologically it joins सम्- (sam-, 'together') with उद्र (udra, 'water', cognate with उदक udaka 'water', Ancient Greek ὕδωρ húdōr, and English water from PIE *wed-), literally signifying 'gathering together of waters'. Colloquial Hindi also preserves its tadbhava doublet समंदर (samandar) alongside tatsama समुद्र.

समुद्री.etymology: Formed in Hindi by attaching the relational adjectival suffix -ई (-ī) to the Sanskrit loanword समुद्र (samudra, 'ocean, sea'). Whereas Classical Sanskrit forms the vṛddhi adjective सामुद्र (sāmudra, 'marine'), Hindi routinely creates transparent invariable adjectives by suffixing -ई directly to nouns (mirroring पहाड़ी 'mountain', बाहरी 'outer'). In cooking it pairs especially with नमक as समुद्री नमक ('sea salt').

समेटना.etymology: Descends from a Middle Indo-Aryan root likely linked to Sanskrit समा-√वेष्ट् (samā-√veṣṭ, "to wrap together, envelop"). It underwent complex phonological reductions to emerge as 'sameṭnā'. It is a highly versatile verb in modern Hindi, applied literally to gathering scattered objects and metaphorically to concluding widespread operations or emotionally composing oneself.

सम्मान.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing सम्मान (sammāna, 'high regard, honour, respect'), from सम्- + मान.

सम्मानित.etymology: सम्मानित (sammānit) is a learned borrowing (tatsama) from Sanskrit सम्मानित (sammānita, 'honoured, esteemed'), the past passive participle of the causative verb सम्-मानयति (from सम्- + मन् 'to think highly of, respect'). In Hindi it serves as a formal, warm adjective for guests of honour and distinguished elders.

सर.etymology: Borrowed from English sir ('respectful form of address to a man, guest, teacher, or senior'), shortened in Middle English from Old French sire ('lord, master'), an unstressed proclitic development of Vulgar Latin *seior < Classical Latin senior ('older, elder').

history.meaning: sir (polite address to a male guest, customer, or teacher)

सर.notes: Distinct from its Perso-Hindi homograph सर / सिर ('head'); often softened even further in polite Indian hospitality as सर जी.

सरकना.etymology: The verb 'सरकना' (saraknā) originates from the Prakrit verb 'सरक्कइ' (sarakkaï), which means 'to slide' or 'to creep'. This Prakrit form descends from the ancient Sanskrit root 'सृ' (sṛ, to flow, glide, or move), specifically from an extended or suffixed form like 'सृक्क' (sṛkka). The Hindi infinitive ending '-ना' (-nā) was subsequently attached to the root to form the modern verb.

सरकाना.etymology: Inherited from a native Indo-Aryan root. It is the causative form of the verb सरकना (saraknā, 'to slide or slip'), which is likely derived from the Sanskrit root सृ (sṛ), meaning to move, glide, or flow.

सरकारी.etymology: सरकारी (sarkārī) is formed with the adjectival suffix -ई (-ī) from सरकार (sarkār, 'government, authority, estate'), borrowed from Classical Persian سرکار (sarkār, literally 'head of affairs', from سر 'head' + کار 'work, business'). In Indian administrative and everyday speech it translates 'governmental' or 'official'.

सरसराना.etymology: सरसराना (sarsarānā) is a reduplicated onomatopoeic verb built on the sound-imitative syllable सर्र / सर- (sar-, 'rustle, whoosh'), mimicking the soft hiss of wind through dry leaves, silk, or paper. Adding the verbalizing suffix -आना to a reduplicated sound stem is a classic Hindi pattern for continuous auditory verbs (compare खटखटाना and झिलमिलाना).

history.meaning: soft rustling sound of wind or leaves

सर्दी.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian سردی (sardī, 'coldness, winter'), from سرد (sard, 'cold').

सर्र.etymology: सर्र (sarr) is a native Hindi onomatopoeic exclamation imitating the crisp, swift rushing sound of wind, sliding paper, or sudden movement. Its geminate final -र्र conveys abruptness and speed, and it serves as the auditory root behind related verbs like सरसराना ('to rustle').

सलामत.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian سلامت (salāmat), which is from Arabic سَلَامَة (salāma), meaning safety, security, or well-being. It is derived from the Arabic root س-ل-م (s-l-m), which is associated with peace and safety.

सलीक़ा.etymology: सलीक़ा (salīqā) entered Hindi via Classical Persian سلیقه (salīqa) from Arabic سليقة (salīqa, 'natural disposition, innate good taste, knack, refined manner'). In Hindi-Urdu it specialized toward neatness, good taste, and proper etiquette, and inflects like native -आ masculine nouns to give the everyday adverbial phrase सलीक़े से ('neatly').

सलीक़ेदार.etymology: सलीक़ेदार (salīqedār) is a Persian-style compound adjective formed in Hindustani from सलीक़े (oblique stem of सलीक़ा, 'neatness, tact', from Arabic سليقة) and the Persian possessive suffix -दार (-dār, 'having'). It describes people, arrangements, or plans marked by orderliness and grace.

सवा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit सपाद (sapāda, 'with a quarter'), from स- ('with') + पाद ('foot, quarter').

rootFamily.gloss: a quarter to; minus a quarter (−¼)
half past; plus a half (with numbers 3 and above)

सवाल.etymology: The noun 'सवाल' (savāl) is a borrowing from Arabic 'سُؤَال' (suʾāl), meaning 'question' or 'inquiry'. It entered the Hindustani language via Persian administration and literature during the medieval period. It remains one of the most widely used terms for 'question' in everyday conversational Hindi, operating as a direct synonym for the Sanskrit-derived 'प्रश्न' (praśna).

सस्ता.etymology: Hindi सस्ता (sastā) is an inherited tadbhava adjective descending from Sanskrit स्वस्थ (svastha, 'comfortable, well-off, easy, abundant') or *सत्थ (*sattha) via Prakrit सस्थ / सत्थ (sattha, 'easy, cheap'). In Sanskrit, स्वस्थ literally meant 'abiding in one's own state' (स्व 'own' + स्थ 'standing'), developing in Middle Indo-Aryan into senses of 'effortless, plentiful, easy to obtain', and hence 'inexpensive'. The initial cluster sv- simplified to s-, while the internal cluster stabilized as -st- in Hindi with the -आ adjectival ending. It is the everyday antonym of महँगा ('expensive').

सहारा.etymology: Inherited (tadbhava) from Sanskrit 'सहकार' (sahakāra, 'cooperation, help, support') or 'सहाय' via Prakrit 'सहाअर / सहार' (sahāra) with the pleonastic masculine ending '-आ'. In Hindi it is a masculine '-आ' noun declining as 'सहारा / सहारे / सहारों', and the postpositional phrase 'के सहारे' commonly expresses leaning physically against a surface or relying on help.

सही.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic صَحِيح (ṣaḥīḥ, 'sound, true, authentic, correct'), via Classical Persian صحیح (sahīh -> sahī).

सही-सलामत.etymology: Paired Arabo-Persian phrase combining सही (ṣaḥīḥ, 'sound') + सलामत (salāmat, 'safe, unharmed').

सा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit सम (sama, 'like, equal, similar'), via Prakrit सअ / सा, reduced to an enclitic degree particle.

rootFamily.gloss: a little; some; a few (in plural)

साँचा.etymology: साँचा (sānchā) descends from Sanskrit सञ्चक (sañcaka, 'mould, stamp, impression') via Prakrit संचअ (sañcaa, 'mould'). The nasal+palatal cluster -ञ्च- simplified in Hindi to -च- with lengthening and nasalization of the preceding vowel, yielding साँच-. It denotes any hollow mould used in baking, brickmaking, or metalwork.

साँस.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit श्वास (śvāsa, 'breath, sigh, respiration'), via Prakrit सास (sāsa) with nasalisation.

साइकिल.etymology: Borrowed from English bicycle, with phonetic adaptation in Hindi.

साइड.etymology: Borrowed from English 'side', from Old English 'sīde' ('flank, side, edge') and Proto-Germanic '*sīdǭ' ('that which hangs down, side'). In Hindi, 'साइड' routinely takes feminine gender (on the pattern of 'तरफ़' and 'ओर') and is very common in spatial phrases like 'एक साइड में' ('to one side') and 'दूसरी साइड' ('the other side').

सागवान.etymology: Inherited/regional Indo-Aryan timber name सागवान (sāgvān, Tectona grandis), connected to Sanskrit शाक (śāka, 'teak tree').

सागौन.etymology: सागौन (sāgaun) derives from Sanskrit शाक (śāka, 'the teak tree, Tectona grandis') and Prakrit साग / सागवण (sāgavaṇa, from शाकवन 'teak-wood'), also giving Marathi सागवान. Widely prized across India for furniture, ships, and architectural joinery, सागौन refers to seasoned teak timber.

साझेदारी.etymology: Hybrid Indo-Persian formation: Hindi साझा ('share, joint venture') + Persian -दारी (-dārī, 'holding').

rootFamily.gloss: with; together with (के साथ); together (एक साथ)

साढ़े.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit सार्ध (sārdha, 'with a half, plus one half'), from स- ('with') + अर्ध ('half').

सात.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit सप्त (sapta, 'seven'), via Prakrit सत्त (satta), from PIE *septḿ̥.

सातवाँ.etymology: The term 'सातवाँ' has entered the common Hindi vocabulary as an important lexical item for daily communication, enriching the language's descriptive power.

साथ.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit सार्थ (sārtha, 'company, caravan, accompanying'), via Prakrit सत्थ (sattha).

rootFamily.gloss: near (के पास); in one's possession ('to have')

साथ-साथ.etymology: साथ-साथ (sāth-sāth) is the distributive reduplication of साथ (sāth, 'company, accompaniment'), which descends from Sanskrit सार्थ (sārtha, 'caravan, company of travellers, companion') via Prakrit सत्थ (sattha). Repeating the word reinforces simultaneity or walking side by side.

rootFamily.gloss: with; together with (के साथ); together (एक साथ)
near (के पास); in one's possession ('to have')

साथी.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit सार्थिक (sārthika, 'fellow traveller, companion'), from सार्थ ('caravan, company').

rootFamily.gloss: with; together with (के साथ); together (एक साथ)

सादा.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian ساده (sāda, 'plain, smooth, unadorned'), from Middle Persian sādag.

rootFamily.gloss: light (in weight, flavour, sound, or brightness); gentle

साधारण.etymology: Learned borrowing (tatsama) from Sanskrit 'साधारण' (sādhāraṇa, 'common to all, general, ordinary'), derived from 'स-' (sa-, 'with, together') + 'आधार' (ādhāra, 'basis, support', from 'आ-धृ' 'to hold, support'). From meaning 'having a common basis' or 'shared by all', it developed the standard Hindi sense of 'ordinary, plain, unpretentious'.

साफ़.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic صَافٍ / صَافِي (ṣāfī, 'pure, clear, limpid, clean'), via Classical Persian صاف (sāf).

साफ़-साफ़.etymology: साफ़-साफ़ (sāf-sāf) is an intensive reduplication of the adjective साफ़ (sāf, 'clean, clear, distinct'), which entered Hindi via Persian صاف from Arabic صافٍ (ṣāfin, 'pure, clear, unclouded'). Repeating the adjective turns it into a crisp manner adverb meaning 'clearly, legibly, or candidly'.

साफ़-सुथरा.etymology: A classic Hindi-Urdu synonymous binominal compound pairing Arabic-derived साफ़ (sāf, from Arabic صَافٍ ṣāfin 'pure, clear, clean') with native Indo-Aryan सुथरा (suthrā, 'neat, orderly, well-arranged', from Prakrit सुट्ठुअ suṭṭhua < Sanskrit सुष्ठु suṣṭhu 'excellent, well-placed'). Such Perso-Arabic + Indic pairings are hallmarks of idiomatic Hindustani, reinforcing meaning through rhythmic coupling. Only the native second component inflects for gender and number.

साबुत.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic ثَابِت (ṯābit, 'firm, fixed, whole'). In Hindi, it specifically came to mean something that is complete, unbroken, or unground.

साबुन.etymology: Entered Hindustani via Classical Persian صابون (sābūn) / Arabic صَابُون and reinforced by Portuguese sabão, all tracing back to Latin sāpō ('soap').

सामग्री.etymology: A Tatsama loan from Sanskrit सामग्री (sāmagrī), meaning 'totality, collection of goods or materials'. It is derived from समग्र (samagra, 'complete, entire'). In modern Hindi, it is primarily used for the ingredients, raw materials, or contents required for a ritual, recipe, or project.

सामने.etymology: सामने (sāmne) descends from Sanskrit संमुखेन / संमुख (sammukha, 'facing, confronting', literally 'with face together', from सम्- + मुख 'face') via Prakrit संमुह / सामुहे (sammuha). The medial cluster simplified with lengthening of the first vowel and oblique -ए marking its adverbial/postpositional role.

rootFamily.gloss: ahead; forward; further on; in front (के आगे)

सामान.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian سامان (sāmān, 'equipment, household goods, order, luggage').

सामान्य.etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit 'sāmānya', meaning general, universal, or common. Formed from 'samāna' (equal, same) with a secondary suffix.

सारा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit सर्व (sarva, 'all, whole, entire'), via Prakrit सब्ब / सार (sāra).

सार्वजनिक.etymology: Learned Sanskrit formation (tatsama) derived via vṛddhi vowel strengthening from सर्वजन (sarvajana, 'all people, the general public', combining सर्व sarva 'all' + जन jana 'person, folk') with the relational suffix -इक (-ika, 'pertaining to'). Vṛddhi lengthens the first syllable (sarva- > sārva-), a classical Sanskrit derivational rule productive across modern Hindi administrative, civic, and journalistic vocabulary. As a tatsama adjective, it does not inflect.

साल.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian سال (sāl, 'year'), from Middle Persian sāl.

सालगिरह.etymology: सालगिरह (sālgirah) is a Classical Persian compound سالگره (sālgereh), combining سال (sāl, 'year') and گره (gereh, 'knot'). It literally refers to the traditional custom of tying a knot on a cord each year to count a person's age or mark each passing year. In Hindi-Urdu it serves as the warm everyday word for an anniversary or birthday.

सालाना.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian سالانه (sālāna, 'yearly, annual'), from سال (sāl, 'year') + suffix -انه.

साहब.etymology: साहब (sāhab) entered Hindi via Classical Persian صاحب (ṣāḥib) from Arabic صاحب (ṣāḥib, 'companion, owner, master, sir'). In South Asia it evolved into a universal term of respectful address and a polite suffix added to names or titles such as डॉक्टर साहब and मोहन साहब.

सिकना.etymology: Inherited from Middle Indo-Aryan vocabulary, likely related to the Sanskrit root सेक् (sek, "to sprinkle, emit") or a specialized regional root for dry heat application. It functions as the passive or intransitive equivalent of the transitive verb सेंकना (sẽknā, "to bake/roast"). The phonetic structure is typical of indigenous culinary terms developed organically in the rural North Indian context.

सिकोड़ना.etymology: Transitive partner of intransitive सिकुड़ना (sikuṛnā, 'to shrink, contract, shrivel'), descending from Prakrit संकुडइ / सिकोडइ via Sanskrit सङ्कुटति / सङ्कोचयति (saṅkucati / saṅkocayati, 'contracts, draws together', from सम्- + कुच् kuc 'to bend, shrink'). Vowel alternation (-u- in intransitive सिकुड़ना vs. -o- in transitive सिकोड़ना) is a regular Indo-Aryan causative-transitive pattern. Common idioms include आँखें सिकोड़ना ('to squint') and नाक-भौं सिकोड़ना ('to turn up one's nose').

सिक्का.etymology: सिक्का (sikkā) entered Hindi via Classical Persian سکه (sekka / sikka) from Arabic سكة (sikka, 'coining die, stamped coin'). The Arabic word originally meant the iron die used to stamp metal currency before shifting to the stamped coin itself. In Hindi it inflects regularly as a masculine -आ noun (सिक्के).

सिखाना.etymology: Causative in -आना from सीखना ('to learn'), inherited from Sanskrit शिक्षयति (śikṣayati, 'teaches, instructs') via Prakrit सिक्खावेइ.

सिटी.etymology: Borrowed from English 'city', via Old French 'cité' from Latin 'cīvitās' ('citizenship, body of citizens, city-state'), derived from 'cīvis' ('citizen'). In Hindi it is feminine (matching the '-ई' ending) and is especially common in municipal and urban compounds such as 'सिटी क्लर्क', 'सिटी बस', and 'सिटी सेंटर' alongside Perso-Arabic 'शहर'.

सिटीबस.etymology: A compound of English borrowings 'city' and 'bus', commonly used together in Indian English and Hindi.

सितारा.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian ستاره (sitāra, 'star'), from Middle Persian stārag, from PIE *h₂stḗr.

सिर.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit शिरस् (śiras, 'head, summit'), via Prakrit सिर (sira), from PIE *ḱérh₂s.

rootFamily.gloss: mouth; face; spout / opening of a vessel

सिरहाना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit शिरोधान (śirodhāna, 'head-rest, pillow-end of a bed'), from शिरस् ('head') + धान ('place, receptacle').

सिरा.etymology: सिरा (sirā) derives from Sanskrit शिरस् / शिरा (śiras, 'head, top, tip, extremity') via Prakrit सिरअ (siraa). As palatal श- shifted to dental स- in Hindi, सिर came to mean 'head' while the -आ extended form सिरा specialized for the tip, end, or extremity of a cord, cloth, or road.

सिर्फ़.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic صِرْف (ṣirf, 'pure, unmixed, mere, sheer'), via Classical Persian صرف (sirf, 'only').

सिलना.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit. From Sanskrit 'sīvyati' (to sew), from the Proto-Indo-European root '*syuh₁-' (to sew, bind).

सीखना.etymology: Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𙀱𙀢𙀒𙀕 (sikkhaï), from Sanskrit शिक्षते (śikṣate, “to learn”).

सीट.etymology: सीट (sīṭ) is borrowed from English 'seat', which entered Middle English from Old Norse 'sæti' ('seat, sitting place', related to Old English 'sittan'). In Indian transport, theatre, and event contexts it is fully naturalized as a feminine noun taking the plural सीटें.

सीढ़ी.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit श्रेणी / श्रि ('series, ladder, flight of steps'), via Prakrit सिड्ढी (siḍḍhī).

rootFamily.gloss: floor / storey of a building; destination

सीधा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit सिद्ध (siddha, 'accomplished, direct, straight'), via Prakrit सिद्ध (siddha).

rootFamily.gloss: to fold; to bend; to turn

सीधे.etymology: Inflected form of सीधा (sīdhā), which is inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit 𙀱𙀢𙀥𙀕 (siddha), from Sanskrit सिद्ध (siddha).

सीलिंग.etymology: Borrowed from English 'ceiling', from Middle English 'selynge / celynge' ('lining or plastering an interior overhead surface'), derived from 'ceil' (ultimately Latin 'caelum', 'sky, vault, canopy', or Old French 'celer', 'to cover'). In Hindi architecture and home décor, 'सीलिंग' is a feminine noun distinguishing an interior ceiling from the exterior roof ('छत').

सुंदर.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing (tatsama) सुन्दर (sundara, 'beautiful, lovely, noble').

सुई.etymology: Descends directly from Sanskrit सूची (sūcī, 'needle, pointer'). Over centuries, through Prakrit 𑀲𑀽𑀈 (sūī), the medial 'c' consonant was elided, leaving a sequence of vowels. It is a fundamental inherited vocabulary word representing ancient Indian sewing technology.

सुकून.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian سکون (sukūn) from Arabic سُكُون (sukūn, 'stillness, calm, serenity'), from root س-ك-ن ('to dwell, be still').

सुखाना.etymology: सुखाना (sukhānā) is the transitive causative verb derived from सूखना (sūkhnā, 'to become dry'), which descends from Sanskrit शुष्यति (śuṣyati, 'dries up', past participle शुष्क śuṣka) via Prakrit सुक्खइ (sukkhai). Adding the causative -आ- suffix regularly shortens the long stem vowel ऊ to उ, producing सुखाना.

सुतली.etymology: Diminutive form of सूत (sūt, 'thread, yarn'), which derives from Sanskrit सूत्र (sūtra, 'thread, string'). The suffix '-lī' is used to form feminine diminutives or specific variations in Hindi. Hence, it refers specifically to coarse twine or packing string, distinguishing it from fine sewing threads.

सुधा.etymology: From Sanskrit सुधा (sudhā, 'ambrosia, nectar'), from सु- ('good') + धा.

सुनना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit शृणोति (śṛṇoti, 'hears, listens'), via Prakrit सुणइ (suṇaï), from PIE *ḱlew- ('to hear').

rootFamily.gloss: to speak; to say; to talk

सुनहरा.etymology: Derived from सोना ('gold', from Sanskrit सुवर्ण suvarṇa 'fair-coloured, gold') + adjectival suffix -हरा.

सुनाई.etymology: Action noun in -आई formed from सुनना ('to hear, listen'), inherited from Sanskrit शृणोति.

सुनाना.etymology: सुनाना (sunānā) is the regular causative verb formed from सुनना (sunnā, 'to hear, listen'), which descends from Sanskrit शृणोति (śṛṇoti, 'hears') via Prakrit सुणइ (suṇai). Meaning literally 'to cause someone to hear', it idiomatically covers telling stories, reading letters aloud, and performing music for an audience.

सुप्रभात.etymology: Learned Sanskrit compound सुप्रभात (suprabhāta): सु- ('good, auspicious') + प्रभात ('dawn, daybreak').

rootFamily.gloss: evening (in polite greeting शुभ संध्या! 'Good evening!')

सुबह.etymology: Borrowed via Classical Persian صبح (subh) from Arabic صُبْح (ṣubḥ, 'dawn, morning').

सुर.etymology: Tadbhava form inherited from Sanskrit स्वर (svara, 'musical note, tone, voice'), via Prakrit सुर (sura).

सुरक्षा.etymology: Learned Sanskrit compound सुरक्षा (surakṣā): सु- ('well, thorough') + रक्षा ('protection, guarding').

सुरक्षित.etymology: Learned Sanskrit borrowing (tatsama) सुरक्षित (surakṣita, 'well-guarded, safe'), from सु- ('well') + रक्षित ('protected').

rootFamily.gloss: to save; to protect; to spare

सुराग़.etymology: From Persian سراغ (sorâğ, 'clue, trace, track'). It is often used in the context of criminal investigations in Hindi.

सुरीला.etymology: Formed in Hindi from 'सुर' ('musical note, tone, pitch', inherited from Sanskrit 'स्वर' svara via Prakrit 'सर / सुर') + the Hindi adjectival suffix '-ईला' (-īlā, 'abounding in, characterized by', as in 'चमकीला' or 'रंग-ईला'). It inflects like a regular '-आ' adjective ('सुरीला / सुरीले / सुरीली').

सुलझाना.etymology: Derived from the native Indo-Aryan verb सुलझना (sulajhnā, 'to become untangled'). The etymology is uncertain, but it may relate to the prefix सु- (su-, 'good') added to a root meaning to loosen or straighten out, forming the transitive causative.

सुलह.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic صُلْح (ṣulḥ, 'peace, reconciliation, settlement'), via Classical Persian صلح (sulh).

सुहाना.etymology: Derived from सुहाना ('to be pleasing, suit'), inherited from Sanskrit शोभन (śobhana, 'pleasing, handsome') via Prakrit सोहण.

सूँघना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit शिङ्घति (śiṅghati, 'smells, sniffs'), via Prakrit सुंघइ (suṅghaï).

सूखना.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit सुक्खइ (sukkhaï), which developed from Sanskrit शुष्यति (śuṣyati, 'becomes dry, withers'), built on the verbal root शुष् (śuṣ, 'to dry, parch'). That Sanskrit root traces back to Proto-Indo-European *h₂sews- ('dry'), making सूखना a distant cognate of English sear and Greek αὔω (aúō). Its transitive partner सुखाना ('to cause to dry') preserves the inherited causative stem derived from Sanskrit शोषयति (śoṣayati).

सूखा.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit शुष्क (śuṣka, 'dry, parched'), via Prakrit सुक्ख (sukkha).

सूचना.etymology: सूचना (sūchnā) is a learned borrowing (tatsama) from Sanskrit सूचना (sūcanā, 'indication, intimation, notice'), derived from the verb सूचयति (sūcayati, 'points out, reveals', from सूचि 'needle, pointer'). In modern Hindi journalism and administration it is the standard word for a bulletin, notice, or piece of information.

सूची.etymology: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit सूची (sūcī, 'needle, pointer; index, list').

सूजन.etymology: Hindi सूजन (sūjan) is a nominalization formed in Hindi-Urdu from the inherited verb सूजना (sūjnā, 'to swell') with the abstract suffix -अन (-an). The base verb सूजना descends via Prakrit सुज्जइ (sujjaï) from Sanskrit श्वयति (śvayati, 'swells') or its passive/denominative stem *शूयते (*śūyate), rooted in Proto-Indo-European *ḱweh₁- ('to swell'). The regular sound shift of Old Indo-Aryan palatal sibilant ś to dental s appears throughout the tadbhava vocabulary. Today सूजन serves as the standard everyday and medical term for inflammation or puffiness.

सूजना.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit सुज्जइ (sujjaï) / *स्वुद्यति, connected in Turner's Comparative Dictionary to Sanskrit श्वयति (śvayati, 'swells, grows strong') or स्फुज् / सुज् (śūna, 'swollen', PIE *ḱewh₁- 'to swell'). The related abstract noun सूजन ('swelling') preserves the same stem with the suffix -अन. As a verb, सूजना is strictly intransitive and its participle सूजा हुआ routinely modifies injured body parts.

सूटकेस.etymology: Borrowed from late nineteenth-century English suitcase ('flat rectangular hinged travelling case originally sized to hold a dress suit'), compound of suit (via Anglo-Norman suite < Vulgar Latin *sequita 'matched set') + case (via Anglo-Norman casse < Latin capsa 'box, receptacle').

morphemes.meaning: hinged box or container (< English case)

सूटकेस.notes: Masculine in Hindi (बड़ा सूटकेस); standard word for rigid or wheeled luggage alongside अटैची ('attaché / small suitcase').

सूना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit शून्य (śūnya, 'empty, void, zero'), via Prakrit सुण्ण (suṇṇa).

cognates.meaning: ultimately calqued from Sanskrit शून्य via Arabic صِفْر

सूप.etymology: Borrowed in its culinary sense from seventeenth-century English soup, itself borrowed from French soupe ('broth poured over slices of bread; soup'), from Late Latin suppa ('bread soaked in broth'), of West Germanic origin (cognate with English sop and supper).
सूप.notes: Masculine in Hindi (गरम टमाटर का सूप, 'hot tomato soup'); in Hindi सूप पिया जाता है ('soup is drunk' with पीना rather than eaten with खाना).

सूरज.etymology: सूरज (sūraj) is the inherited semi-tatsama / tadbhava development of Sanskrit सूर्य (sūrya, 'the sun', cognate with Greek 'hēlios' and Latin 'sōl') via Prakrit सूरिय / सूरज (sūriya / sūraja). Breaking the Sanskrit cluster -र्य- into -रज- yielded the warm everyday word सूरज, which sits alongside formal सूर्य in modern Hindi.

से.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit सहुं / सइं or Sanskrit समम् ('together with') blended with ablative तो.

rootFamily.gloss: to; for; definite direct-object marker; at (times of day)
until; up to; as far as; even

सेंकना.etymology: Hindi सेंकना (sẽknā) is an inherited New Indo-Aryan verb tracing back to Middle Indo-Aryan *सिंकइ / *सेक्कइ (*sekkai) and ultimately connected by philologists with Sanskrit स्वेद / स्यन्दते or *शेक्- / सिक्त ('warmed, fomented, toasted'), though Turner treats *seṅk- / *sekk- ('to warm, foment, bake') as a distinct Prakrit verbal base with expressive nasalization. Compare Punjabi सेकणा and Gujarati शेकवुं ('to warm, toast, bake'), where the non-nasalized root *sekk- appears clearly. In Hindi, nasalization spread into the stem सेंक-, covering dry-heat baking on a griddle, oven baking, and warming oneself by a fire.

सेंटीमीटर.etymology: सेंटीमीटर (senṭīmīṭar) is borrowed via English 'centimetre' from French 'centimètre', coined in 1793 from Latin 'centum' ('hundred') and Greek 'métron' ('measure'). Adopted into Indian metric measurement, carpentry, and architecture, it takes masculine grammatical gender.

सेंट्रल.etymology: सेंट्रल (senṭral) is borrowed from English 'central', derived via Old French from Latin 'centrālis' ('in the centre', from 'centrum'). In Indian railway and civic naming (such as सेंट्रल स्टेशन or सेंट्रल पार्क), it functions as an established proper place-name component.

सेकंड.etymology: Borrowed from English second, from Medieval Latin secunda.

सेकना.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit सेक्कइ (sekkaï) or *सिक्कइ, deriving from Sanskrit सिच्यते / सेक (seka, 'sprinkling, fomentation') or *śek- / *svidyati ('heats, sweats, warms'). Turner links Hindi सेकना / सेंकना with Sanskrit स्वेदयति ('warms, steams, applies heat') and सेक ('pouring warm liquid, fomentation'). In modern Hindi kitchens, it is the core native verb for dry-heat cooking on a tawa or inside an oven, as well as applying a warm compress.

सेब.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian سیب (sēb, 'apple'), from Middle Persian sēb.

rootFamily.gloss: sweet; pleasant (of voice, music, or scent)

सेवा.etymology: Learned borrowing from Sanskrit सेवा (sevā, 'attendance, care, service'), from root सेव् ('to attend upon').

सैंड.etymology: Borrowed from the English verb 'sand' ('to smooth or polish with sandpaper'), derived from Old English 'sand' ('fine grains of rock'). In carpentry and workshop Hindi, 'सैंड' enters as an invariable complement in the conjunct verb 'सैंड करना' ('to sand down').

सैकड़ों.etymology: सैकड़ों (saikaṛon) is the oblique plural collective form of सैकड़ा (saikaṛā, 'a group of a hundred, century'), which derives from Sanskrit शतक (śataka, 'a hundred', from शत 'hundred') via Prakrit सअडा / सैकड़ा. Used before nouns without a postposition, सैकड़ों expresses an indefinitely large count of 'hundreds of'.

सैर.etymology: Borrowed from Arabic سَيْر (sayr, “walking, journey, stroll”).

सॉफ्ट.etymology: Borrowed from English 'soft', from Old English 'sōfte' ('quiet, gentle, tender') and Proto-West-Germanic '*samftī', related to German 'sanft' ('gentle'). In Hindi, 'सॉफ्ट' is used as an invariable adjective for texture, light, sound, and baked goods alongside native 'नरम' and 'मुलायम'.

सोख़्ता.etymology: Borrowed from Classical Persian سوخته (soxta, 'burnt, consumed'). In the Indian subcontinent, its meaning shifted from 'consumed' to 'absorbing material' or 'blotting paper'.

सोचना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit शोचति (śocati, 'ponders, reflects, grieves'), via Prakrit सोचइ.

rootFamily.gloss: to understand; to realise; to figure out

सोडा.etymology: Borrowed from English soda (soda water / carbonated water).

सोना.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit स्वपिति (svapiti, 'sleeps'), via Prakrit सोवइ (sovaï), from PIE *swep- ('to sleep').

सोमवार.etymology: Learned Sanskrit compound सोमवार (somavāra, 'day of the Moon / Monday').

सोलह.etymology: सोलह (solah) descends from Sanskrit षोडश (ṣoḍaśa, 'sixteen', compound of षष् 'six' + दश 'ten') through Prakrit सोळह (soḷaha). As regular in Indo-Aryan numerals, Sanskrit -ड- shifted to -ल- and -दश weakened to -ह, giving modern Hindi सोलह.

सोलहवाँ.etymology: सोलहवाँ (solahvān) is formed by adding the regular Hindi ordinal suffix -वाँ (descending from Sanskrit -तम via Prakrit -अम / -वँ) to the cardinal numeral सोलह ('sixteen', Sanskrit षोडश). Like other -वाँ ordinals from पाँचवाँ onward, it inflects for gender and case: सोलहवाँ, सोलहवीं, सोलहवें.

सौ.etymology: Inherited from Sanskrit शत (śata, 'hundred'), via Prakrit सअ (saa), from PIE *ḱm̥tóm.

सौंपना.etymology: Inherited from Prakrit 'sampaai'. From Sanskrit 'samarpayati', causative of 'sam-ṛ' (to deliver, hand over).

स्कूल.etymology: Borrowed from English school, ultimately from Greek skholḗ.

स्केच.etymology: Borrowed directly from English 'sketch'. It has been seamlessly integrated into Hindi vocabulary, especially in art and police investigations.

स्केल.etymology: Adopted from English scale, which unites two historical streams: measuring graduated marks (from Latin scāla 'ladder, flight of steps', via scāndere 'to climb') and weighing pans (from Old Norse skál 'bowl, weighing dish'). Because the markings along a graduated instrument resembled the rungs of a ladder, Latin scāla easily yielded both 'ruler' and 'musical ladder of pitches'. In modern Indian school, carpentry, and music vocabulary, स्केल serves naturally as a masculine noun for both a straightedge ruler and a musical octave progression.

स्क्रीन.etymology: Borrowed from English screen, from Middle French escren.

स्टील.etymology: Adopted from English steel, descending from Old English stēle / stīele and Proto-Germanic *stahliją ('hardened iron, steel'), derived from *stah- ('to stand firm', from Proto-Indo-European *stek- 'to resist, be stiff'). English steel entered Indian households and industry prominently through stainless-steel cookware (commonly called स्टील के बर्तन) and modern tools. In Hindi it functions as an uncountable masculine noun.

स्टूडियो.etymology: Hindi स्टूडियो (sṭūḍiyo) is a borrowing from English 'studio', which entered English in the early nineteenth century from Italian 'studio' ('study, artist's workroom'). The Italian noun continues Latin studium ('zeal, eager application, study'), derived from studēre ('to be eager, apply oneself'). In Hindi, initial st- triggers no prothetic vowel in standard urban spelling (स्टूडियो), and the final vowel -o renders the word invariable for plural. Today it designates an artist's workshop, recording studio, or compact apartment.

स्टूल.etymology: Borrowed from English stool, descending from Old English stōl ('chair, seat, throne') and Proto-Germanic *stōlaz ('seat, stand'), built on Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- ('to stand', cognate with Sanskrit स्था sthā, Latin stāre, and German Stuhl). Before backrests became standard on household chairs, a stool was the primary seat. In Hindi it refers specifically to backless seats and step-stools as a masculine noun.

स्टेशन.etymology: Borrowed from English station, from Latin statiō ('standing place').

स्टैंड.etymology: स्टैंड (sṭainḍ) is borrowed from English 'stand' (from Old English 'standan', 'to stand'). In modern Hindi it is widely used for easels, display stands, cycle stands, and bus stops, behaving as a regular consonant-final masculine noun.

स्टॉप.etymology: Borrowed from English 'stop', from Old English 'stoppian' ('to plug up, close, halt'), ultimately from Late Latin 'stuppare' ('to plug with tow/oakum', from 'stuppa', 'coarse flax'). From stopping a hole, the English word broadened to halting movement; in Hindi, 'स्टॉप' is a masculine noun used for bus stops, playback buttons, and conjunct 'स्टॉप करना'.
